Reading 1 Corinthians 1:24-29, watch him gather every thread of the chapter, foolish and wise, weak and strong, and tie them all to one Person. 1 Corinthians 1:24 Open ↗ but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God. There it is, the sentence the whole week has been building toward. To the people who actually answer God's call, Jews and Greeks alike, the crucified Christ is not weakness and foolishness. He is the power of God and the wisdom of God. The Greek word for wisdom here is sophia, the very thing the Greeks prized above almost everything, the deep insight into how life really works. Paul takes that treasured word and says it was never a system to be mastered. It was a Person to be known. The same Jesus who is God's power to rescue us (1 Corinthians 1:18) is also God's wisdom, the answer to the question every philosopher kept circling. The gospel is the power of God for everyone who believes (Romans 1:16). Stop hunting for a cleverer answer than the cross. There is not one. There is only a better look at the One already hanging on it. 1 Corinthians 1:26 Open ↗ Brothers, consider the time of your calling: Not many of you were wise by human standards; not many were powerful; not many were of noble birth. Paul asks them to take an honest look around the room. Be real, he says. Most of you were not the brilliant, the powerful, or the well-born. You were ordinary people the world had no special use for. That is not an accident, and it is not a problem to hide. It is exactly how God planned it. He deliberately chose the overlooked, so that when the church filled up with changed lives, no one could chalk it up to human talent or family name. The credit would have nowhere to land except on God Himself. That is why Paul ends the thought by saying the only thing left to brag about is the Lord (1 Corinthians 1:31). Even God's so-called foolishness outclasses our best wisdom (1 Corinthians 1:25), so the wise have nothing to add and the simple have nothing to fear. 1 Corinthians 1:30 Open ↗ It is because of Him that you are in Christ Jesus, who has become for us wisdom from God: our righteousness, holiness, and redemption. Paul will not leave wisdom floating as an abstraction, so he spells out what it means that Christ became wisdom for us. He breaks it into three gifts. Righteousness, being counted right with God when we were guilty. Sanctification, being slowly remade into the people we were meant to be. Redemption, being bought back and set free. That is what the wisdom of God actually does, and not one piece of it came from us. It is all from Him, received in Christ. The world's smartest thinking could diagnose the human problem a hundred ways and never once cure it (1 Corinthians 1:21). Only Christ takes a guilty person and makes them righteous, free, and new. This is the wisdom that finally makes someone wise enough to be saved (2 Timothy 3:15). Street Level The Part That Was Never in the Manual Think back to your first real day at a job that mattered. They probably handed you a manual, a binder, a folder of training videos, the whole system written down, and you read it. Then a situation came up that the manual did not cover, and you froze, because the page in front of you had plenty of words and no wisdom. What saved you was not a thicker document. It was the veteran across the room who had done this for twenty years, who caught your eye, walked over, and showed you the thing that was never written down anywhere because it could not be. You did not need more information. You needed a person. That is the quiet turn the whole week has been moving toward. People kept hunting for wisdom as if it were a system to download, a method to master, a binder finally thick enough to explain life. Paul says the wisdom of God was never a what. It is a Who. You do not study your way to it from a safe distance. You get it the way an apprentice gets a trade, by belonging to the master, standing close, letting His life rub off on yours over time. Christ does not hand you wisdom and walk away. He becomes your wisdom, and the only way to have the gift is to have Him. Today’s World The Puzzle the Experts Could Not Crack For more than ten years, a team of scientists was stuck. They needed the three-dimensional shape of an enzyme from an AIDS-like virus, a structure that could open the door to new drugs, and the world's trained biochemists kept hitting a wall. So in 2011 they tried something that sounds like a joke. They handed the problem to a video game. Foldit lets anyone fold virtual proteins like a puzzle, no science degree required, and most of its players were exactly that, regular people. Retirees, students, and hobbyists, twisting shapes on their home computers for fun. The crowd of amateurs solved the structure in about three weeks, and the result ran in a respected scientific journal with the gamers listed as co-authors. Paul would have loved that story. He told a church full of nobodies to take an honest look around the room and notice that God had not stocked it with the brilliant and the well-connected. He had chosen the overlooked on purpose, so that when the impossible got solved, no one could pin the credit on human talent or a famous name. The wisdom the Greeks chased was never a prize for being clever. It was a gift handed to the humble, the ones willing to sit down at the table and simply receive it. A wall the experts could not get over, a roomful of amateurs walked right through. God still loves to hand the breakthrough to the people the world walked straight past. Christ at the center Every other day this week we have looked at the cross. Today we look at the Person on it and realize the cross was never the point all by itself. Jesus is the point. Paul does not say the cross is the wisdom of God in the abstract. He says Christ is. Power and wisdom are not forces God hands out from a distance, they are things you only get by getting Him. This is the difference between Christianity and every self-improvement plan ever sold. We are not handed a better philosophy to apply or a stronger willpower to summon. We are given a Person to belong to, and everything we need, the rightness, the freedom, the slow remaking, comes bundled up in Him. So the answer to a confused, exhausted, striving life is not more information. It is Jesus. He did not come to make us wise. He came to be our wisdom. Application Today, notice where you are reaching for your own wisdom and strength to fix something only Christ can. Maybe it is a habit you keep trying to white-knuckle, a relationship you keep trying to manage, a guilt you keep trying to argue yourself out of. Name it, and then pray something simple. "Jesus, You are my wisdom and my power here. I have run out of mine." Then take one concrete step that leans on Him instead of on you, whether that is asking for help, confessing it to someone, or simply stopping the striving for a day. Discussion Question "Where are you still trying to be wise enough or strong enough to save yourself in some corner of your life, and what would it look like this week to trade your own wisdom for simply belonging to the One who became wisdom for you?" Closing Prayer Father, we have spent so much energy trying to be wise enough and strong enough on our own, and we are tired. Thank You that You never asked us to manufacture either one. Thank You that Christ Himself is our wisdom and our power, that everything we lack is found by being found in Him. Forgive us for treating the gospel like a starter kit we outgrow instead of the Person we lean on for every step. Make us people who boast in nothing but You. And when we feel small or overlooked, remind us that this is exactly the kind of person You love to fill with Yourself. In Jesus' name, Amen.
docs.2026-07-10.html: Week in Review This week we took the one symbol the ancient world found too shameful to name and watched Paul plant the entire Christian faith on it. ☩Sabbath: The Message of the Cross. The same cross Rome reserved for slaves and rebels, Paul called the power of God, and he set the scandal of it at the center of the whole week. ☩Sunday: The Gospel of the Cross. Paul refused to out-talk a city that loved clever speakers, because a dressed-up cross is a disarmed cross. ☩Monday: Foolishness to Those Who Are Perishing. The message the smartest people mocked was God's deliberate way of humbling proud minds and saving everyone willing to believe. ☩Tuesday: Power to Those Who Are Being Saved. Two short verses spelled out what the cross accomplished, reconciling us to God, bearing our sins, and healing us, a debt paid in full. ☩Wednesday: A Messiah Crucified. A crucified Messiah offended Jews, Greeks, and even Jesus' own disciples, proof that God's strangest paths are often His deepest rescue. ☩Thursday: Christ, the Power and Wisdom of God. Paul named the hidden power at last. Not a system but a Person, Christ Himself, our wisdom, righteousness, and freedom. Historical Context Every Reason It Should Have Failed Step back and take in the whole landscape this week walked through. A Roman world where the cross was so shameful that respectable people would not say the word. A Greek world where eloquence was entertainment and a traveling speaker could draw a crowd like a star athlete. A Jewish world aching for a warrior Messiah who would break Rome, not be broken by it. And a little church in Corinth made up mostly of the people all that grandeur looked straight past, slaves and tradesmen and women with no titles. Into the middle of it Paul set one unspeakable thing, a crucified Messiah, and refused to move it or dress it up. Every force in that world said the message was too shameful, too foolish, too weak to survive. It did more than survive. It outlasted the empire that invented the cross, and it is still standing here, being read on a screen two thousand years later. What This Week Clarifies Six days at the foot of one cross leave a few tensions pulled tight. Three deserve a slower look before Sabbath opens, and the week has already done the work of resolving them. The Power Leaks Out Through the Polish Sunday handed us a strange refusal. Paul walked into a city that treated its speakers like celebrities, carrying the one message he most needed people to believe, and he deliberately left his best rhetorical tools at home. Every instinct says the opposite. Precious things get our best packaging. The better the news, the better the presentation it deserves. 1 Corinthians 1:17 Open ↗ For Christ did not send me to baptize, but to preach the gospel, not with words of wisdom, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power. The verse explains the refusal. Clever words do not add power to the cross. They empty it, and Sunday gave us the picture behind Paul's warning, a full cup of God's power drained by a slow leak nobody notices. Decoration is not neutral. It moves the room's attention from the message to the messenger, the way a singer can bury a beloved anthem under vocal runs until the crowd walks out praising the voice and humming nothing. So Paul sang it straight. A city that graded speakers for sport heard one plain sentence about a crucified Savior, with nothing impressive wrapped around it to take the credit. He was not lowering his standards. He was guarding the cup. God Turned Down Both Wish Lists Wednesday laid the two wish lists on the table. Jews wanted a sign from heaven, the kind of power display that settles arguments. Greeks wanted a wisdom elegant enough to satisfy the mind. Any sensible messenger would have led with one or the other. God declined both orders and sent a crucified Messiah, the one answer guaranteed to offend every audience at once. 1 Corinthians 1:22-23 Open ↗ 22Jews demand signs and Greeks search for wisdom, 23but we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles, The week's answer is that both wish lists carried the same fine print. A Messiah who performed on demand would have left the audience in the judge's seat, grading God against their expectations and approving Him only when He flattered them. Rescue on those terms would have crowned the very pride that was sinking us. So God sent a stumbling block instead. Even Jesus' closest friends tripped over it, three plain predictions of the cross that would not fit any slot their minds had ready, and they needed an empty tomb before the words made sense. The offense was never a failure of messaging. It was the rescue refusing to flatter what it came to heal. And the stone they tripped on turned out to be a doorway, forgiveness announced to the whole room and light carried to the ends of the earth (Acts 13:47). The Wisdom They Were Chasing Had a Face By Thursday the week had swung a wrecking ball through nearly everything Corinth called smart. God promises to frustrate the intelligent, fills His church with people no recruiter would chase, and calls the world's best thinking foolish. Follow that trail far enough and it starts to sound like God has a quarrel with the mind itself. 1 Corinthians 1:30 Open ↗ It is because of Him that you are in Christ Jesus, who has become for us wisdom from God: our righteousness, holiness, and redemption. The week's target was never the mind. Tuesday showed what God actually tears down, the self-rescuing wisdom that was quietly dismantling the people who trusted it, the kind He destroys because it was destroying us. Thursday showed what He hands back. Paul does not say Christ teaches wisdom from a safe distance. He says Christ became wisdom for us, then unpacks the gift into three things no argument has ever produced. A guilty record declared right. A life being remade toward holiness. A captive bought back and walked home free. That is wisdom doing what wisdom was always for, and it comes the way a trade comes to an apprentice, by belonging to the Master and standing close. The week never asked us to stop thinking. It asked us to stop expecting our thinking to do a Savior's job. Still Speaking The Thing You Almost Walked Past Almost everyone has a story about the unimpressive thing that turned out to be everything. The job nobody wanted that became a career. The blind-date setup you almost canceled. The plain little house with the ugly carpet that became home. We are strangely good at walking past the very thing that would have changed our lives because it did not look the part. The cross is that, on the scale of the universe. Two thousand years of art and jewelry have made it beautiful to us, but it began as the single most off-putting object in the Roman world, and people walked past it by the thousands because it looked like weakness and defeat. That same sorting still happens every day, quietly, in living rooms and group chats and our own hearts. The message of a crucified Savior asks something the modern world finds just as awkward as Corinth did, that we are not okay on our own, that we cannot save ourselves, that the help we need comes through surrender instead of strength. To the person determined to be self-made, it still sounds like foolishness. To the person who has run out of their own strength and knows it, it sounds like the first true thing they have heard in years. Same message, same crossroads, and the dividing line was never intelligence. It is humility. Here is what made the difference for Paul. He did not just grit his teeth and survive the pull of a corrosive city. He had seen something. Somewhere along the road he had caught a clear look at the love of God poured out in the death of His Son, and once you have really seen that, the opinion of the room loses its grip. The cross stops being the embarrassing part of your faith and becomes the most precious thing you own. The world will keep calling it foolish. The people being saved will keep calling it home. Christ at the Center of the Week Pull the week together and every day lands on the same Person. Sabbath set the cross at the center of everything, the offense that is actually the power of God. Sunday found Paul refusing to dress it up, because Christ crucified needs no decoration. Monday watched the world laugh at Him and call Him foolish, never guessing they were mocking their own rescue. Tuesday spelled out what He did, reconciling us by His blood and healing us by His wounds. Wednesday stood amazed at how far He went, a God willing to be tripped over and nailed up to bring us home. Thursday gave Him His full title, the power of God and the wisdom of God in person. Six days, one thread, one Name. The whole week has been a long, slow look at Jesus, because the message of the cross was never really a message about an event. It was always a message about Him. Weekend Practice This weekend, do one thing that puts the cross back at the center. Pick the single area of your life where you are most tempted to be impressive, self-sufficient, or in control, and deliberately bring the cross into it. Tell God plainly that you cannot save yourself there. Then, sometime before Monday, say the plain, unimpressive truth of the gospel out loud to one person, without dressing it up or apologizing for it, that Jesus was crucified for us and it is the best news there is. Let the week's lesson move from your head to your mouth and your hands. Closing Prayer for the Week Father, thank You for a week spent looking at the cross. Thank You that what the world called foolish turned out to be Your power, and what looked like weakness turned out to be a wisdom we could never have invented. Forgive us for the times we have been embarrassed by the very thing that saves us. Give us eyes like Paul's, eyes that have truly seen Your love poured out in the death of Your Son, so the opinion of the room loses its hold on us. Keep the cross at the center of how we think and live, this weekend and into the week ahead. And make us bold enough to carry a message the world still calls foolish, because we have tasted its power and found it to be life. In Jesus' name, Amen.
docs.2026-07-11.html: In brief Picture a church where people wear a favorite teacher's name like a team jersey, one crowd for Paul, another for Apollos, each sure they picked the winner. That was Corinth, and Paul treats it as an emergency. Before he corrects a single belief, he goes after the divisions, because a church split into fan clubs has forgotten what it is. This week he joins no camp and instead pulls everyone back to the one name that was ever crucified for them. The church was never built to rally around a leader, only around the Lord crucified for it. Last week Last week the cross stood alone at the center, the one message Paul refused to dress up or trade away, God's power hidden inside the very thing the world called weak. We ended on a hard line, that humility, not intelligence, is what decides who receives it. Now watch where Paul carries that cross next. Not into a debate with philosophers, but into a church quietly tearing itself apart, members lining up behind their favorite teachers like rival fan clubs. His answer to their divisions is the same cross we just studied. Before he untangles a single quarrel, he reminds them that only one name was ever nailed up for them, and it was not Paul's. Historical Context Everyone in Corinth Wore Someone Else's Name A man in Roman Corinth rarely introduced himself by what he did. He told you whose he was. This was a city wired for patronage, held together by a web of powerful patrons and the clients who leaned on them for money, protection, legal muscle, and a foothold in the world. Clients gathered at the patron's door before dawn, walked him to the forum, cheered when he spoke, and carried his name through the streets like a badge. Your patron was your identity and your insurance at once. And because standing ran on it, the whole system bred rivalry. To belong to one great man was, quietly, to be measured against the followers of another. Now drop a young church into that world. These were people who had spent their whole lives sorting themselves by whose name they carried, and old reflexes die hard. They had swapped their patrons for apostles, but they were still keeping score. One group flew Paul's banner, another Apollos's, another Cephas's, each certain their teacher outranked the rest. They had turned the men who first pointed them to Jesus into competing celebrities, and the family of God back into a status game. Paul's whole answer this week is to remind them that only one name was ever nailed to a cross for them, and no apostle's will do. The name you wear is supposed to be His. This Week’s Memory Text 1 Corinthians 1:10 Open ↗ I appeal to you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that all of you agree together, so that there may be no divisions among you and that you may be united in mind and conviction. Notice how Paul opens. Not with a command but a plea. The word is parakaleo, Greek for coming alongside someone to urge and steady them, the same root that names the Holy Spirit as the Helper called to our side. Paul could have pulled rank as the founding apostle and ordered them to knock it off. Instead he begs them, and he begs "in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ," because that name is the whole point. The cure for a divided church is never a stronger boss. It is a shared Lord. And look closely at what he actually asks for. Not that everyone become identical, not one flavor of personality or opinion, but that they stop splitting into camps and line up "united in mind and conviction," their minds settled on the same Person. Hold that plea over everything we read this week. Paul names the fracture out loud, a church chanting "I belong to Paul" or "I belong to Apollos" (1 Corinthians 1:12-17). He files their infighting in the same breath as the ugliest sins he can list, right beside envy and malice (Romans 1:29). He calls it what it is, spiritual infancy, a church still stuck on milk because jealousy and quarreling have stunted its growth (1 Corinthians 3:1-4). Then he lifts their eyes to the only mind that heals division, the mind of Christ, who did not grab at status but emptied Himself and obeyed all the way down to a cross (Philippians 2:5-8). And he redraws what leadership even means, not the polished patron the city admired but a man beaten, imprisoned, and worn thin by his care for the churches, filling up in his own body what was still owed in the afflictions of Christ (2 Corinthians 11:23-28, Colossians 1:24). One body, one Lord, one name worth wearing. This Week’s Road Map ☩Sunday: The Problem of Cliques in the Church. Paul names the divisions out loud and shows why splitting into camps around leaders is not a small flaw but a denial of the gospel. ☩Monday: Centered on Jesus. The cure for factions is not picking the right leader, but remembering that only Christ was crucified for us and only He is Lord. ☩Tuesday: Wisdom and Maturity. Paul traces the quarreling back to spiritual immaturity, a church still on milk, and calls them up into the wisdom of God. ☩Wednesday: Christlike Servanthood. Real leaders are not celebrities to rally behind but servants and stewards who empty themselves the way Christ did. ☩Thursday: A Lifestyle That Reflects the Cross. True ministry is marked by suffering rather than status, and the cross is the only power that breaks our hunger for rank. ☩Friday: Further Thought & Discussion. The week lands on why the world will believe we are His when it finally sees us love one another. Christ at the center Here is the question to carry all week. What could possibly hold together people this different, this quick to pick sides? Paul's answer is not a better program or a stronger personality. It is a Person, and specifically a Person on a cross. On the night before He died, Jesus prayed for people He had never met, that they would be one the way He and the Father are one, so that the world would believe. He did not pray that we would all think alike. He prayed that we would be His. The cross does what no leader ever could. It takes people who would never have chosen each other and makes them one body by making them all debtors to the same blood. This week, watch every division in Corinth turn out to be the same failure underneath, a set of eyes that slid off Jesus and onto a man. And watch Paul mend them the only way that ever works, by turning every face back toward the One who was lifted up for them all. Application Before Sunday, name your camp. Most of us keep a quiet lineup of the Christians we consider a step below us, the ones in the wrong tradition, the wrong politics, the wrong worship style, the ones who follow the wrong teacher. Pick one person or group you have written off that way. Then do one concrete thing this week to move toward them instead of away, a message, an honest conversation, a real prayer for them by name. You do not have to agree with everything about them to belong to the same Lord they do. Opening Question for the Week "Where have you let loyalty to a person, a tradition, or a 'side' quietly become part of your identity as a believer, and what would change this week if the only name you needed to wear was Christ's?" Opening Prayer for the Week Father, before we open this letter, we admit how easily we split into sides. We pick our favorites and quietly look down on everyone who chose differently. We have wanted to be right more than we have wanted to be one. This week, show us how much our divisions cost You. Remind us that only one name was ever nailed to a cross for us, and it was not the name of any teacher we admire. Teach us to hold our convictions without turning them into camps, and to love the people You have joined us to, even the ones we would never have chosen. Pull every eye back to Jesus, until He is bigger to us than every side. In Jesus' name, Amen.
docs.2026-07-12.html: In brief Listen closely to the Corinthian church and you can hear chanting. I belong to Paul. I belong to Apollos. It sounds like team spirit, until Paul cuts in with a question no favorite teacher survives. Was he crucified for you? The divisions had already spilled into lawsuits and the communion table, and Paul treats none of it as minor. He files "strife" right next to idolatry. The fix is not picking the best leader. It is remembering that only one Person ever bled for you. Cliques feel like loyalty, but they are really the church forgetting who was crucified for it. Yesterday Yesterday we watched a whole city size people up by whose name they carried, and we saw a young church catch the same disease, wearing "Paul" or "Apollos" like a badge of rank. Today Paul quotes the slogans back to them, and you can almost hear the chant rise. I belong to Paul. I belong to Apollos. Then he interrupts the cheering with three questions that stop the room cold. Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Were you baptized in Paul's name? Every honest answer is no, and every no pulls the floor out from under the factions. This is where Paul starts his repair work, not with the surface quarrels but with the cross buried underneath them all. Historical Context They Would Rather Sue a Brother Than Lose Face Two men who once broke bread at the same table now stand on opposite sides of a Corinthian courtroom, in front of a pagan magistrate, airing the church's dirty laundry for the whole city to enjoy. In the Roman world this was almost ordinary. Going to court was less about justice and more about honor, a public arena where a man could humiliate a rival and climb a rung by dragging him down. The wealthy sued to flex their influence, juries could be tilted by status and quiet bribes, and the whole affair was a bloodsport of reputation. Winning was the point. Being right was optional. That instinct did not evaporate when people were baptized. It walked straight through the church doors and sat down. A community trained from childhood to treat every relationship as a contest simply found new contests, and the slogans of chapter 1 were only the loudest symptom. Long before Paul ever mentions a courtroom or a communion table, he is dealing with people who kept score for a living and could not stop keeping score once they were saved. Their team spirit was not harmless enthusiasm. It was the first visible crack in a wall that was already coming down. Into the Word You can hear the factions before you see them. One corner of the room belongs to Paul, another swears by Apollos, a third lines up behind Cephas, and a fourth trumps everyone by claiming to belong to Christ, as if Jesus were the most exclusive club of all. Paul has already begged them to stop splitting apart (1 Corinthians 1:10). Now he shows them how absurd their scorekeeping really is, and he does it by asking a question none of their heroes can survive. Did any of these men bleed for you? Watch him refuse to enjoy his own fan club, and watch how fast he changes the subject from himself back to the cross. 1 Corinthians 1:12-17 Open ↗ 12What I mean is this: Individuals among you are saying, “I follow Paul,” “I follow Apollos,” “I follow Cephas,” or “I follow Christ.” 13Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Were you baptized into the name of Paul? 14I thank God that I did not baptize any of you except Crispus and Gaius, 15so no one can say that you were baptized into my name. 16Yes, I also baptized the household of Stephanas; beyond that I do not remember if I baptized anyone else. 17For Christ did not send me to baptize, but to preach the gospel, not with words of wisdom, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power. Paul lets them hear their own chant, then drops three questions like a hammer. Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Were you baptized in Paul's name? The answer to each is obviously no, and each no dismantles a faction. The word underneath all of it is the Greek schisma, a tear or a split, the very word you would use for ripping a piece of cloth clean in two. That is what their team spirit was quietly doing to the body of Christ. Then Paul does something almost funny. He is relieved he baptized hardly any of them, because the last thing he wants is a single soul walking around thinking they belong to him. His job was never to build a following. It was to preach a cross, and a preacher who collects fans has buried the very thing he was sent to lift up. Read the slogans again and the tragedy is plain (1 Corinthians 1:12-27). This was not a rumor Paul went looking for. Word had reached him from Chloe's household that the church was consumed with rivalry (1 Corinthians 1:11), and the fault lines ran everywhere. Believers were hauling one another before pagan judges to win petty disputes (1 Corinthians 6:1-3), a thing Paul says should leave them ashamed (1 Corinthians 6:5). Even the Lord's Supper had curdled into a place where the divisions showed, the well-off eating their fill while the poor went hungry (1 Corinthians 11:17-22). None of it was harmless. Paul wants them to see that what they are calling loyalty keeps very dark company. Galatians 5:20 Open ↗ idolatry and sorcery; hatred, discord, jealousy, and rage; rivalries, divisions, factions, Look at the neighborhood strife lives in. When Paul lists the works of the flesh, contention and factions show up wedged between idolatry and fits of rage, filed right alongside sorcery and jealousy as things that war against the Spirit. This is the same ugliness he keeps naming in the Corinthians' quarrels, and he drops it into vice list after vice list so no one can pretend it is a minor flaw (Romans 1:29, Romans 13:13, 2 Corinthians 12:20). To Paul, a church that fights and cliques up is not merely awkward or immature in a harmless way. It is carnal, still ruled by the very flesh it was supposed to leave behind (1 Corinthians 3:3). We like to rank sins and set "division" down near the harmless end. Paul sets it next to idolatry. Street Level The Two Tables Picture the first big holiday after two sisters stop speaking. Nothing gets announced. The invitations just quietly go out to two houses now instead of one, and everyone in the family understands they are supposed to pick a side. Cousins who grew up inseparable start keeping their distance. An aunt rehearses which subjects are safe to bring up. The grandmother who hosted the whole family for forty years sets a smaller table and looks at the empty chairs. And here is the strange part. Nobody feels like they are tearing the family apart. Each person is simply being loyal to the sister they love most. That is exactly what was happening in Corinth, and exactly why Paul treats it as an emergency. Choosing a side felt like devotion. It felt like loyalty to Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas. But every time someone picked a human name to rally behind, the one family Jesus died to gather got a little more torn. Loyalty to a leader you admire is not the same thing as love for the body he pointed you to. So Paul asks the question that empties every camp. Was your favorite teacher the one nailed up for you? Only one name was ever paid in blood, and it was not the name on anybody's banner. When you catch yourself lining up against other believers, it is worth asking whether your loyalty is quietly setting a second table in a family that was only ever meant to have one. Today’s World The Body That Attacks Itself Your immune system has one job. It learns to tell you from everything that is not you, then defends you against the invaders. In an autoimmune disease that defense misfires. The body's own soldiers stop recognizing home tissue as friendly and start attacking it as though it were the enemy. In 2023 a study in The Lancet tracked the health records of 22 million people and found that roughly one in ten now lives with one of these conditions, from rheumatoid arthritis to type 1 diabetes to multiple sclerosis, and more than eighty types are known. In every case the damage does not come storming in from outside. It comes from the very cells built to protect the body turning against it. That is the exact danger Paul saw in Corinth, and it is why he refused to treat their cliques as harmless team spirit. The church was not being killed by Rome or by persecution from the outside. It was doing it to itself, members who were meant to guard one another turning into each other's enemies, loyalty misfiring into friendly fire. A body can usually survive an outside attack. What it often cannot survive is its own defenses turned inward. When believers start treating other believers as the threat, the very love that was supposed to hold the body together becomes the thing pulling it apart. Paul drags the problem into the light because a church at war with itself is not a lively church with strong opinions. It is a body slowly consuming the one life it was given. Source The Lancet Incidence, prevalence, and co-occurrence of autoimmune disorders over time and by age, sex, and socioeconomic status: a population-based cohort study of 22 million individuals in the UK. The Lancet, 2023. Read the source. Christ at the center Go back to the one question that silenced the room. Was Paul crucified for you? He asks it because he knows the answer resets everything. No teacher, however gifted, ever hung on a cross for the Corinthians, and no leader you admire ever hung on one for you. Only Jesus did. Every faction, in the end, is a case of mistaken identity, a group of rescued people crediting the wrong rescuer. When a church splinters into camps, it is not just being petty. It is forgetting whose blood bought it. And here is the deeper wound. The cross was the place God tore heaven's best to make us one, His own Son's body broken so that enemies could be folded into a single family. To take that hard-won oneness and shred it over which speaker we prefer is to trample the very thing that saved us. Paul is not scolding them for bad manners. He is walking them back to Calvary, where the only name that matters was written in blood. Application Pick a conflict you are currently invested in somewhere in the body of Christ, an online argument, a church disagreement, a grudge against another believer over how they do things. Ask yourself one blunt question about it. Did the person on the other side get crucified for you, or did Jesus? Then take one step today to lower the temperature, apologize for your part, mute the argument, or reach out to the person directly. You can hold your convictions with everything you have and still refuse to let them turn a brother or sister into an enemy. Discussion Question "Think of one Christian, or group of Christians, you quietly treat as the 'wrong' kind of believer (a different denomination, worship style, political lean, or the followers of a teacher you distrust). What would it look like this week to treat them as someone Christ was crucified for, rather than as a rival to be corrected?" Closing Prayer Father, we confess that we love our sides. We enjoy being right, we enjoy our teams, and we have treated other believers as rivals to beat instead of family to love. Forgive us for cheapening the cross by splitting the very people it was meant to unite. Remind us today that no one else was crucified for us, only Jesus, and that His blood runs thicker than every difference we use to divide. Give us the humility to lower our weapons first. Make us people who would rather lose an argument than lose a brother or sister. In Jesus' name, Amen.
docs.2026-07-13.html: In brief Yesterday's question left a hole. If the church is not supposed to rally around Paul or Apollos, what actually holds it together? Today Paul answers with a Person. We were called into fellowship with the Son of God, baptized into His name and no leader's. The word he uses for "united" means mending a torn net or setting a broken bone, not filing everyone down until they match. He wants a body, not a set of clones, where wildly different people are anchored to the same Lord. Unity is not everyone becoming the same. It is everyone facing the same Jesus. Yesterday Yesterday Paul emptied the factions with a single question. Was Paul crucified for you? No, and neither was Apollos or Cephas. But a question like that leaves a hole behind it. If the church is not supposed to gather around its favorite teachers, then what does hold it together? Today Paul fills the hole, and the answer is a Person. We were never called into a fan club for Paul. We were called into fellowship with the Son of God Himself. The problem in Corinth was never that they loved their leaders too much. It was that they had let a leader slide into the one place where only Christ belongs. Historical Context Rome Told the Body Story to Keep People in Their Place Long before Paul, the Romans already had a famous story about a body. As the legend went, the common people of early Rome once went on strike and marched out of the city, furious at being used by the elite. A senator coaxed them back with a fable. Once upon a time, he said, the hands and the mouth resented the lazy stomach and refused to feed it, until the whole body wasted away and they learned their lesson. The moral was blunt. Know your place, do your job, and stop complaining, because the people at the top are the stomach and you are the hands. For generations the "body" was a tidy image for keeping the lower ranks quiet and content at the bottom. Paul knew that image, and he detonated it. When he tells the Corinthians they are one body with many members, he is not telling the little people to keep serving the important people. He says the opposite. The parts that look weakest are the ones you cannot live without, the members that seem least honorable get the most honor, and nobody gets to say to anyone else, "I don't need you." In Rome the body kept people in their lane. In Christ the body makes the lowliest member essential. A church busy ranking its teachers had the picture exactly upside down, and Paul flips it right side up by pointing them past every member to the Head. Into the Word So what does Paul actually want in place of the factions? His words sound almost impossible at first, that a church full of different people would be "united in the same mind and the same judgment." It sounds like he is asking everyone to become identical. He is not. Read him closely and you find something far better than uniformity, a real unity that runs underneath our differences because it is anchored in one shared Lord. The center of the church was never meant to be a personality. It is a Person, and everything Paul says here is working to move Christ back to the middle where He belongs. 1 Corinthians 1:10 Open ↗ I appeal to you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that all of you agree together, so that there may be no divisions among you and that you may be united in mind and conviction. Here is the verse the whole week keeps circling. Notice what Paul is and is not asking for. The Greek word behind "united" is katartizo, the word for mending a torn fishing net, setting a broken bone, or easing a dislocated joint back into place. It does not mean grinding everyone down until they think and sound the same. It means taking something fractured and restoring it to working order. Paul is not after a church of clones. He is after a church that functions, where people who disagree about a hundred smaller things are still set solidly on the same foundation. And that phrase "the same mind and the same conviction" is not about matching opinions on every subject. It is about one settled agreement underneath everything else, that Jesus is Lord and all the rest bends to Him. Unity is not everyone becoming the same. It is everyone facing the same direction. 1 Corinthians 1:9 Open ↗ God, who has called you into fellowship with His Son Jesus Christ our Lord, is faithful. This is the ground the whole appeal stands on. God did not call the Corinthians into the Paul movement or the Apollos movement. He called them into fellowship with His Son. And notice that Paul cannot stop calling Jesus "Lord." In just the opening lines of the letter he repeats it over and over (1 Corinthians 1:2, 1 Corinthians 1:7, 1 Corinthians 1:8), driving the point home before he ever touches the quarrels. Every believer in that fractured church already possessed the one thing that could unite them. They belonged to the same Lord. They had simply let smaller loyalties crowd Him toward the edge of the room. Paul's cure is not complicated. Put Christ back in the center, and the factions lose their oxygen. 1 Corinthians 12:27 Open ↗ Now you are the body of Christ, and each of you is a member of it. Paul's favorite picture for the church is a body. Not a crowd of look-alikes, but a body, where an eye and a foot and an ear are wildly different and every one of them is needed, and not one of them works alone. That is a unity with room for difference built right into it. It also explains why the factions were so deadly. A body divided against itself is not a body anymore, it is just scattered parts. And remember how they joined this body in the first place. Not one of them was baptized into Paul (1 Corinthians 1:13). Every one of them was baptized into the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19). They were stamped as Christ's from the very start. The heartbreak in Corinth was a body full of members who kept acting like they belonged to different owners, when they had all been claimed by the same Lord. Street Level Why Strangers Talk Around a Fire Think about the last time you stood around a real fire at night, a backyard fire pit or a ring at a campground. Look at who is there. People who would have nothing to say to each other in a bright kitchen. Different ages, different politics, some loud, some shy, a few of them strangers. And yet a fire on a cold night does something a lit room never quite manages. It turns a random cluster of people into a circle. Nobody had to agree on anything first. Nobody became like anyone else. They just turned their chairs toward the same warmth, and somewhere in facing the same center, they quietly became an "us." That is the unity Paul is begging the Corinthians to recover, and notice what it is not. He is not asking a room full of very different people to become identical. The word he reaches for means mending a torn net or setting a broken bone, putting something fractured back into working order, not filing everyone down until they match. A church is a circle around a fire, and the fire is Christ. Face Him together and a hundred differences stop dividing you, because you are all being warmed by the same thing. Turn away from the center to argue about who is sitting where, and the circle breaks and the cold comes back in. Unity was never everyone becoming the same. It is everyone leaning toward the same fire. Today’s World The Eye as Wide as the Earth A black hole sits so far away and looms so small in our sky that no single telescope on Earth could ever photograph one. So in 2019 a team did something stranger. They took radio dishes scattered across the planet, from Hawaii and Arizona to Chile, Spain, Mexico, Greenland, and the South Pole, run by different countries and institutions, and aimed every one of them at the same spot in the sky at the same instant, all synchronized by atomic clocks. When their separate streams of data were combined, the scattered dishes acted like one telescope the size of the whole Earth, and it captured the first image ever taken of a black hole. In 2022 they did it again for the giant one at the center of our own galaxy. Behind that work stood a sprawling collaboration, some 760 scientists and engineers from nearly 200 institutions, spanning 32 countries or regions. Notice what actually made it work. Nobody melted the telescopes down and rebuilt them as identical machines. They stayed exactly what they were, wildly different instruments in different nations, run by people speaking different languages. Their unity came from one thing only. Every last one of them was fixed on the same center. That is the picture Paul is reaching for. He is not asking the Corinthians to become copies of one another, matched in shape and size and opinion. He is asking them to aim their lives at the same Christ. A church becomes one body the way those scattered dishes became a single eye, not by sameness but by a shared center. Turn the instruments toward each other and you get nothing. Turn them all toward the same point and suddenly they see what none of them could see alone. Source Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration Telescopes Unite in Unprecedented Observations of Famous Black Hole (data collected by a team of 760 scientists and engineers from nearly 200 institutions, spanning 32 countries or regions). Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration, 2021. Read the source. Christ at the center Every problem in Corinth traces back to one misplaced center. A church is only ever as unified as the Person it is built around, and the Corinthians had quietly swapped the Son of God for their favorite spokesmen. Paul's fix is not to find a better leader or broker a cleverer compromise. It is to move Christ back to the middle. Think about what that means. The thing that binds Christians together is not agreement, not personality, not shared taste in music or politics or preachers. It is a shared Lord who was crucified and raised for every one of us. Two believers who cannot agree on much of anything are still joined at the deepest possible point, because the same Jesus died for both and the same Spirit lives in both. When He is the center, the differences become a body. When He is not, they become a battlefield. Unity was never something the church had to manufacture. It was something they already had in Him and kept forgetting to live. Application Take an honest inventory today of what actually sits at the center of your faith. Sometimes it is a favorite teacher, podcast, author, or tradition, and it has quietly become the lens you judge every other Christian by. Name it. Then deliberately set Christ back in that spot. Here is one practical test. Before you share, repost, or argue for your favorite voice this week, ask whether you are pointing people to Jesus or to your team. And take two minutes today to thank God not for your preferred leader, but for the Lord you share with believers who are nothing like you. Discussion Question "What has quietly drifted into the center of your faith in the place that belongs to Christ (a favorite teacher, a tradition, a cause, a way of doing church), and how would your attitude toward other believers change if Jesus, and not that thing, were unmistakably at the center?" Closing Prayer Lord Jesus, we confess how easily You slip from the center. We build our faith around voices we admire and wake up having quietly made them more important to us than You. Forgive us. You are the One who was crucified for us, the One we were baptized into, the Lord we all share. Draw us back to the middle where You belong. Teach us to hold on to You so tightly that the smaller loyalties lose their grip, and to recognize as family everyone else who belongs to You. Make our differences into a body again, joined to You as our Head. In Jesus' name, Amen.
docs.2026-07-14.html: In brief A church that prided itself on being wise gets handed the most deflating word Paul has. Babies. Still on milk, not ready for solid food, and the proof is the bickering, the jealousy, the endless "I follow Paul" and "I follow Apollos." To Corinth that partisanship felt sophisticated. To Paul it was a nursery squabble. Real maturity, he says, is not knowing more facts or admiring smarter teachers. It is being trained by walking with God until you can actually tell what matters. The taking of sides they thought made them look wise was the clearest sign they had never grown up. Yesterday Yesterday Paul handed us the cure in a single line. Put Christ back in the center and the factions lose their oxygen. But that leaves a painful question hanging. If the answer is that simple, why could the Corinthians not just do it? Today Paul tells them, and it stings. They could not act like a mature church because they were not one yet. They were still spiritual infants, and their fan clubs were the evidence. The very slogans they were so proud of, I follow Paul, I belong to Apollos, were baby talk. Paul loves them too much to flatter them, so he calls them back to the solid food they keep pushing away. Historical Context Milk and Solid Food Were a Teacher's Everyday Shorthand In the ancient world, teachers reached for the same picture Paul uses here all the time. A beginner got milk, the simple first lessons anyone could swallow. The advanced student, weaned onto solid food, could finally chew on the hard and heavy things. Rabbis used it, philosophers used it, and everybody understood the insult buried inside it. A grown adult still demanding a bottle was a picture of someone who had refused to grow up. And in Corinth, of all places, that stung, because this was a city where being counted wise and mature was a genuine status symbol, something people competed for the way they competed for money and titles. So Paul's diagnosis lands with surgical precision. The Corinthians were sure their sophistication showed in their taste for impressive teachers and their skill at picking sides. Paul says it shows the opposite. All that clever partisanship is not the mark of wise adults. It is a nursery full of toddlers squabbling over which grown-up they like best. And here is the quiet tragedy underneath it. They wanted to be seen as wise more than they wanted to actually become wise, and the road to real maturity ran straight through the one thing their pride would not allow. Admit you are still on milk. Into the Word Paul has been fairly gentle so far. Here he stops cushioning it. He looks at a church that prided itself on wisdom and calls them babies, not as an insult thrown in anger but as a diagnosis given in love, the way a doctor names a condition so it can finally be treated. The factions, the sides, the whole competitive circus, all of it was evidence of one thing. They had never grown up. So Paul reaches for the oldest picture in the book, milk and solid food, to show them how far they still have to travel, and to call them toward the real wisdom they keep trading away for something cheaper. 1 Corinthians 3:1-4 Open ↗ 1Brothers, I could not address you as spiritual, but as worldly—as infants in Christ. 2I gave you milk, not solid food, for you were not yet ready for solid food. In fact, you are still not ready, 3for you are still worldly. For since there is jealousy and dissension among you, are you not worldly? Are you not walking in the way of man? 4For when one of you says, “I follow Paul,” and another, “I follow Apollos,” are you not mere men? Paul picks the most deflating word he can find. He calls a church obsessed with looking wise a room full of nepioi, the Greek word for babies, infants who can only take milk because they cannot yet chew. Then he points to the evidence sitting right in front of them. The jealousy. The strife. The chant of "I follow Paul" and "I follow Apollos." To the Corinthians all that partisanship felt like discernment, a sign they had refined taste in teachers. To Paul it was a nursery squabble. Grown-up faith does not fracture into cliques over personalities, and only the immature mistake taking sides for depth. And what were they fighting to own? A church that was never theirs to divide, God's own field and building and temple, the place where we all belong to God through Christ (1 Corinthians 3:9, 1 Corinthians 3:11, 1 Corinthians 3:16-17). Hebrews 5:13-14 Open ↗ 13For everyone who lives on milk is still an infant, inexperienced in the message of righteousness. 14But solid food is for the mature, who by constant use have trained their senses to distinguish good from evil. Paul is not the only one who used this picture. The book of Hebrews scolds a different set of believers the very same way, telling people who ought to be teachers by now that they still need someone to walk them through the ABCs of the faith (Hebrews 5:12). Here is the sharp part. Staying on milk is not a harmless holding pattern. It leaves a person inexperienced with the deeper things of God, unable to handle real weight, because those things belong to the mature, the ones whose spiritual senses have been trained by practice to tell good from evil. So maturity is not about how many years you have been a Christian or how much Bible trivia you can recite. It is about whether your walk with God has actually trained you to live wisely. You can carry a Bible for fifty years and still be crying for a bottle. 1 Corinthians 2:6-7 Open ↗ 6Among the mature, however, we speak a message of wisdom—but not the wisdom of this age or of the rulers of this age, who are coming to nothing. 7No, we speak of the mysterious and hidden wisdom of God, which He destined for our glory before time began. So what is the solid food they keep refusing? Real wisdom, but not the kind Corinth was chasing. Paul says there is a wisdom he speaks among the mature, and it is nothing like the slick wisdom of this age that is already on its way out. It is God's own hidden wisdom, a plan He laid before time began, and it reaches us not through raw brainpower but through His Spirit, who alone lets us grasp the things of God (1 Corinthians 2:13-14). And where is that wisdom found? Not in a lecture hall. In the cross (1 Corinthians 2:1-4), the very thing the clever called foolish. This is the whole point Paul is making before he circles back to their unity (1 Corinthians 3:1-17). The Corinthians desperately wanted to be wise. The door to real wisdom stood open the entire time, and it was shaped like a cross they kept walking past on their way to argue about their favorite teachers. Street Level What the Old Farmer Feels Coming Put two people at the edge of the same field. One just finished an agriculture degree and can recite the science of soil chemistry and rainfall. The other never went to college but has worked this ground for forty years. A gray smudge shows up on the horizon. The graduate pulls out a phone to check the forecast. The old farmer has already started moving, because they felt the shift in the wind and smelled the rain long before the app will admit it is coming. Bend down and crumble the dirt between your fingers, and the veteran knows by the way it holds together whether the ground is ready. The book learning is real. It is just not the same thing as knowing. That is the difference Paul is pressing on a church that was very proud of how wise it was. The Corinthians could debate theology and rank their favorite teachers with real skill, and they mistook that for maturity. Paul calls them babies anyway. Real growth, he says, is not how many facts you have stacked up. It is whether your senses have been trained, by actually walking with God through a lot of ordinary years, to tell what matters from what does not. You can memorize the whole field guide and still panic at the first yellow leaf. You can sit in a pew your entire life and still never learn to read the ground under your own feet. The solid food was never more information. It is the slow, trained wisdom that finally shows up in how you treat the people around you. Today’s World The Board a Master Reads in Five Seconds Show a chess grandmaster a real game position for just five seconds, then take it away, and they can rebuild it on an empty board almost perfectly, some thirty pieces back in their right places. It looks like a superhuman memory. Then researchers tried something clever. They scattered the same number of pieces across the board at random, with no real game behind them, and gave the master another five-second look. Suddenly the grandmaster remembered no more than a rank beginner. The famous experiments by Adriaan de Groot and later Chase and Simon showed the master's gift was never a bigger memory or a higher IQ. It was thousands of hours of play that had trained the eyes to see the board in meaningful patterns. Experts, as the researchers put it, do not search more. They see more. Paul is pressing that exact distinction on people who were sure their cleverness made them mature. And here is the sharp edge of the chess research. Take the master off a real board and hand them a random one, and all that brilliance simply evaporates, because the gift was never raw brainpower. It was pattern, earned slowly in one specific arena. Spiritual maturity works the same way. It is not imported from being generally smart, well-read, or quick in an argument. It grows up close, over years of walking with God, until a person can read a situation the way a master reads the board. The Corinthians had plenty of intelligence and almost no discernment, and they could not tell the two apart. Growing up in Christ is learning to see what is really in front of you, and that kind of sight comes only one slow way. Source Chase & Simon, Cognitive Psychology Perception in Chess (masters recall real game positions near-perfectly but random ones no better than novices; expertise as trained pattern recognition, building on de Groot; reconfirmed in world-class players 2023). Chase & Simon, Cognitive Psychology, 1973. Read the source. Christ at the center Notice where Paul says the deepest wisdom of God is actually kept. Not in a library, not in a philosophy, not in the teacher with the best arguments. In a crucified Man. The smartest people in Corinth looked at Jesus dying on a cross and saw the dumbest story ever told, and Paul says that is exactly where the wisdom of God was hiding all along. This is the solid food a divided church could not stomach, that the way up is down, that greatness looks like a Savior washing feet and bleeding for enemies. You cannot grow up in that wisdom while you are busy competing for rank, because the cross is the death of rank. Real maturity is not measured by how much you know about Christ. It is measured by how much you have let the mind of the crucified Christ reshape the way you actually treat people. The Corinthians wanted to look wise. Jesus offered to make them wise, and the classroom was Calvary. Application Here is an honest gut-check for today. Think about your spiritual "diet" over the last month. Are you actually growing, or just collecting content, sermons, podcasts, hot takes, while the way you treat people has not changed at all? Pick one area where you know God has been asking you to grow up, maybe how you handle disagreement, or a grudge you keep nursing, or a habit you excuse. Take one concrete step in it today. Maturity is not the information you gather. It is the obedience you finally practice. Discussion Question "Where in your life are you still 'on milk,' knowing a lot about a part of your faith but not yet living it (for example, preaching patience while staying easily offended, or valuing unity while quietly keeping score)? What would one step toward solid food look like this week?" Closing Prayer Father, we admit that we often mistake being informed for being mature. We can discuss You, quote You, and take sides about You while still acting like toddlers with the people around us. Forgive us for wanting to look wise more than we want to become wise. Wean us off the milk we keep clinging to. Train our senses through the ordinary practice of following You, so that we learn to tell what really matters. And keep drawing us back to the cross, where Your deepest wisdom is hidden, until the mind of Christ reshapes how we live. In Jesus' name, Amen.
docs.2026-07-15.html: In brief On the night He was betrayed, Jesus' disciples were arguing about which of them was greatest, and He answered by kneeling to wash their feet. That is the picture Paul drops on a status-obsessed church. Stop ranking your leaders like celebrities. A real leader is a servant and a steward, handed Someone else's treasure to pass on faithfully and owning none of it. And the model is Christ, who held the highest place there is and emptied Himself all the way down to a cross. You cannot claw for rank while wearing the mind of a Savior who climbed down for you. Yesterday Yesterday ended at the cross, with Paul insisting that God's deepest wisdom is a crucified Man, and that growing up means letting His mind reshape how we treat people. Today he shows us exactly what that mind looks like when it actually runs a life. It looks like a servant. The Corinthians kept ranking their leaders like celebrities and arguing over whose was greatest, and Paul hands them a completely different job description. A true leader is not a star to rally behind. He is a servant and a steward, someone trusted with Someone else's treasure, and the pattern for all of it is Jesus, who had every reason to grasp for status and instead let all of it go. Historical Context The Manager of the Estate Usually Owned Nothing In a wealthy Roman household, the most capable person on the property was often the estate manager, and he was frequently a slave. He held the keys, kept the accounts, directed the staff, and was trusted with the master's entire fortune. Real authority ran through his hands every single day. And yet he owned none of it. The house was not his, the money was not his, the land was not his. Everything he managed belonged to someone else, and his whole standing hung on one question, whether he was faithful to his master. A brilliant steward who started skimming for himself was not clever. He was a thief. Paul reaches for exactly that figure to reset how Corinth sees its leaders. An apostle is not a celebrity to be ranked and cheered. He is the household manager, handed the master's treasure, the gospel itself, to distribute faithfully rather than to build a personal following on. The one thing asked of a steward is not brilliance or charisma or a bigger crowd than the steward down the road. It is faithfulness to the owner. And a steward who starts collecting fans for himself is quietly robbing the Master. In a city that measured leaders by applause, Paul measures them by loyalty to Someone else, and reminds everyone that the treasure was never theirs to fight over in the first place. Into the Word Two pictures sit at the heart of today, and together they take the whole competition apart. First Paul tells the Corinthians how to think about their leaders, not as headliners but as servants and stewards. Then he shows them where a posture like that even comes from, the mind of Christ Himself, who held the highest status in the universe and spent all of it going down. Put the two side by side and the factions look absurd. Just before this Paul had branded the Corinthians' quarreling a mark of spiritual infancy, the worldly behavior of people still lining up behind rival names and boasting that they belonged to Paul or to Apollos (1 Corinthians 3:1-4). You cannot rank servants the way Corinth was ranking them, and you cannot scramble for status while following a Master who emptied Himself. Watch Paul move from the job description of a leader to the heart of the Leader who defines the whole thing. 1 Corinthians 4:1-2 Open ↗ 1So then, men ought to regard us as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. 2Now it is required of stewards that they be found faithful. Paul hands the church a whole new way to see the people they were so busy ranking. Not celebrities. Servants and managers. The word for manager is oikonomos, the household steward, the trusted servant who ran a wealthy master's entire estate, and the word behind our "economy." He carried the keys and the accounts and real authority, and still he owned none of it. Everything he managed belonged to someone else. That, Paul says, is the job. Leaders are stewards handed the mysteries of God to pass along faithfully, not treasure to hoard and not a fan base to build. And look at the single thing actually required of a steward. Not brilliance, not charisma, not a bigger crowd than the steward next door. Faithfulness to the Master. Rank the servants against each other and you have missed the entire point. There is only one Owner, and none of it was ever yours to fight over. So where does a servant heart like that even come from? Paul has already dropped the astonishing claim that we have the mind of Christ (1 Corinthians 2:16). Now he shows that mind in full motion, in maybe the most breathtaking description of downward movement ever written. Philippians 2:5-8 Open ↗ 5Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus: 6Who, existing in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be grasped, 7but emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in human likeness. 8And being found in appearance as a man, He humbled Himself and became obedient to death—even death on a cross. Here is the mind that heals a divided church. Jesus began with the highest status there is, equal with God, and He refused to clutch it. He let it go. He emptied Himself, took the nature of a servant, and kept descending, all the way down to a criminal's cross. Trace it as a straight line and it is dizzying. From the throne of heaven, to a servant's place, to a Roman execution, there was no bottom Jesus was unwilling to reach. And Paul aims this directly at the quarreling. He tells the Philippians, who had their own divisions simmering, to count others more important than themselves and to watch out for one another's interests (Philippians 2:1-4). That is what the mind of Christ does inside a real church. It quits asking who is greatest and starts asking whom it can serve. You cannot climb over other believers while wearing the mind of a Savior who climbed down for them. Street Level The Name That Is Never on the Wall Behind a famous painting there is almost always a person no one thinks about. The conservator. She is trusted with a canvas worth more than she will earn in ten lifetimes, and she handles it more closely than anyone alive, cleaning it under careful light, mending a hairline crack with a brush a few hairs wide. She wears gloves so her own skin never touches the surface. And when the work is finished, the painting goes back on the wall with the artist's name beside it, never hers. Millions will stand in front of it and feel something, and not one of them will know she existed. That is the whole job. The treasure was never hers. She was only ever meant to keep it and hand it on unharmed. Paul hands the Corinthians that exact picture of a leader, and it lands like cold water on a church busy ranking its teachers like celebrities. A real leader, he says, is a steward. Someone trusted with a treasure that is not his, the good news itself, and given one assignment. Be faithful with it. Do not hoard it, do not sign your name across it, do not build a personal following on the back of it. And this is the mind of Christ running all the way down. The One who owned everything took the lowest place and worked unseen, so that we could see the glory of Someone else. A leader who starts collecting admirers has quietly reached up and pried his own name onto a masterpiece he was never meant to sign. Today’s World The Founder Who Gave the Whole Company Away In September 2022 Yvon Chouinard, the founder of the outdoor company Patagonia, did something almost nobody sitting on three billion dollars does. He gave the entire company away. He did not sell it, did not take it public, did not hand it to his children to keep. He and his family signed all of it over to a trust and a nonprofit built to guard the company's mission, and announced that from then on every dollar of profit not reinvested, around a hundred million a year, would go to fight the climate crisis. "Earth is now our only shareholder," he said. A man who could have cashed out and lived like a king instead handed away the thing he built and kept working to run it for a purpose far bigger than his own name. That startles us for the same reason Paul's message startled Corinth. Everything in us assumes a builder should cash in, put his name on the tower, and climb. Chouinard walked the other direction on purpose, and the whole world stopped to stare, which is exactly the point. A life poured downward is so rare it makes headlines. Yet Paul insists downward is simply the shape of Christian leadership, running straight from the example of Christ, who owned everything and grasped at none of it. The Corinthians were scrambling upward, fighting over whose teacher outranked whose. The gospel calls a leader the opposite way, toward the low place, measuring greatness not by what you can pile up and keep but by what you can hold loosely and give away. Source Patagonia Works / CNBC Patagonia's Next Chapter: Earth Is Now Our Only Shareholder (Yvon Chouinard transfers all ownership to the Patagonia Purpose Trust and the nonprofit Holdfast Collective). Patagonia Works / CNBC, 2022. Read the source. Christ at the center Sit with the timing of it. On the same night Jesus was walking toward the cross, His disciples were arguing about which of them was the greatest. He answered them not with a lecture but with a towel, kneeling to wash the feet of men too busy competing to wash His. That is the mind Paul is describing. Everything the Corinthians were fighting over, rank, recognition, a place above the others, Jesus already held by right and gave away on purpose. He is God, and He chose the basin and the cross. So the deepest offense in a divided church is not simply that we bicker about status. It is that we bicker about status while the Son of God is kneeling in front of us with a towel in His hands. The cross does not only forgive our pride. It exposes it, and then it offers to trade it for something far better, a heart that finds its glory in going low for people who can never pay it back. Application Find one place today where you are quietly competing for rank, at work, in your family, in your church, or even inside your own head, keeping score of who gets the credit or who is ahead. Then pick one concrete act of low, unglamorous service you can do there this week, the kind nobody applauds. Clean the thing no one wants to clean. Hand someone else the credit. Serve a person who cannot return the favor. The mind of Christ is not admired into you. It is practiced into you, one basin at a time. Discussion Question "Where are you right now technically 'serving' (in a church role, a job, a family responsibility) while secretly keeping score of the credit you feel you are owed? What would it look like this week to do that same work as a steward who answers only to Christ, whether or not anyone ever notices?" Closing Prayer Lord Jesus, You had every right to be served, and You reached for a towel. We confess how far our instincts run from Yours. We angle for credit, we keep score, and we want to be the greatest even in rooms where You are kneeling to wash feet. Forgive our endless scramble for rank. Give us Your mind, the mind that released its status and went low for people who could never repay it. Teach us to measure ourselves by faithfulness to You instead of applause from others, and to find our joy in serving the way You served us. In Jesus' name, Amen.
docs.2026-07-16.html: In brief In a world where leaders advertised their honors, Paul brags about his beatings. Five floggings, three shipwrecks, hunger, cold, and the daily weight of worry for churches like Corinth. He pictures the apostles as prisoners at the tail of a Roman parade, marched out last to die while the crowd watches. Why hand a status-drunk church a résumé of scars? Because that is what a life shaped like the cross actually looks like, and it looks like Jesus. The wounds are not an interruption of the ministry. They are where the love becomes visible. Yesterday Yesterday we watched Jesus trade a throne for a towel, and Paul told a status-hungry church that real leaders go down, not up. Today he shows us how far down. Servanthood is not just a humble attitude you put on for church. Lived all the way out, it costs you something, and Paul has the scars to prove it. He stops debating leadership in the abstract and lays his own body on the table, beaten, imprisoned, shipwrecked, worn thin with worry for churches like Corinth. If you want to know what a life shaped like the cross actually looks like, he says, stop picturing a stage and look at the wounds. Historical Context The Parade Everyone Cheered Ended With the Condemned When a Roman general won a great victory, the city threw him a triumph, one of the grandest spectacles the ancient world could stage. He rode through Rome in gold and purple, wagons of plunder rolling behind him, the streets packed and roaring. But the parade had a back end nobody envied. At the very rear, in chains, came the conquered enemies, the captured kings and soldiers, dragged along as living proof of the victory. And for many of them, the parade route ended at the arena or the executioner. The front of the procession was pure glory. The back was a death sentence performed for a cheering crowd. Paul deliberately puts himself at the back. When he says God has displayed the apostles "at the end of the procession, like prisoners appointed for death," this Roman parade is the picture in his head, the doomed captives at the tail of the triumph, the part of the show the crowd came to watch die. And here is the scandal he presses on Corinth. They pictured themselves near the front, robed and reigning, and they wanted leaders who matched that fantasy. Paul says the true apostles are marching at the back with the condemned, and that is exactly what makes them look like their Lord, who was Himself paraded to a cross while a crowd looked on. In Corinth everyone wanted the front of the parade. In Christ the glory was waiting at the back. Into the Word Paul has just said a real leader is a steward, not a star. Now he shows the price tag on that kind of life, and it is not a stage. It is a cross-shaped existence. He insists that God Himself sets the standard for Christian leadership, not the applause of a crowd (1 Corinthians 4:1-5), and he points out that even Jesus, during His time on earth, handed every scrap of glory back to the Father (John 17:4). Then Paul does the one thing no self-promoter would ever do. He builds his entire credibility not on his triumphs but on his scars, and quietly dares the Corinthians to notice which résumé actually looks like the crucified One they claim to follow. 2 Corinthians 11:23-28 Open ↗ 23Are they servants of Christ? (I am speaking as if I were out of my mind.) I am so much more: in harder labor, in more imprisonments, in worse beatings, in frequent danger of death. 24Five times I received from the Jews the forty lashes minus one. 25Three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, three times I was shipwrecked. I spent a night and a day in the open sea. 26In my frequent journeys, I have been in danger from rivers and from bandits, in danger from my countrymen and from the Gentiles, in danger in the city and in the country, in danger on the sea and among false brothers, 27in labor and toil and often without sleep, in hunger and thirst and often without food, in cold and exposure. 28Apart from these external trials, I face daily the pressure of my concern for all the churches. Watch what Paul brags about. In a culture where leaders advertised their honors, their wealth, and their winning streak, Paul lists his beatings. Five floggings, three rods, a stoning, three shipwrecks, a night and a day adrift in open water. Hunger, cold, sleeplessness, constant danger. And then, as if it weighs more than all the rest, the daily pressure of worry for the churches he loves. This is not a man fishing for sympathy. He is redrawing the whole idea of what proves a ministry is real. The Corinthians wanted leaders who looked victorious. Paul says the marks of a true servant of Christ are the wounds he took while following a crucified Lord. His credentials are his scars. The most Christlike thing on his résumé is everything the world would file under failure. Colossians 1:24 Open ↗ Now I rejoice in my sufferings for you, and I fill up in my flesh what is lacking in regard to Christ’s afflictions for the sake of His body, which is the church. Stranger still, Paul says he rejoices in all of it. Not grits his teeth through it. Rejoices. He can even speak of "completing what is lacking in Christ's afflictions" for the sake of the church, and he does not mean the cross fell short of paying for sin, because that work was finished. He means the love that poured out on the cross keeps pouring out through people willing to suffer to carry it to others. Paul's pain was never meaningless. It was the shape love takes when it actually costs something. When a shepherd bleeds for the flock, the flock sees in flesh and blood what Jesus did for them all. This is why suffering, not status, is the real trademark of ministry. Anyone can chase applause. Only love will bleed. 1 Corinthians 4:9-13 Open ↗ 9For it seems to me that God has displayed us apostles at the end of the procession, like prisoners appointed for death. We have become a spectacle to the whole world, to angels as well as to men. 10We are fools for Christ, but you are wise in Christ. We are weak, but you are strong. You are honored, but we are dishonored. 11To this very hour we are hungry and thirsty, we are poorly clothed, we are brutally treated, we are homeless. 12We work hard with our own hands.
