When we are vilified, we bless; when we are persecuted, we endure it; 13when we are slandered, we answer gently. Up to this moment we have become the scum of the earth, the refuse of the world. Then Paul turns the whole thing into theater, on purpose. He says God has put the apostles on display like prisoners at the very end of a Roman parade, the condemned marched out last to die in the arena. The word he uses is theatron, a spectacle, a public theater show, the source of our word "theater." The whole world, he says, is watching the apostles be humiliated. Meanwhile he skewers the Corinthians' self-image with heavy irony, picturing them as rich, reigning kings while the men who brought them the gospel go hungry, beaten, homeless, and slandered, treated like the filth scraped off the world (1 Corinthians 4:8). Sit in that contrast. They imagined they had already arrived, and the apostles were being counted as garbage. Underneath the whole mess Paul names the actual disease, pride (1 Corinthians 4:6), the very root the factions had grown from. A church chasing thrones had stopped recognizing the cross even when it walked through the door. Street Level The Helmet He Won't Replace Walk into a firehouse and you can usually spot the veterans without a word, just by their helmets. The rookie's is clean and bright, barely scuffed. The veteran's is a wreck. Scorched down one side, the paint bubbled and discolored, the brim warped from heat. And here is what surprises people. He could get a brand new one anytime he wanted. He keeps the battered one on purpose. In that world a scarred helmet is not an embarrassment. It is a record. Every burn on it is a door he walked through, a night he went into the smoke while everyone else was pouring out, a person he carried down a ladder. To the people who know, the scars are the credential. Now you can see what Paul is doing when he answers a status-drunk church by bragging about his beatings. Five floggings, three shipwrecks, a stoning, years of hunger and cold and worry for people who rarely thanked him. In a city that measured leaders by how polished and victorious they looked, Paul holds up his scars and says these are my credentials. Not in spite of the wounds. Because of them. They are the proof he actually went into the fire for people, that love cost him something and he paid it. A faith with no marks on it at all might just be a faith that never went in after anyone. Paul's wounds were never the thing that spoiled his standing. They were the proof that he loved. Today’s World The Wound That Becomes the Credential In many addiction recovery programs now, some of the people best able to draw someone still using toward help are not the ones with a framed degree on the wall. They are the peer recovery specialists, and their qualification is the one thing you cannot earn in a classroom. They have been an addict themselves. They have been to the bottom the other person is living in and clawed their way out. Recent reviews of these programs keep pointing the same direction. Peers who share that lived experience build a trust and credibility that helps draw people into treatment and keep them engaged. The very thing the world would file under failure, a life once wrecked by addiction, becomes the exact thing that opens a door to someone in the same pit. Paul is making that same upside-down claim to a church dazzled by status. Corinth wanted leaders who looked impressive and strong, and Paul answered by pointing to his beatings and his sleepless nights of worry over people who rarely thanked him. He was not apologizing for those wounds. He was holding them up as the one thing that proved he had actually gone to people in their pain instead of performing for them from a safe distance. Scars cannot be faked, and a watching world quietly knows it. The person who has bled a little for you is the one you finally believe. The mark of real ministry was never a spotless, winning image. It was a love that had already paid for itself, the kind a hurting person can trust precisely because it cost the one who offered it. Source Current Addiction Reports (Springer) Peer Recovery Support Services and Recovery Coaching for Substance Use Disorder: A Systematic Review (peer support from lived experience builds trust and credibility and improves treatment engagement and retention). Current Addiction Reports (Springer), 2025. Read the source. Christ at the center Everything Paul says about himself was true first of Jesus. If the apostles march at the back of the parade, it is only because their Lord walked there first. Jesus was the truly condemned One, paraded through Jerusalem, stripped, mocked, and nailed up as a public spectacle for a jeering crowd. The King of glory took the last place in the procession on purpose. And that is the pattern Paul is pressing into a church drunk on status. The road to real glory runs straight through the place everyone is scrambling to avoid. Jesus did not suffer because His mission had failed. He suffered because love, when it is real, absorbs the cost instead of passing it on. So a leader who reflects the cross will never look like a winner on the world's scoreboard. He will look like Jesus, poured out for people who may never thank him. The wounds are not the interruption of the ministry. They are the ministry, because they are where the love becomes visible. Application Think of one place where following Jesus is currently costing you something, a relationship strained because you did the right thing, a thankless role you keep showing up for, a hurt you absorbed instead of passing on. Rather than resenting the cost or advertising it, offer it to God today as your actual ministry. Then find one small way this week to serve someone exactly where you will get no credit for it. A cross-shaped life is not measured by how impressive it looks. It is measured by how much love it is willing to pay out. Discussion Question "When you picture a 'successful' Christian life, how much of your image looks like winning (comfort, respect, influence) and how much of it looks like the cross (sacrifice, service, absorbing hurt for others)? Where might God be inviting you this week to measure your life by Jesus' scoreboard instead of the world's?" Closing Prayer Father, we like the idea of following Jesus far more than we like the cost of it. We want the crown without the cross, the influence without the wounds. Forgive us for chasing a comfortable, impressive faith while Your Son walked to the back of the parade for us. Thank You that Jesus did not count the cost too high, that He poured Himself out all the way to death so we could be brought home. Give us the courage to serve where it hurts, to absorb wrongs instead of returning them, and to find our glory where He found His, in a love that is willing to bleed. In Jesus' name, Amen.
docs.2026-07-17.html: Week in Review This week Paul faced a church splintering into rival fan clubs and refused to fix it with a better leader, pointing them instead to the one crucified Christ who is the only center strong enough to make a divided people one. ☩Sabbath: Unity in Christ. Corinth wore its leaders' names like jerseys, and Paul made the divisions his very first emergency, calling everyone back to the one name that was actually crucified for them. ☩Sunday: The Problem of Cliques in the Church. The slogans "I belong to Paul" collapsed under a single question, "Was Paul crucified for you?", and Paul filed their strife right next to idolatry. ☩Monday: Centered on Jesus. The cure was never a better leader but a shared Lord; the word for "united" means mending a torn net, restoring a fractured body around its one Head. ☩Tuesday: Wisdom and Maturity. Their clever side-taking was not sophistication but spiritual infancy, and the solid food they kept refusing was the wisdom hidden in the cross. ☩Wednesday: Christlike Servanthood. A real leader is a servant and a steward, not a celebrity, modeled on the Christ who emptied Himself from the throne all the way to a cross. ☩Thursday: A Lifestyle That Reflects the Cross. Paul staked his credibility on his scars instead of his successes, because suffering love, not status, is the true trademark of a ministry shaped like Jesus. Historical Context A City That Turned Everything Into a Ranking Step back and the whole week was walking through one city built on a single obsession, rank. Corinth ran on the question of who was above whom, and every institution was a way to climb it or show it off. You belonged to a patron and wore his name. You dragged rivals into court to win honor. You bragged about the teacher you studied under. You measured a household by the fortune its manager controlled, and you cheered the victorious general while the losers were marched to their deaths at the back of his parade. From top to bottom, the culture was a ladder, and everyone was climbing. Into that ladder Paul dropped a crucified Messiah and told the church the ladder itself was the disease. The factions were not a random flare-up. They were Corinth's status game smuggled into the body of Christ. That is why Paul does not answer their divisions with better management. He answers with the cross, the one place where the whole ranking system dies, because the God at the top of everything went all the way to the bottom on purpose. What This Week Clarifies A week about unity leaves three loose threads, and a week that talked this much about mending nets deserves to have them tied. A plea for one mind that can sound like a demand for sameness. A love for good teachers filed dangerously close to idolatry. A sentence about Christ's afflictions that seems to say the cross left something undone. All three tie off cleanly. Take them one at a time before Sabbath. A Mended Net Still Has a Thousand Knots Paul's opening plea can read like a demand for sameness. Agree together. No divisions. United in mind and conviction. To modern ears that sounds like a church of matching opinions and interchangeable people, and the same week seems to argue against it, celebrating a body whose parts are nothing alike. The plea and the picture appear to pull in opposite directions. 1 Corinthians 1:10 Open ↗ I appeal to you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that all of you agree together, so that there may be no divisions among you and that you may be united in mind and conviction. The word Paul chose settles it. Monday found katartizo underneath united, the fisherman's word for mending a torn net and the doctor's word for setting a broken bone. It means restored to working order, never ground down to sameness. So the memory text asks for one settled agreement, that Jesus is Lord and everything else bends to Him, and it leaves a hundred honest differences standing. The week kept handing us that picture from new angles. A body needs its eye and its foot to stay unalike. The scattered telescopes that photographed a black hole stayed different instruments in different countries and became one eye only because every dish aimed at the same point. That is the unity Paul begs for. Not clones, and not camps. Different people facing one center, joined at the deepest possible point because the same Lord was crucified for them all. The Teacher Was a Gift. The Jersey Was the Theft. Sunday filed the church's team spirit next to idolatry, and that filing can feel unfair. Apollos was a real gift to Corinth. So was Paul. Loving the teacher who first pointed you to Jesus looks like plain gratitude, and nobody in those camps felt like a divider. Every one of them felt loyal. The week owes a reader the line where devotion crossed over. 1 Corinthians 4:1-2 Open ↗ 1So then, men ought to regard us as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. 2Now it is required of stewards that they be found faithful. Wednesday drew the line with a job description. Regard us, Paul says, as servants and stewards, and the steward picture does the work. The estate manager in a Roman house held the keys and ran the accounts, and owned none of it. Honor him rightly and your thanks still lands on the master of the house. Follow him as owner and something has been stolen, which is why a preacher who collects fans has quietly signed his own name across treasure he was hired to hand on. That is where gratitude tips into idolatry. Not in loving a teacher, but in wearing him, letting a servant occupy the center only Christ can hold. Sunday's question still measures every loyalty on the shelf. Nobody's favorite voice was crucified for them. Thank the stewards warmly. Wear the one name that bled. Nothing Was Missing From the Cross Thursday saved the week's strangest sentence for its quietest verse. Paul rejoices to fill up what is lacking in Christ's afflictions, and a careful reader stops cold right there. The whole gospel rests on a finished cross. A sentence that sounds like the cross came up short cannot be allowed to drift past unexamined. Colossians 1:24 Open ↗ Now I rejoice in my sufferings for you, and I fill up in my flesh what is lacking in regard to Christ’s afflictions for the sake of His body, which is the church. The week's answer holds both truths at full strength. The atonement lacked nothing. That work was finished, and Paul of all people is not reopening the account. What remains unfinished is the delivery. The love that poured out at Calvary still has addresses it has not reached, and it travels the only way love travels, through people willing to absorb cost to carry it. That is what Paul's floggings, shipwrecks, and sleepless worry were, not payments toward sin but the cost of delivering a finished gift to people who had not yet received it. It is why the scorched helmet outranks the polished one, and why the apostles march at the back of the parade where their Lord walked first. The suffering was never the tragedy of the ministry. It was the love becoming visible. That is the week's closing word to a church that wanted the front of the parade. The center holds the body together, the stewards hand on the treasure, and the love gets delivered by whoever will carry it, at whatever cost. Tomorrow the family gathers again, different as ever, one Lord in the middle. Take your seat in that circle gladly, and thank the stewards who handed the treasure down to you. The net was tied together at a cross, by a Lord who walked to the back of the parade to gather every knot. Still Speaking The Argument the World Can Actually See We tend to think the church's witness rises or falls on having the best arguments, the sharpest answers, the most polished presentation. Jesus said something far more uncomfortable. The proof He staked His reputation on was not our logic but our love, specifically our love for each other. A watching world cannot fact-check our theology or sit in on our prayer times, but it can see, with its own eyes, whether people who have every reason to split apart somehow refuse to. Unity across the lines the world cannot cross, race, class, politics, temperament, old grudges, is an argument a skeptic cannot easily wave off. Which means our divisions are not a private family matter. Every time the church splinters into the same tribes as everyone else, cheering our camp and writing off the others, we hand the world a reason to shrug. And every time believers who should not get along somehow do, held together by nothing but a shared crucified Lord, the world catches a glimpse of something it cannot explain away. That kind of oneness unsettles the very forces that thrive on division. In an age addicted to taking sides, the most convincing thing a church could possibly do is to belong, visibly and stubbornly, to Jesus before it belongs to anything else. Christ at the Center of the Week Trace the week and it keeps landing on the same Person. On Sabbath the cross was the center strong enough to hold a fractured church together. Sunday reminded us that only Jesus, not any teacher, was ever crucified for us. Monday named Him the one Lord we were all baptized into, the Head that makes the body one. Tuesday found the wisdom the Corinthians were chasing hidden in His cross, the solid food they kept refusing. Wednesday watched Him step down from the throne, empty Himself, and take the form of a servant. Thursday saw Him at the back of the parade, the condemned One whose wounds turned out to be the whole point. Every answer to division, all week long, was not a strategy. It was a Savior. The church becomes one the only way it ever has, by everyone looking away from themselves and back to Him. Weekend Practice This weekend, do one concrete thing to close a gap instead of widening it. Pick a believer or group you have quietly written off, the wrong tradition, the wrong politics, the wrong style, and take a real step toward them. Reach out to someone you have drifted from over a disagreement. Pray, by name, for a Christian you tend to look down on, and keep praying until your heart softens. Or serve in a role this week where nobody will know it was you. Then, before Sabbath ends, sit with one honest question. If the watching world judged the gospel by how I treat other Christians, what verdict would I be handing them? Closing Prayer for the Week Father, thank You for a week that held up a mirror. We have seen our love of sides, our hunger for rank, our quiet habit of following people instead of following You through them. Forgive us for the ways we have splintered the body Your Son died to make one. Teach us to hold our convictions without turning them into weapons, to serve without keeping score, and to measure our lives by the cross instead of the applause. Make us one, not by pretending our differences away, but by fixing every eye on Jesus, until the watching world sees Him in how we love each other. In Jesus' name, Amen.
docs.2026-07-18.html: In brief A report crosses the sea to Paul. A man in the Corinthian church is sleeping with his father's wife, a scandal so ugly even pagan Corinth would not excuse it, and the church's response is to feel proud of how accepting it is. This week Paul refuses to look away. He walks straight into sexual scandal, church discipline, lawsuits between believers, and hard questions about marriage, and underneath all of it he plants one enormous claim. Your body is where the Holy Spirit lives. You are not your own. You were bought at a price. Last week Last week ended with the world watching. Jesus staked His credibility on our visible unity, and Paul spent four chapters pulling a church out of its fan clubs and back to the one name crucified for it (1 Corinthians 1-4). Now the same watching city gets an eyeful of something else. A scandal is being tolerated inside God's family that even Corinth's pagans would call shameful, and the church is not grieving. It is proud. Paul saw pride at the root of the factions, and he finds the same root here. So the cross he has been preaching turns from the church's divisions to the church's compromises (1 Corinthians 5-7), and the surgery goes deeper. Historical Context The Temples in Corinth Never Closed A sailor stepping off a grain ship could walk the few miles up into Corinth and never once lose sight of a god. The seven heavy columns of Apollo's temple, already ancient when Rome rebuilt the city, stood over the forum like the bones of an older world. There were shrines to Asklepios the healer, altars to Poseidon who ruled the seas that made the city rich, and street-corner spirits whose names nobody bothered to carve. High overhead, on the gray rock of Acrocorinth, sat a sanctuary of Aphrodite, the goddess of desire. Worship here was not a weekly appointment. It was the water the city swam in, woven into the butcher's stall, the dinner party, the business deal, and the bedroom. Greek comedians had long since turned the city's name into a verb for sleeping around, and the new Roman city, flush with harbor money, did little to retire the joke. Now notice what was missing from that skyline. The God of Israel owned no marble in Corinth. No columns, no statue, no smoking altar. And when He finally claimed a temple in the city, He did it in the strangest way imaginable. He moved into people. A tentmaker, a former synagogue ruler, a dockworker washed clean of an old life, each one now a dwelling where the Spirit of the living God actually lived. That is the claim this whole week stands on. The city's appetites had followed the converts through the church door, a scandal here, a lawsuit there, old habits waiting in the dark. Paul answers every one of them with the same staggering fact. The holiest ground in Corinth was no longer up on the hill. It got up every morning, put on sandals, and went to work. This Week’s Memory Text 1 Corinthians 6:19-20 Open ↗ 19Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have received from God? You are not your own; 20you were bought at a price. Therefore glorify God with your body. Read the question the way Corinth would have heard it. Everyone in that city knew what a temple was. Paul's word here is naos, Greek for the inner room of a temple, the small dark chamber where the god was believed to actually dwell, not the courtyards and columns but the holy center itself. Paul lifts that word off the marble and sets it on your body. The Holy Spirit does not visit you. He lives in you. Then comes the ownership claim, "bought at a price," the language of the marketplace, where a purchase changed whose hand held your whole life. Nobody walks into a shrine and scratches their own name over the god's. A temple belongs to the One who fills it. That one sentence carries everything we are about to read. It is why a hidden scandal cannot be waved through as a private matter (1 Corinthians 5:1-13), and why discipline, done the way God intends, ends with a broken man being welcomed home (2 Corinthians 2:5-10). It is why believers dragging each other before pagan judges stung Paul so badly, and why he answers both the lawsuits and the brothel with the same word about the body (1 Corinthians 6:1-13). It is why holiness is not a hobby for the extra devout but God's will for every believer (1 Thessalonians 4:1-8), and why the week ends with two commands that make sense of desire, flee what destroys and honor what God designed (1 Corinthians 6:19-7:9). A temple does not get to be casual about what happens inside it. It was built for Someone. This Week’s Road Map ☩Sunday: Dissonance Between Faith and Practice. A scandal the church should have grieved becomes something it quietly brags about, and Paul shows how far practice can drift from faith. ☩Monday: Dealing With Scandals. The hard instructions, remove, hand over, do not even eat together, turn out to be aimed at one goal, bringing the man home. ☩Tuesday: Protecting the Church's Identity. Believers are suing each other in front of pagan judges, and Paul asks what that spectacle is teaching the city about who Jesus' people are. ☩Wednesday: Antidote Against Sexual Immorality. Paul traces the church's problems to a misused freedom and answers with sanctification, the Spirit setting a whole life apart for God. ☩Thursday: Marriage and Singleness. Fleeing immorality is half the answer. Honoring God's design for marriage and desire is the other half. ☩Friday: Further Thought & Discussion. The week lands on seven questions Paul expects us to already know the answer to. Christ at the center Hold the phrase "bought at a price" up to the light and the cross shows through it. Paul never names the figure, because Corinth already knew how people were purchased, in silver, on a block, in public. God purchased differently. The price was His own Son, and the receipt is written in blood. Watch how every hard word this week stands on that purchase. The scandal matters because the man involved was bought, and so were the people shrugging at him. The discipline aims at rescue because the Owner wants His temple back, not burned down. Even the strangest sentence of the week, that Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed (1 Corinthians 5:7), turns cleaning out sin into an act of worship. Here is the question to carry through the week. If Jesus paid that much for you, what does He now want with what He bought? By Friday the question will no longer be how much is forbidden. It will be who you belong to. And the answer is Him. Application Before Sunday, run an honest intake audit. Our minds soak up whatever we hand them, and most of what we hand them arrives by habit, the feed we scroll at night, the shows running in the background, the voices we let talk to us for hours. Pick the one steady input you suspect has been quietly resetting your sense of normal. Cut it for the week, or swap it for something that feeds the temple instead of the appetite. Write down what you chose, so by Friday you can tell what changed. Opening Question for the Week "Where has the culture around you quietly reset your sense of normal, so that something that would have grieved you ten years ago barely registers today (a kind of entertainment, a way of talking about people, a habit you defend as harmless)? And if your body really is the place where God's Spirit lives, what would honoring Him with it look like this week?" Opening Prayer for the Week Father, this week is going to be uncomfortable, and we ask You to keep us in the room. Paul is about to talk about sex, scandal, lawsuits, and discipline, the subjects we usually lower our voices around, and every one of them touches something we would rather keep private. So before we begin, we hand You the key. Remind us all week that we are not our own, that You paid for us at the cross, and that Your Spirit has actually moved in. Where we have grown comfortable with what grieves You, make us tender again. Where we have confused tolerance with love, teach us the difference. And where something in us needs to be cleaned out, do it gently, but do it. We would rather be Your temple than our own landlords. In Jesus' name, Amen.
docs.2026-07-19.html: In brief The report reaches Paul in Ephesus and the news is ugly. A man in the Corinthian church is sleeping with his stepmother, a sin so far past the line that even pagan Rome banned it, and the church's reaction is not grief. It is pride. They think their tolerance proves how gracious they are. Paul hears something else, yeast working through dough, a congregation quietly learning to call blindness love. A church that can no longer blush at sin has not become more loving. It has stopped seeing. Yesterday Yesterday ended with a staggering picture. The holiest ground in Corinth was not the temple on the hill. It was people, bought at a price, walking around with the Spirit of God living inside them. Today we find out what provoked the letter's hardest chapter. A report has crossed the Aegean to Paul, and it is not about worship styles. Something is happening inside one of those temples, and the church that should be on its knees about it is congratulating itself instead. This first case study is not really about how bad sin can get. It is about how blind a proud church can become to it. Historical Context A Scandal Even the Pagans Refused to Excuse When the Roman orator Cicero wanted to make a jury's skin crawl, he told them about a wedding. A mother-in-law had married her own daughter's husband, and Cicero could barely get the words out. Unbelievable, he called it, unheard of in all his years. Rome was not a prudish place. Its poets joked about affairs, its generals collected mistresses, and its gods behaved worse than its citizens. But even Rome kept a short list of things beyond the pale, and the family line sat at the top of the list. Taking your father's wife was not on the menu of Roman vice. Their own law forbade it, and their own moralists gagged at it. That is what makes the Corinthian case so devastating. This was not a church stumbling over the ordinary temptations of a port city. A man had taken his father's wife, crossing a line Israel's law had drawn in ink centuries earlier and pagan Rome had never dared erase. The one place in that whole city where the affair raised no eyebrows was the congregation of Jesus. So today's question is not how such a thing could happen in a church. People fail everywhere. The question is how a church could watch it happen and feel proud of itself. When God's people lose the ability to blush, the world notices before they do. Into the Word For four chapters Paul has been coaxing a divided church, reasoning with it, pleading with it. Then a report stops the quill cold, and you can almost hear the tone change. It is actually reported. Not rumored, not whispered, reported, and the news has already crossed the sea. The whole chapter that follows (1 Corinthians 5:1-13) is Paul dealing with the fallout, and today we sit with the two shocks at the top of it. The first is what a church member was doing. The second, and Paul treats it as the worse one, is what the church was feeling about it. 1 Corinthians 5:1-2 Open ↗ 1It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and of a kind that is intolerable even among pagans: A man has his father’s wife. 2And you are proud! Shouldn’t you rather have been stricken with grief and have removed from your fellowship the man who did this? Paul names the problem with the broadest word Greek had for it, porneia, sexual immorality of every kind, the word that eventually gave us "pornography." Then comes the detail that made even hardened Corinth blush. A man has his father's wife (1 Corinthians 5:1), his stepmother, crossing a line the Torah had drawn in ink (Leviticus 18:7-8) and even pagan law refused to cross. The report came through people from Chloe's household (1 Corinthians 1:11), so this was no anonymous smear. But watch where Paul aims his shock. Not first at the man. At the congregation. And you are arrogant (1 Corinthians 5:2)! They knew, and the knowing had curdled into a strange pride, as if tolerating what even outsiders condemned proved how free in Christ they were. Grief was the sane response. They chose applause. Why would a church do that? Paul never tells us, and honesty beats guessing too hard. Maybe the man was wealthy, a patron the congregation depended on and did not dare confront. Maybe they had twisted the slogan making the rounds in Corinth, everything is permissible for me (1 Corinthians 6:12), into a license grace never issued. We simply do not know. What we do know is the outcome. A church stared at a flagrant violation of God's design and trained itself to see nothing. Worse than nothing. It learned to call the blindness love. 1 Corinthians 5:6 Open ↗ Your boasting is not good. Do you not know that a little leaven works through the whole batch of dough? Every Jewish family knew the ritual. Before Passover you swept the house for leaven, every crumb of it, because the feast required bread with nothing working through it. Paul reaches for that picture on purpose. Yeast is quiet. It never announces itself. It just spreads, cell by cell, until the whole batch rises on its influence. Tolerated sin behaves exactly the same way. The affair was one household's scandal, but the tolerance belonged to everyone, and tolerance teaches. Every week the matter went unaddressed, the whole congregation was quietly learning a new definition of normal, the way dough learns from a pinch of yeast. Paul is not panicking over one man's failure. He is watching a church's conscience ferment. What a church refuses to name, it eventually stops noticing. And what it stops noticing, it starts producing. Street Level The Train You Stop Hearing Ask anyone who has ever moved into a house beside train tracks. The first night, the 2 a.m. freight sounds like it is coming through the bedroom wall. The windows rattle, the dog barks, and you lie there wondering what you have done. Two weeks later you barely stir. A month in, you hear nothing at all. Then a friend stays over, staggers into the kitchen the next morning and asks how on earth you slept through that, and you answer with a straight face. Through what? You are not pretending. Your brain filed a freight train under normal without ever asking your permission. The whole street sleeps the same way. Kids who grow up there never hear the train at all. That is the church in Corinth. The scandal came thundering through the congregation on schedule, week after week, and the members slept right through it. Nobody voted to approve it. Nobody preached a sermon defending it. They just adjusted, a little at a time, until the unthinkable became part of the house. And when visitors winced, the church smiled the way locals smile at jumpy houseguests, quietly proud of how unbothered it had become. Paul's letter is the friend at breakfast asking how anyone in this house is still sleeping. Sin's favorite trick is not persuasion. It is repetition. Keep a thing close enough, long enough, and it stops sounding like anything. The train never got quieter. The house went deaf. Today’s World Four Missing Bolts and a Factory That Stopped Noticing On January 5, 2024, a panel the size of a refrigerator door tore off the side of Alaska Airlines Flight 1282 a few minutes after takeoff from Portland. The cabin depressurized in an instant. A teenager's shirt was ripped off his body, phones were sucked into the night sky, and only a nearly empty row beside the hole kept the story from turning deadly. Investigators traced the failure to something almost unbelievable. Months earlier, workers at Boeing's Renton factory had opened that door plug for a repair and reinstalled it without the four bolts that hold it in place. No paperwork recorded the job. No inspection caught it. The jet then flew 154 flights with nothing but friction keeping the panel on. When the National Transportation Safety Board announced its findings at a board meeting in June 2025, the probable cause was not one careless mechanic. It was a factory culture, years of inadequate training, guidance, and oversight in which skipped steps and missing records had quietly become normal. The board's chair said the deficiencies should have been evident and should have been preventable. Here is the detail worth losing sleep over. For 154 flights, the missing bolts seemed fine, and every safe landing testified that nothing was wrong. Tolerated deviation always works that way. It rewards you right up until it ruins you. The Corinthian church's scandal was flying fine too, and their pride was 154 smooth landings deep. The blowout is never the moment the failure happens. It is only the moment the failure stops being deniable. Source National Transportation Safety Board Boeing's Inadequate 'Training, Guidance and Oversight' Led to Mid-Exit Door Plug Blowout on Passenger Jet. National Transportation Safety Board, 2025. Read the source. Christ at the center Follow Paul's leaven picture one verse further and you land at the cross. Clean out the old leaven, he writes, for Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed (1 Corinthians 5:7). Notice the tense. The Lamb is not about to die, waiting on our housecleaning. He has already been sacrificed. In every Jewish home the order was fixed. The lamb died, and the leaven went out the door, because you do not keep the feast with old rot in the walls. Paul is saying the church lives permanently inside that moment. Calvary has already happened. The blood is already on the doorposts. The only question left is whether we will sweep the house. That is why tolerating the scandal was not extra grace. It was forgetting what grace cost. A church that shrugs at sin is not being generous with Jesus' mercy. It is being careless with His blood. The Lamb has died. Sweep the house. Application Somewhere in your life there is a thing you have renamed. Scripture calls it sin, and you have been calling it a quirk, a coping mechanism, a private matter, no big deal. Today, before God, use its real name. Say it out loud in prayer, without the softer word. Then take one concrete step against it before the day ends, delete the app, end the conversation, pour it out, make the call. Grief over sin is not self-hatred. It is the first honest step home. Discussion Question "What has your church family, or your own heart, drifted into tolerating that Scripture clearly condemns, all under the banner of love and acceptance (a habit everyone jokes about, a relationship pattern nobody questions, a business practice that pays too well to examine)? And if you pictured actually addressing it, what would grieving it look like, instead of either shrugging at it or attacking the people caught in it?" Closing Prayer Father, we have been reading about Corinth, but You have been reading us. We confess that we have our own tolerated things, sins we have relabeled until they sound like personality. We confess that we have sometimes been proud of our tolerance, calling it love, calling it grace, while something You died to remove settled deeper into the house. Give us the gift we least want and most need, the ability to blush again. Teach us to grieve sin without despising sinners, starting with the one in the mirror. Keep us tender toward the man in this story, because his road, repentance and restoration, is the road we all walk home. And thank You that the Lamb has already been sacrificed, that the price is already paid. Help us sweep the house. In Jesus' name, Amen.
docs.2026-07-20.html: In brief Circle the verbs in this chapter and they read like a courtroom. Remove. Judge. Hand over. Do not even eat together. Then one small clause turns the gavel into a stretcher, so that his spirit may be saved. Paul is not throwing a man away. He is refusing to let a church's warmth keep lying to him, and one letter later a repentant man is being forgiven, comforted, and hugged back into the family. Discipline in God's house is never the opposite of love. It is love that refuses to lie. Yesterday Yesterday we watched a congregation applaud itself for tolerating what even pagans condemned, and we heard Paul name the real danger, a pinch of yeast quietly teaching the whole batch a new normal. The Lamb has died, he said. Sweep the house. Today he hands the church the broom. What follows is the hardest set of instructions in the letter, remove him, hand him over, do not even share a table, and to modern ears every one of them sounds like cruelty. Read them slowly anyway. Hidden inside the harshest sentence is a purpose clause that changes everything, and at the end of this road there is a welcome-home nobody saw coming. Historical Context A Shared Table Was a Signed Statement In Corinth a business deal did not close with a signature. It closed with a dinner. To recline at another man's table was to tell the whole street something about yourself, that his people were your people, that his standing vouched for yours, that whatever he was known for, you could live with it. Meals ran on this logic across the ancient world. Treaties were sealed over bread and salt. A patron fed his clients, and the feeding announced who belonged to whom. A wedding feast bound two families, not just two people. Israel felt the weight of the table too, which is why the psalmist's bitterest line about betrayal is not about stolen money but a shared loaf, the trusted friend who ate my bread and then turned on me (Psalm 41:9). So when Paul writes do not even eat with such a one, he is not inventing a punishment. He is unplugging an endorsement. As long as the church kept passing the bread to a man living in open, unrepentant sin, every meal was a public statement that Jesus' people could live with it. The table was the church's signature, and Corinth could read it from across the street. Withdrawing it was not about hating the man. It was about refusing to let the family's warmth keep telling him, and the watching city, a lie. Sometimes the most honest thing a table can do is sit empty. Into the Word Read the chapter again and circle the verbs (1 Corinthians 5:1-13). Remove. Judge. Hand over. Put away. They land like a gavel, one blow after another, and it is fair to admit they sound severe to us. Paul knew they would sound severe in Corinth too. He wrote them anyway, because a church that had learned to applaud a scandal was never going to be healed by a shrug. So today's question is what all that severity is actually for. Follow the hardest sentence in the chapter to its final clause and you will find out. This surgery has a survival plan. 1 Corinthians 5:5 Open ↗ hand this man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved on the Day of the Lord. This is the verse people quote to prove Paul was harsh, and it ends in a rescue. Handing the man over to Satan is not a curse or a dark ritual. It is a transfer of custody. Inside the church, a person lives under the shelter of God's people, their worship, their warnings, their love. By refusing to repent, this man had already chosen Satan's territory. Paul tells the church to stop pretending otherwise and let him stand on the ground he picked. The destruction of the flesh is not torture. It is a sinful life collapsing under its own weight, the far country doing what the far country always does. Then comes the clause that flips the whole verse. So that his spirit may be saved. Paul had already made the judgment call (1 Corinthians 5:3) that the church kept dodging (1 Corinthians 5:2). The goal was never to lose the man. It was to lose the lie that was keeping him. The boundary had teeth, and Paul had drawn it before. An earlier letter had already told them not to associate with the sexually immoral (1 Corinthians 5:9), and they had managed to misread it, so now he spells it out. He never meant the people of the world. You would have to leave the planet to avoid them, and Jesus did not leave His people here to avoid anybody. He meant the one who wears the family name while living in open defiance of the family's Lord, the so-called brother (1 Corinthians 5:11). With him, do not even share a meal. In a world where a meal was a signature, the church's table had to stop signing. 1 Corinthians 5:13 Open ↗ God will judge those outside. “Expel the wicked man from among you.” Paul closes the chapter with a division of labor. God judges outsiders. The church tends its own house. Notice how that reverses the posture churches often fall into, loud about the world's sins and silent about their own. Paul does not tell Corinth's believers to police the morals of a pagan city. That is God's business, in God's time. He tells them to take responsibility for what carries Jesus' name. The final command is borrowed from Moses, the old covenant formula spoken when the community's life with God was at stake (Deuteronomy 17:7), purge the evil from among you. The church is not the world's judge. It is the guardian of its own witness. A family cannot control the whole neighborhood. It can decide what happens under its own roof. 2 Corinthians 2:5-10 Open ↗ 5Now if anyone has caused grief, he has not grieved me but all of you—to some degree, not to overstate it. 6The punishment imposed on him by the majority is sufficient for him. 7So instead, you ought to forgive and comfort him, so that he will not be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow. 8Therefore I urge you to reaffirm your love for him. 9My purpose in writing you was to see if you would stand the test and be obedient in everything. 10If you forgive anyone, I also forgive him. And if I have forgiven anything, I have forgiven it in the presence of Christ for your sake, Now read what happened next, quite possibly to this very man, met again one letter later. The discipline did its work. He repented. And the church, so slow to act before, has swung to the opposite pole, so slow to welcome him back that Paul has to intervene again, this time on the sinner's behalf. The punishment was sufficient, he writes. Forgive him and comfort him before the sorrow drowns him. Reaffirm your love. Paul's word for forgive is charizomai, Greek for granting something freely, forgiveness given the way you give a gift, grace with hands on it. And he anchors the reunion in the presence of Christ, because that is where every real restoration happens. Here is the test of church discipline. If the welcome-home was never in the plan, it was never discipline. It was just an exile with better paperwork. Street Level The Month the Money Doesn't Come A mother sits at her kitchen counter with her thumb over the transfer button. Her grown son has overdrafted again, the third time this year, and the banking app is waiting for her to make it quietly disappear. She has covered it every time. She calls it helping. But the overdrafts keep growing, the calls only come when the account is empty, and somewhere along the way her rescues stopped rescuing anything. They just moved the weight of his choices from his shoulders to hers, one month at a time. So tonight she does the hardest thing love has ever asked of her. She closes the app. Days later, in a checkout line across town, his card is declined in front of strangers, and for the first time in years the bill lands on the man who ran it up. Everyone watching thinks she gave up on him. The truth is she never fought harder for him in her life. That is the logic of 1 Corinthians 5:1-13. The congregation's kindness had become the sin's life support, so Paul says stop the transfers. Let the consequences finally reach him, not to crush him, but because they are sometimes the last voice a person can still hear. And notice what the mother never cancels. The porch light stays on. His room stays his room. The whole time, the plan was the homecoming. She did not stop loving him the night she closed the app. That was the night the loving got serious. Today’s World The Prison That Plans the Homecoming Norway's correctional service sums its philosophy up in one sentence. "The punishment is the restriction of liberty; no other rights have been removed by the sentencing court." The consequence is real. The gate locks, and the years are genuinely lost. But the same service runs on what it calls the principle of normality, that life inside should resemble life outside as much as possible, the school, the library, the doctor, the chaplain all brought in from the surrounding community, and a contact officer assigned to assist the prisoner rather than merely watch him. The idea has crossed the ocean. At a Pennsylvania state prison outside Philadelphia, a unit nicknamed Little Scandinavia, built in partnership with Norwegian researchers, now runs on the same principles, with residents assigned at random so a study can measure what happens. The Marshall Project reported in 2025 that early results are promising, including a single physical altercation since the unit opened. Notice what this model refuses to do. It refuses to cancel the consequence, and it refuses to cancel the person. The sentence lands with full weight, and from day one the system designs backward from the homecoming, because the man in that cell is not garbage to be warehoused. He is a neighbor in the making. That is 1 Corinthians 5:1-13 and 2 Corinthians 2:5-10 wearing a corrections uniform. Hand him over, let the far country do its honest work, so that his spirit may be saved, and when he turns, forgive him, comfort him, reaffirm your love. The systems that actually change people are the ones that never stopped picturing them restored. Paul would recognize the blueprint. He drew it first. Sources The Marshall Project, Norwegian Correctional Service (kriminalomsorgen.no) Fish Tanks, Plants and Podcast Studios — Some States Try a New Approach to Incarceration. The Marshall Project, 2025. Read the source. About the Norwegian Correctional Service. Norwegian Correctional Service (kriminalomsorgen.no), 2026. Read the source. Christ at the center Handed over. Notice how strange that phrase should feel by the end of this chapter. The church hands a man over to Satan so that his spirit may be saved, and if that sounds severe, remember that God did something far more severe first. He did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all (Romans 8:32). On the night of His arrest, Jesus looked at the torches coming for Him and named the moment as the hour when darkness reigns (Luke 22:53). He was handed over to the dark, not for His sins but for ours, so that every sinner who ever gets handed over to consequences would have somewhere to come home to. That is why discipline in the church can never run on disgust. The Man overseeing the process has scars. He knows exactly what being given up costs, He paid it willingly, and He stands in the middle of every reunion, which is why Paul forgives in the presence of Christ. No one wants the prodigal home more than the One who walked into the far country to carry him back. Application Paul's word to a church that finally disciplined well was reaffirm your love. So today, think of one person who has genuinely turned, from an affair, an addiction, a season of wreckage, and who still walks into rooms wondering whether they are actually welcome. Send the message their shame says will never come. Name the change you see in them, tell them you are glad they are back, and if you can, invite them to a real table this week. And if you are the one standing outside right now, take one honest step back toward the family today. The door is not locked. Discussion Question "When you have seen correction go wrong in a church or a family, which half usually failed, the courage to confront or the grace to restore (the scandal everyone ignored for years, or the repentant person still treated as suspect a decade later)? And which half are you personally more likely to get wrong this year, with the actual people God has placed around you?" Closing Prayer Father, thank You for loving us too much to lie to us. We confess that we get this backwards in both directions. We tolerate what is destroying people because confrontation frightens us, and then, when someone finally repents, we hold the door half-closed because trust feels risky. Give our churches the courage to grieve sin, the honesty to name it, and the speed to forgive it. For anyone we love who is living under hard consequences right now, we ask You to make the far country loud enough to wake them and Your mercy loud enough to call them home. And when the prodigals head for the door, make us the family that runs to meet them, because that is how You met us. Teach us the kind of correction that plans the welcome-home from the start. In Jesus' name, Amen.
docs.2026-07-21.html: In brief Picture the scene the city could not stop watching. Two members of the same small church stand in Corinth's forum, suing each other before a pagan judge while the neighbors enjoy the show. Paul is nearly speechless. Is there really no one wise among you? People destined to judge angels are hiring the world to referee a business squabble. Underneath the lawsuits he finds the real problem, a church forgetting who it is, and he answers with a list of everything they used to be. You were washed. Do not let a dispute talk you out of your name. Yesterday Yesterday the church learned the difference between God's jurisdiction and its own. God judges outsiders, Paul said. The family tends what happens under its own roof. Today we watch the Corinthians run that principle exactly backwards. Matters that belonged inside the family, disputes between brothers, are being marched downtown and handed to outsiders to decide. The same church that had no stomach for judging a scandal inside its walls found plenty of stomach for suing its own members in front of pagans. Tolerance where there should have been grief, and litigation where there should have been family. Paul reads both as symptoms of the same amnesia. They have forgotten who they are. Historical Context The Synagogue Next Door Settled Its Own Quarrels Two Jewish merchants in a Roman city had a problem, a shipment paid for and never delivered, and everyone in their community knew exactly where that problem would go. Not to the governor's tribunal. To a quiet room near the synagogue, where a panel of respected elders would hear both men out, weigh the Torah, and settle the matter. For centuries, scattered Jewish communities had carried their own justice with them, a court of their own wherever enough families gathered. Rome, pragmatic as ever, mostly let them. Moses had commanded Israel to appoint judges within the community back in the wilderness years, and the habit survived exile, empire, and every hostile neighborhood in between. Family matters stayed in the family. Dragging a fellow Jew before a pagan magistrate was close to unthinkable, a public announcement that your community could not govern itself. The church in Corinth was born inside that inheritance. Its first members had watched internal justice work their whole lives, patient, private, anchored in God's law. And they walked away from it. Believers with disputes went downtown instead, to the public tribunal where orators performed and rank quietly tipped the scales, and where the city could watch Jesus' people tear at each other for sport. Paul's astonishment in this chapter is not that Christians had conflicts. Every family does. It is that the family with the oldest tradition of settling its own matters, and the greatest Judge to imitate, had chosen the world's stage for its fights. The church did not just have a legal problem. It had an identity problem. Into the Word There is a question hiding in the middle of this passage that drips with irony. Is there really not one wise person among you? This is Corinth, the church that boasted about wisdom, sorted itself by clever teachers, and rated preachers like entertainment. Paul has spent three chapters deflating that pride, and now it lands with a thud. All that wisdom, and nobody can arbitrate a dispute between brothers. Today's reading (1 Corinthians 6:1-13) follows the lawsuits down to the appetites underneath them, and it keeps asking the church one question. Do you remember whose you are? 1 Corinthians 6:1 Open ↗ If any of you has a grievance against another, how dare he go to law before the unrighteous instead of before the saints! Paul's word for the dispute is pragma, Greek for a thing, a matter, an ordinary piece of business, and the ordinariness is part of his point. This was not a criminal case. Crimes belonged to the state's courts, whose God-given authority Paul affirms elsewhere (Romans 13:1-5). This was civil, a contract, a debt, a property line, the small change of life together. And for that, believers marched each other in front of judges Paul calls the unrighteous, not because every magistrate was corrupt but because they stood outside the covenant, strangers to the Lord both parties claimed. How dare you is strong language for a small-claims fight. Paul uses it because of what the venue announced. Taking the family's matter to the world's referees told the whole city that the family had no Father worth consulting. We never learn what the case was about. The passage sits bracketed by sexual scandal on both sides (1 Corinthians 5, 1 Corinthians 6:12-20), so the matter may have been tangled in the same mess, and some readers have wondered whether the litigants were the father and son of the affair itself (1 Corinthians 5:1). Paul never says, and he does not need to. Whatever the case was (1 Corinthians 6:1-11), his grief was the spectacle, brother against brother, in front of unbelievers (1 Corinthians 6:6), in courts where rank and rhetoric tipped the scales while the city kept score. Even Paul's outline here is borrowed. Moses, too, set legal process right beside sexual sin (Deuteronomy 22:22-24), and Paul walks the same path, handling the church's problems on the Torah's rails rather than Rome's. 1 Corinthians 5:12-13 Open ↗ 12What business of mine is it to judge those outside the church? Are you not to judge those inside? 13God will judge those outside. “Expel the wicked man from among you.” Here is the principle underneath both days. The church has a jurisdiction, and it is not the world. Paul refuses to hand out verdicts on outsiders, because God will handle the world's judgment in His own time. But insiders are different. Those who are inside have taken one Lord, joined one body, and handed each other their trust, and that gives the family both the right and the responsibility to settle its own matters. Paul had exercised exactly that inside-jurisdiction over the scandal, judging the case from a distance (1 Corinthians 5:3) while the locals dithered. Now he lays the same map over the lawsuits. A dispute between brothers is inside business. Marching it downtown does not just misplace a court case. It redraws the family's borders and seats the world on the bench. 1 Corinthians 6:9-10 Open ↗ 9Do you not know that the wicked will not inherit the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived: Neither the sexually immoral, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor men who submit to or perform homosexual acts, 10nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor verbal abusers, nor swindlers, will inherit the kingdom of God. Why does a paragraph about lawsuits suddenly break into a list of sins? Because Paul can smell what is underneath the litigation, greed, swindling, taking what is not yours, the same appetites driving the sexual chaos, and he has already filed lists like this while dealing with the scandal (1 Corinthians 5:10-11). Notice that sexual sins sit shoulder to shoulder with theft, greed, drunkenness, and abusive speech. Corinth ranked sins by respectability. Paul refuses to, because every entry on the list is the same move, an appetite enthroned where the Lord belongs. The unrighteous, he warns, do not inherit God's kingdom, and unrighteous is the very word he just used for the pagan judges. Act like the world long enough and the question stops being rhetorical. Whose are you? But the list is not a wall to keep sinners out, and the next breath proves it. That is what some of you were (1 Corinthians 6:11). Were. You were washed, sanctified, justified in the name of the Lord Jesus. The vice list is a mirror with a caption underneath. Not anymore. Street Level The Name on the Front of the Jersey Late in a blowout loss, the cameras find two teammates on the same sideline, helmets off, chests together, screaming at each other over a blown assignment. Every phone in the stadium is already up and recording. By morning the clip has ten million views and a one-word caption. Meltdown. Nobody in the comments knows what the assignment was. Nobody cares. The score is forgotten, the opponent is forgotten, and all anyone remembers is that this team turned on itself in public. Which is why every veteran locker room lives by the same unwritten rule. Have it out in here if you have to. Grab a facemask, clear the air, say the hard thing behind that door. Never out there. Paul is the old captain in this chapter. He never pretends believers will not collide. Families do, teams do, churches do. His grief is the venue. Two brothers marched their quarrel into Corinth's forum and let a city that despised their Lord hand down the family's verdict, and whatever that verdict was, the loss was already total, because the city did not learn who was right. It learned that Jesus' people fight like everyone else. Remember what a team jersey teaches. The name on the back is yours. The name on the front belongs to everybody, and it is the only one the crowd can read from the stands. You can win the argument and stain that name, or take the loss and keep it clean. The captain only ever cares about the front of the jersey. Today’s World The Fight Two of Every Five Websites Watched WordPress is the free software quietly running roughly two of every five websites on earth, built over twenty years by a worldwide community of volunteers who mostly liked each other. Then, in September 2024, at the community's own flagship conference, WordPress's co-founder stood on stage and publicly declared war on one of the ecosystem's biggest hosting companies, WP Engine, calling it "a cancer to WordPress" in a dispute over trademarks and contributions. Within weeks the fight was everywhere the public could see it. Blocked access that stranded thousands of sites, a federal lawsuit, a court injunction, banned contributors, resignations, and a running stream of blog posts and interviews. An independent timeline that tracks the conflict had logged 74 separate events by early 2026, with the case still grinding through court. Meanwhile the trackers that measure such things recorded a turn of their own. WordPress's long-growing share of the web has been slipping across the same stretch, a fact the usage charts report without explaining. Here is the detail worth sitting with. Almost nobody watching ever learned the merits. Whether the original grievance was righteous is a question the internet never answered, because it never asked. What the watching world saw was simpler and worse, the family that built the open web tearing at itself in public. No tracker can prove what the fight has cost the platform, and a slipping market share can have many causes. But a witness does not wait on proof. That is Paul's grief in Corinth, updated. When brothers take the family quarrel to a venue the world can watch, the world does not learn who was right. It learns that the name on the front cannot hold its own house together. You can win the case and lose the witness. Twenty years of trust can shrink in one keynote. Sources wpvswpe.report (independent timeline, updated March 2026), W3Techs WordPress vs WP Engine Conflict Timeline: Complete History. wpvswpe.report (independent timeline, updated March 2026), 2026. Read the source. Usage Statistics and Market Share of WordPress (usage trend, share of all websites). W3Techs, 2026. Read the source. Christ at the center The most Jesus-shaped sentence in this chapter is a question nobody wants to ask. Why not rather be wronged? (1 Corinthians 6:7). Paul dares to suggest that losing on purpose can be the most Christian move on the table, and he learned that from his Lord. Jesus once refused to arbitrate an inheritance fight between brothers, asking who had appointed Him their judge (Luke 12:14), and then went on to do something far stranger than judging. He absorbed the loss Himself. Falsely accused, He offered no defense. Entitled to armies of angels, He took the nails. The only man who ever deserved to win every case chose to be wronged, cheated, and condemned, and that unjust verdict is the reason we can be called justified at all. Paul tips the same irony toward Corinth, reminding them that the saints will one day judge the world and even angels (1 Corinthians 6:2, 1 Corinthians 6:3). People with that future can afford to lose a property dispute. The cross does not just forgive our fights. It embarrasses them. Application Name the dispute you are closest to right now, the simmering conflict with another believer, the money someone owes you, the public callout you have half-drafted. Before you take the next step, do the math Paul forces on Corinth. What would it cost you to absorb this wrong, and what will winning it cost the family's witness? Then take one concrete de-escalating step today. Propose a mediator you both trust, make the phone call instead of the post, or decide, in writing, what you are willing to lose to keep a brother. Discussion Question "Where are you in a standoff with another believer right now, and who is the audience watching you fight it (a comment section, a family text thread, the coworkers who hear your side first)? And in that one specific conflict, what would it actually cost you to take Paul's question seriously, why not rather be wronged?" Closing Prayer Father, we confess how much we like to win. We keep score in our churches, our marriages, our group chats, and we can turn even Your family into a courtroom when we feel shortchanged. Forgive us for the fights we have staged in front of a watching world, and for the times we made unbelievers the referees of Your household. Remind us who we are, washed, sanctified, justified, not because we won our case but because Jesus lost His on purpose, for us. Give us one wise friend when conflict comes, the humility to sit down with them, and the strange courage to be wronged rather than to wound. Guard Your church's name in our neighborhoods this week, and let the way we handle our worst disagreements make somebody curious about our Lord. In Jesus' name, Amen.
docs.2026-07-22.html: In brief Somewhere in Corinth a believer is quoting slogans over dinner. Food for the stomach, the stomach for food, the body is just appetite hardware, so what you do with it means nothing. Paul answers with the strangest sentence in the whole argument. The body is for the Lord, and the Lord is for the body. Then he stacks three facts underneath it, you were washed, you are members of Christ, you are a temple of the Spirit. Your body is not a shell you happen to use. It is a place God lives. Yesterday Yesterday ended with a list and a caption. Sexually immoral, idolaters, thieves, greedy, that is what some of you were, and then the caption, not anymore. You were washed. But anyone who has carried a strong habit into a new life knows the morning-after question. If I am washed, why does the old pull still feel so loud? Today Paul answers with the word underneath this entire week. Sanctification. Not a rule book bolted onto grace, but the Spirit's slow, deliberate work of setting a whole person apart for God. The antidote to a corrupted culture was never going to be willpower. It is belonging, worked all the way down into the body. Historical Context The Philosophers Called the Body a Tomb Somewhere at a Corinthian dinner party, a man with a cup of wine is explaining the universe. The real you, he says, is the soul. The body is a costume, a tomb the soul is locked inside until death finally opens the door. Greek thought had played variations on that tune for centuries, the spirit noble, matter beneath notice. And the doctrine came with a convenient corollary. If the body is just temporary packaging, then what you do with it is spiritually beside the point. Some thinkers took that logic toward harsh self-denial, starving the costume to free the soul. Corinth, being Corinth, mostly took it the other direction. Feed the appetite, visit the brothel, follow the urge. The soul stays clean. The meat does what meat does. Half the church's slogans in this letter are that philosophy wearing Christian clothes. Food for the stomach and the stomach for food. Everything is permissible for me. The new converts had carried the city's body-shrug right through the baptistry with them, and it was quietly licensing everything from the scandal to the brothel visits Paul is about to name. That is why his counterattack sounds so physical. Bodies washed. Bodies joined to Christ. Bodies indwelt by the Spirit. Scripture refuses to treat flesh as packaging, because God does not save souls out of bodies. He redeems people, and people come embodied. In a city that called the body a tomb, Paul called it a temple. Only one of those gets cleaned for company. Into the Word Why did one church generate this many problems? A scandal, lawsuits, brothel visits, and more questions waiting in line. Paul's diagnosis is not that Corinth was uniquely wicked. It is that the church had misread its own freedom. So before he finishes his argument about the body, we step sideways into a letter he wrote to another young church breathing the same Greek air (1 Thessalonians 4:1-8). There Paul lays out the antidote in a single word, and the word is not willpower. It is God's own will for every believer, worked by God's own Spirit. Sanctification. 1 Thessalonians 4:1-8 Open ↗ 1Finally, brothers, we ask and encourage you in the Lord Jesus to live in a way that is pleasing to God, just as you have received from us. This is how you already live, so you should do so all the more. 2For you know the instructions we gave you by the authority of the Lord Jesus. 3For it is God’s will that you should be holy: You must abstain from sexual immorality; 4each of you must know how to control his own body in holiness and honor, 5not in lustful passion like the Gentiles who do not know God; 6and no one should ever violate or exploit his brother in this regard, because the Lord will avenge all such acts, as we have already told you and solemnly warned you. 7For God has not called us to impurity, but to holiness. 8Anyone, then, who rejects this command does not reject man but God, the very One who gives you His Holy Spirit. Thessalonica was not Corinth, but it marinated in the same assumptions, which is why these instructions travel so well. At the center sits a sentence worth memorizing. This is God's will, your sanctification. The word is hagiasmos, Greek for being set apart, the ongoing work of making someone holy, and notice whose project it is. God wills it, God empowers it, God gives you His own Holy Spirit for it. What He asks reads almost embarrassingly practical, keep away from sexual immorality, learn to govern your own body in holiness and honor, refuse the lustful autopilot of people who do not know God. Knowing God changes what desire is allowed to drive. And Paul adds a line our culture forgets, that sexual sin always takes advantage of somebody, a brother, a sister, a future spouse, a person reduced to fuel. So rejecting all this, he finishes, is not rejecting a preacher's opinion. It is rejecting the God who moved in. Now back to Corinth, where freedom had gone feral. Some believers reasoned that since the gospel set them free, they were free to do anything, and they had slogans to prove it. Just as the stomach was made for food, they said, the body was made for sex (1 Corinthians 6:13). Paul calls that a misuse of the gift. Christ frees us from the law of sin (Romans 8:2), and that freedom is not an opening for the flesh but a call to serve one another in love (Galatians 5:13). Set free from sin, Scripture says, we became servants of righteousness, bound to God, with sanctification as the payoff (Romans 6:18, Romans 6:22). Free was never the same as unclaimed. The body is for the Lord, and the Lord is for the body, and the rest of the chapter (1 Corinthians 6) unpacks that one claim three ways. 1 Corinthians 6:11 Open ↗ And that is what some of you were. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God. First way, you were washed. Paul has just read Corinth its own rap sheet (1 Corinthians 6:9-10), and half the church is on it. Then come three verbs that changed everything, washed, sanctified, justified, and all three arrive in the passive voice. You did not scrub yourself clean, set yourself apart, or argue your own acquittal. It was done to you, in the name of the Lord Jesus and by the Spirit of our God. That is why the immorality Paul spends this chapter dismantling (1 Corinthians 6:12-20) has no place left to live. Not because God is stingy with pleasure, but because those behaviors belong to a person who no longer exists. The washing was real. The only honest thing left is to live like it. 1 Corinthians 6:15 Open ↗ Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I then take the members of Christ and unite them with a prostitute? Never! Second way, your body is a limb of Christ. Not your soul on Sundays, your body, the hands and skin and nervous system reading this sentence. Union with Jesus runs that deep, one spirit with Him (1 Corinthians 6:17). Which is why Paul asks the question that made Corinth flinch. Take a part of Christ's body and join it to a prostitute? Absolutely not, the strongest no he knows how to write. Sex, Scripture insists, is never casual contact between shells. It makes two people one body, the very words spoken over the first marriage (1 Corinthians 6:16). There is no version of following an appetite somewhere that Jesus is not carried along, because the third way says it plainest, your body is a temple of His Spirit, bought at a price (1 Corinthians 6:19-20). So offer it, all of it, as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God (Romans 12:1). Worship was never just a soul activity. Street Level The Collar Was Never the Cage The gate gets left open one morning, and the dog is gone before anyone notices. For the first twenty minutes it is glorious. No fence, no leash, nobody saying no. He tears down three streets with his ears back, drunk on it. But watch what that freedom does to him by late afternoon. He is miles past anything he recognizes, thirsty, footsore, flinching at traffic. By dark he is shaking under a stranger's porch, and the liberty that felt like flying at nine in the morning feels exactly like being lost. Because that is what it was. Meanwhile, two neighborhoods over, a family is driving slow with the windows down, calling his name into the dark. Corinth's slogans were an open gate. Everything is permissible for me, the body is only appetite, run wherever it pulls. Paul answers with a collar. You are not your own. You were bought at a price. And before that sounds confining, remember what a collar actually is. Not the cage. The claim. The tag on it tells the whole world that somebody loves this one, somebody paid for him, and if he turns up lost there is a home to call. Nobody looks at a dog with no claim on him and calls him free. They call him a stray. Appetite promises open country and delivers the far porch, shaking in the dark. But the Owner who bought you is already in the street with the windows down, calling your name. Freedom was never the absence of a master. It is belonging to the One who comes looking. Today’s World The Revolution Ended in a Famine For fifty years the culture has been running something very like Corinth's experiment at national scale, dismantling boundary after boundary around sex on one promise, that a body freed from covenant would finally be satisfied. The numbers coming back are strange. Analyzing the 2024 General Social Survey, researchers at the Institute for Family Studies reported in 2025 that the share of American adults having sex even once a week has fallen from 55 percent in 1990 to 37 percent today, a level the researchers call a record low. Among adults under thirty, one in four reported no sex at all in the past year, double the rate of 2010. Whatever else the era of fewer rules has delivered, more sex is not on the list. And buried in the data sits the punchline nobody ordered. The people having the most sex are the married ones, the folks who signed the lifelong covenant the culture kept calling a cage. Paul heard Corinth's slogan, food for the stomach and the body for sex, and answered that a body is not appetite hardware. It is a temple, built for union and belonging, joined to Christ Himself. The researchers themselves point to prosaic suspects for the decline, fewer marriages, less face-to-face social life, more hours alone with screens. A survey can count the retreat. It cannot rule on the cause, and honesty says so out loud. But read the trend from Paul's side of the argument and it looks like a parable, a culture that learned to treat bodies like hardware, swiped, rated, and returned, quietly losing its appetite for the very thing it deregulated. The design was never a restriction on joy. It was the address of it. The ancient claim is aging very well. Source Institute for Family Studies The Sex Recession: The Share of Americans Having Regular Sex Keeps Dropping. Institute for Family Studies, 2025. Read the source. Christ at the center If the body were really just packaging, God would never have worn one. That is the doctrine that detonates every body-shrug philosophy in Corinth, and it is the heartbeat under this whole chapter. The Word became flesh. Jesus did not beam truth down from a safe spiritual distance. He took on lungs, hunger, fingerprints, and fatigue, and when they demanded a sign from Him, He pointed at Himself and called His own body the temple (John 2:19-21). Destroy it, He said, and in three days I will raise it. He meant it literally. Easter morning did not release Jesus from His body. It raised that body, scars included, and He wears it still. Heaven judged human flesh worth keeping forever. So when Paul tells you that your body is a temple, he is not flattering you. He is tracing your body's dignity straight back to the Man who bought it with His. The cross was a bodily act. So is following Him. Application Pick the one bodily arena where your private logic still runs on my body, my business, what you eat or drink, what you look at late at night, how you treat sleep, how you treat touch. Today, deliberately present that exact arena to God as worship. Say it in plain words, this body is Yours, bought at a price, and then live the next hour like it is true. If it helps, write bought at a price where you will see it all week, on the mirror, the lock screen, the dashboard. Discussion Question "Where in your life has the world's body-logic quietly set the rules, it is my body, it is natural, everyone does it (what you consume, what you watch, who you let define your worth)? And if that one area really is a temple where the Spirit lives, what is the first piece of furniture that would have to move?" Closing Prayer Father, we bring You our actual bodies today, the tired ones, the aging ones, the ones we have criticized in mirrors and misused in the dark. Thank You that You do not deal in souls only, that Your Son wore flesh, that Your Spirit chose these bodies for a home. We confess the places we have lived like tenants with no landlord, feeding appetites and calling it freedom. Wash us again in what You have already declared over us, washed, sanctified, justified. Where the old habits shout, let Your quiet ownership be louder. Teach us to govern our own bodies in holiness and honor, not as a performance for You but as worship with You. And for everyone among us carrying sexual regret, speak the old word over them once more today. Clean. In Jesus' name, Amen.
docs.2026-07-23.html: In brief A slave in Egypt is cornered day after day by his master's wife, and one afternoon she grabs his coat. Joseph leaves it in her fist and runs. A thousand years later, Paul hands a tempted church the same strategy in one word. Flee. Not negotiate, not linger, not prove how strong you are. Run. Then he opens the church's letter about marriage and answers with a design worth honoring, mutual, faithful, and unashamed. Flee what would defile the temple, and honor the home God built for desire. Yesterday Yesterday stacked up three facts about a believer's body. Washed clean, joined to Christ, and occupied by His Spirit. Beautiful doctrine, but every reader knows the next morning's question. What do I actually do when desire pulls against all three? Today Paul gets ruthlessly practical. His strategy has two verbs, and neither one is complicated. Flee what would burn the temple down. Honor the design God built for desire to flourish in. One verb for the ambush, one verb for the architecture. And behind both stands a church that had written Paul a letter full of real questions about marriage, singleness, and sex, proof that these conversations belong inside the family of God, not exiled from it.
