Long fuse, kindness, no scorekeeping, not seeking your own, whichever one names the place your love goes thin. Then aim it at one person before the day ends. Answer the slow text without the edge. Do the kind thing for the family member who irritates you fastest. Tear up one grudge you have been keeping in the drawer. One verb, one person, on purpose. That is how a feeling becomes a way. Discussion Question "Which of love's fifteen verbs breaks down first in your closest relationships (the long fuse in traffic with your family, keeping no record in your marriage, not seeking your own with friends)? And what would practicing that single verb on one specific person look like this week?" Closing Prayer Lord Jesus, we have wanted the gifts more than the love, and we confess it. We have practiced our abilities and left our patience unrehearsed. We have kept records You died to erase. Today Your word read us, verb by verb, and we felt where our sentences break. Thank You for being the portrait we could not paint, patient with us, kind to us, keeping no record against us. Now write those verbs into our reflexes. Give us the long fuse at home, where it is hardest. Give us kindness that costs something before sundown. Where our gifts have been making noise, wire them to love until they start making disciples. We do not ask to feel more loving. We ask to love, the way You love us, until the feeling catches up. In Jesus' name, Amen.
docs.2026-08-05.html: In brief Across the gulf from Corinth, pilgrims paid to hear a priestess whose answers needed official interpreters, because in that world the stranger the speech, the stronger the god. Corinth's church dragged that scale into worship and cranked its loudest gift. Paul honors the gift itself, real languages given by the Spirit, and then takes the scale away. Words nobody understands build nobody up. So speak to be understood, take turns, let someone interpret, keep the gathering in order. God has never tried to sound impressive. He wants to be understood, because understanding is how love builds. Yesterday Yesterday love got its fifteen verbs, and the chapter ended with the only measure that matters. Not how a gift sounds, but what it builds. Today that measure meets its first real test case, the gift Corinth had turned up the loudest. Tongues had become the congregation's showpiece, the proof of spirituality, the sound that filled the living room whether anyone understood it or not. Paul walks in carrying yesterday's chapter like a level against a crooked wall. Love is patient, love is kind, and love asks one question of every word spoken in worship. Did that build the person beside you? Historical Context The Priestess Nobody Could Understand A day's journey from Corinth, on the slopes across the gulf, sat the most famous religious address in the Greek world. Delphi. Kings and farmers alike queued there to put their questions to the god Apollo, and the answers came through a woman seated on a tripod in the temple's inner room. What came out of her was not conversation. Ancient writers describe utterances that had to pass through the shrine's official interpreters before a pilgrim could carry them home, and the arrangement bothered nobody. Just the opposite. In that world, speech you could not follow was the whole point. The ecstatic cults that danced through Corinth's own streets ran on the same instinct, frenzied cries, clashing cymbals, language dissolving as the god took over. Losing intelligibility was the proof of contact. Now picture Corinth's converts, raised on that scale, walking into Christian worship. When a brother stood and poured out praise in a language nobody present knew, every pagan-trained nerve in the room said the same thing. This must be the peak. The stranger the speech, the stronger the spirit. Paul spends a whole chapter dismantling that scale, because the God of Israel has always been the talking God, the One who speaks in order to be heard. Paul would rather say five understandable words than ten thousand nobody can follow (1 Corinthians 14:19). In Corinth's religion, mystery was the product. In Christ's church, meaning is. Into the Word So what about tongues? Of all the gifts on this week's lists, this is the one the Corinthians pushed to the front and the one that still stirs the most questions. Paul refuses both easy exits. He will not despise the gift, and he will not let it run the room. Today's passage watches him do something harder than either, honor a true gift while retraining an entire congregation on what worship is for. His argument starts with what the gift actually is, and it ends with two or three sentences of house rules that still hold. Begin where the gift began. Jesus promised that new tongues would follow the gospel out into the world (Mark 16:17), and at Pentecost the promise landed with an audience. Visitors from a dozen nations heard Galilean fishermen declaring the magnificent acts of God, each in his own native language (Acts 2:1-13). The same sign fell at a Roman officer's house (Acts 10:44-48) and on a handful of disciples in Ephesus (Acts 19:6). In line with those scenes, the tongues of 1 Corinthians are best understood as the Spirit-granted ability to speak real languages the speaker never learned. The gift was a bridge to human ears, never a fog machine. Now watch how much ink Paul gives it. Tongues appears in the gift list (1 Corinthians 12:8-10), in the ranked catalog (1 Corinthians 12:28) with its own rhetorical question (1 Corinthians 12:30), and twice in the love chapter (1 Corinthians 13:1, 1 Corinthians 13:8). Then chapter fourteen says the word tongue fifteen times, more than the rest of the letter combined, and even reaches for a rare term for foreign speech drawn from the prophets (1 Corinthians 14:21). Writers linger where the wound is. The gift was real, and its misuse was tipping public worship into disorder and confusion. 1 Corinthians 14:9 Open ↗ So it is with you. Unless you speak intelligible words with your tongue, how will anyone know what you are saying? You will just be speaking into the air. Speaking into the air. It is one of Paul's bluntest images, a room full of sound and not one syllable arriving anywhere. His logic is almost embarrassingly simple. Words exist to be known. A flute has to hold a melody, a trumpet has to sound the right call, and a mouth has to make meaning, or the noise benefits exactly no one (1 Corinthians 14:6). This is why Paul insists the gift of tongues travel with its partner gift, interpretation, and why he tells the tongue-speaker to pray for the ability to interpret (1 Corinthians 14:13). He is not criticizing the gift. He is refusing to let a bridge be used as a wall. Sound that never becomes meaning is not deep. It is weather. 1 Corinthians 14:26 Open ↗ What then shall we say, brothers? When you come together, everyone has a psalm or a teaching, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation. All of these must be done to build up the church. Here is the sentence that governs the whole chapter, and the word carrying it is the Greek oikodomē, the ordinary term for putting up a building, a house going up beam by beam. Everything in the gathering exists to raise the house. Notice first what Paul does not say. He does not cancel the participatory service. Each one still arrives carrying something, a hymn, a teaching, a revelation, a tongue, an interpretation, the same crowded living room we walked into on Sabbath. The variety stays. What changes is the test every contribution must pass at the door. Not, is it impressive. Not even, is it real. Does it build? A gathering is a construction site, and love reads every gift like a work order. Whatever you carried in this week, it was meant to leave a wall taller than it found it. 1 Corinthians 14:27 Open ↗ If anyone speaks in a tongue, two, or at most three, should speak in turn, and someone must interpret. Paul gets astonishingly practical. Two, or at the most three. Each in turn. Someone interprets, or the speaker stays quiet and speaks to God privately. You can feel the Corinthian service reshaping around those instructions, volume giving way to order, performance giving way to communication. And tucked inside the rules sits a correction the church has needed ever since. Paul wished everyone had this gift (1 Corinthians 14:5), yet the Spirit gives it to some and not others, exactly as He decides (1 Corinthians 12:10). So no believer's baptism in the Spirit is ever proven or disproven by this one gift. And the gift itself still walks among us in its plainest clothes. The member who can welcome a visitor in her own language, or carry the gospel across a counter in a second tongue, is holding the Corinthian gift the way Pentecost held it. As a bridge. 1 Corinthians 14:40 Open ↗ But everything must be done in a proper and orderly manner. The chapter closes with eight words that have steadied two thousand years of church services. Order is not the enemy of the Spirit. Order is His signature, for God is not a God of disorder but of peace (1 Corinthians 14:33). Paul has already imagined the alternative, a visitor stepping into wall-to-wall uninterpreted tongues and concluding the church is out of its mind (1 Corinthians 14:23). Chaos costs souls. But order, taking turns, making sense, leaving room, is love wearing its work clothes, the same care for one another that Monday's body required. A service a stranger can walk into and understand is not less spiritual than a dazzling one. It is more, because the Spirit who fills the room is the same Spirit who wants the stranger home. Street Level Every Announcement Was True and You Were Still Lost Land in an airport where you do not speak the language and you find out what it feels like to drown in accurate information. The ceiling speakers never rest. Gate changes, boarding calls, final warnings, all of it real, all of it urgent, none of it landing. Somewhere in that river of sound is your name, your flight, your one chance at the connection, and you cannot find it. A whole crowd stands up and moves and you do not know whether to follow. Then a gate agent looks at the boarding pass shaking in your hand, points down the corridor, and says four words in rough English. Other gate. B4. Run. You will remember her face for the rest of your life. That is the scene Paul is worried about, except the airport is a church. The gift in Corinth was real speech carrying real praise, and Paul never doubts it. He just asks the lost traveler's question. Did it reach anyone? Words that never become meaning cannot build a person, no matter how true they are, and there is always somebody in the room holding a boarding pass. The visitor. The teenager. The friend who has never opened a Bible. Church vocabulary can turn into ceiling speakers, constant, correct, and landing on no one. Love does what the gate agent did. It sees one lost face, drops the fluency, and points. Ten thousand words filled that terminal. Four of them saved your trip. Today’s World The Words That Only Sound Like Sense In 2025 researchers Cruz and Lombrozo published a study in Nature Human Behaviour on what technical language does to the people reading it, and they found something unsettling. Jargon makes a weak explanation feel more complete than it is, masking the gaps so readers walk away satisfied while actually understanding less. The impressive words do not hand over knowledge. They counterfeit the feeling of having received it. Read that next to Paul and the overlap is uncanny. A room can be full of true, technically flawless speech and leave everyone in it a little more lost and a little more sure they are the problem. That is speaking into the air, and it happens in churches every week, not in ancient tongues but in insider vocabulary, in answers pitched over the visitor's head, in words chosen to sound weighty rather than to land. Paul's fix was never to say less that is true. It was to make the truth reach the person in the next chair. Being understood is not a lower calling than sounding profound. In Paul's math it is the higher one, because only the words that actually land can build. Source Nature Human Behaviour How laypeople evaluate scientific explanations containing jargon. Nature Human Behaviour, 2025. Read the source. Christ at the center Translation is not a side project for God. It is His habit. He spoke through prophets in the language of shepherds and kings, and when the time fully came, He did the unthinkable. The Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14), God translating Himself into a life we could read, a face we could watch, hands we could touch. Jesus taught in the dialect of farmers and fishermen. His parables ran on seed, bread, sheep, and lamps, the vocabulary of everybody. When the Spirit came at Pentecost, the first miracle of the church age was a translation miracle, every visitor hearing the mighty works of God in the language their mother sang over their cradle. And the cross speaks the one language that needs no interpreter anywhere on earth, love that gives everything. Corinth wanted a God impressive enough to be incomprehensible. In Jesus, God chose the opposite glory. He has never once spoken over our heads on purpose. Application Today, translate one truth. Take something Jesus means to you and say it in one sentence a twelve-year-old could repeat, no church words allowed. No blessed, no saved, no fellowship. Write the sentence down, then test it out loud on one actual person, a kid, a coworker, the friend who never darkens a church door. If their eyes don't glaze, you built something. If they do, revise and try again tomorrow. Speaking to be understood is not dumbing it down. It is love doing carpentry. Discussion Question "Where does your faith-talk most often turn into speaking into the air, true words that land on nobody (insider vocabulary around guests, answers to questions nobody asked, volume where clarity was needed)? And who in your life needs one truth about God translated into their language this week, whether that means Spanish, teenager, or plain English?" Closing Prayer Father, thank You for being the God who speaks to be heard. You could have stayed incomprehensible, and instead You sent prophets, then Your Son, plain enough for fishermen and children and us. Forgive us for the times our worship and our witness have been sound aimed at nobody, words that impressed the room and built no one in it. Teach us the difference between reverence and fog. Where our congregations gather, give us order that welcomes the stranger, turns taken in love, and every voice raising the same house. Give the members among us who carry second languages a holy restlessness for the people who need You in exactly those words. And keep us from ever measuring Your Spirit by volume. We would rather say five words that land than ten thousand that echo. In Jesus' name, Amen.
docs.2026-08-06.html: In brief A traveling stranger stands at the church door claiming to speak for God, and the first believers kept a rule book ready, because this gift was too precious to abandon and too easy to fake. Paul ranks prophecy above the gifts Corinth loved loudest, then defines it by what it does to people. Strengthening. Encouragement. Consolation. Scripture supplies the tests for anyone claiming it, words that come true, agreement with what God already said, a life that looks like Christ, fruit that feeds. God still speaks to build His people, and every voice claiming His name gets measured against His Book. Yesterday Yesterday closed with a service a stranger could finally walk into, tongues taken in turn, someone interpreting, everything raising the house. But turning one gift's volume down was never Paul's whole project. All along he has been clearing the floor for a different gift, the one the Corinthians kept shoving to the back while chasing the showpiece. Prophecy. Every time Paul compared the two, the comparison tilted the same direction, and today we find out why. The gift Corinth neglected is the one that speaks to people for their strengthening. The loudest room in Corinth was starving for the quieter gift. Historical Context Every Road Had a Prophet on It The first-century Mediterranean was crawling with people who spoke for the gods, at a price. Oracle-mongers worked the festival crowds with books of ready-made predictions. Dream interpreters set up tables in the market. And once the gospel began to spread, a new figure appeared on the roads between churches, the traveling Christian prophet, arriving at the door with a greeting in the Lord's name and, sometimes, an appetite. Most were sincere. Enough were not. The young churches faced a problem Israel had known for a thousand years, wrapped in fresh clothes. What do you do when a stranger says, God sent me? One of the earliest Christian handbooks outside the New Testament, written close enough to the apostles to remember them, answers with rules so practical they still make you smile. A visiting prophet who stays three days without working is false. A prophet who orders a meal in a trance and then eats it himself is false. A prophet whose life does not match the Lord's ways is false, however impressive the words. The early church was not being cynical. It was being biblical, reaching back to the tests Moses and the prophets had already written. Prophecy was too precious to throw away and too dangerous to leave unweighed. So the church did what love always does with precious things. It refused to abandon the gift, and it refused to stop testing it. Into the Word Say the word prophecy and most people picture a crystal ball with a religious paint job, someone predicting next year's headlines. Scripture's picture is at once bigger and closer to home. Today's passages, Paul's definition of the gift (1 Corinthians 14:3) and the risen Christ's staffing plan for His church (Ephesians 4:11-13), show a gift that has less to do with forecasting the future and everything to do with carrying God's voice to people who need it now. Notice first where prophecy sits in Paul's mind. In list after list it comes before tongues (1 Corinthians 12:10, 1 Corinthians 12:28), even among the gifts that will one day retire (1 Corinthians 13:8). And when tongues does get named first, the order only sharpens the contrast. The uninterpreted tongue builds its own speaker while prophecy builds the church (1 Corinthians 14:4). Paul would rather the whole congregation prophesied (1 Corinthians 14:5). A visit full of impressive sound profits nothing next to a word of revelation or teaching (1 Corinthians 14:6), and even as signs the two gifts serve different audiences (1 Corinthians 14:22). The gift Corinth benched was the one Paul kept moving to the front. 1 Corinthians 14:3 Open ↗ But he who prophesies speaks to men for their edification, encouragement, and comfort. Here is the gift defined by its fruit, and not one item on the list is a prediction. Strengthening, encouragement, consolation. The Greek verb behind the gift, prophēteuō, can mean to say something in advance, but just as often it means to say something on behalf of someone else, and Scripture uses it both ways. Peter says David spoke in advance, foreseeing the resurrection (Acts 2:29-31), the same pattern as the Lord who does nothing without revealing His counsel to His servants the prophets (Amos 3:7). But when Judas and Silas are called prophets, their prophesying looks like encouraging and strengthening the brothers with many words (Acts 15:32). Prophecy is less about predicting the future and more about how to live in the present. It is God's voice arriving through a person, aimed at the exact place another person is buckling. Ephesians 4:11-13 Open ↗ 11And it was He who gave some to be apostles, some to be prophets, some to be evangelists, and some to be pastors and teachers, 12to equip the saints for works of ministry and to build up the body of Christ, 13until we all reach unity in the faith and in the knowledge of the Son of God, as we mature to the full measure of the stature of Christ. Look at the word until. The ascended Christ gave these gifts, prophets included, with an expiration condition attached, and the condition is not the death of the last apostle. It is the church reaching unity in the faith, maturity, the full stature of Christ. Look around. We are not there. So the gifts were never meant to retire in the first century, and Peter said as much at Pentecost, the promise is for you and for your children and for all who are far off, as many as the Lord our God will call (Acts 2:39). A church that assumes God went silent after the apostles has misread the delivery schedule. The scaffolding stays up until the building is finished. The building is not finished. 1 John 4:1-3 Open ↗ 1Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God. For many false prophets have gone out into the world. 2By this you will know the Spirit of God: Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, 3and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God. This is the spirit of the antichrist, which you have heard is coming and which is already in the world at this time. An ongoing gift demands an ongoing filter, and Scripture hands us four tests that work together. First, the words come true. A prophet whose unconditional predictions fail was never sent (Deuteronomy 18:22), the standard Jeremiah threw down when Hananiah promised easy peace (Jeremiah 28:8), let the fulfillment identify the sent one (Jeremiah 28:9). Second, the message agrees with what God already said. Even a wonder-worker who tugs people toward other gods fails (Deuteronomy 13:1-3), for if they do not speak according to the law and the testimony, there is no dawn in them (Isaiah 8:20). Third, the life confesses Christ, here in John's test. Fourth, the fruit feeds somebody, for you will recognize them by their fruit (Matthew 7:15-20). Test the spirits is a command, not a suggestion. So is the word that comes right before it. Dear friends. Revelation 19:10 Open ↗ So I fell at his feet to worship him. But he told me, “Do not do that! I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers who rely on the testimony of Jesus. Worship God! For the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.” The Bible's last book will not let prophecy fade into history. When the dragon makes war on God's people at the end, they are identified by two marks, keeping the commandments of God and holding firmly to the testimony of Jesus (Revelation 12:17), and the angel defines that second mark in today's verse. The testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy. God's people at history's close are a prophecy-marked people, still strengthened, encouraged, and consoled by His voice. History bears the pattern out. Whenever God's people have needed guiding, He has kept His promise to reveal His counsel, and every voice that has ever claimed the gift, in any century including ours, stands before the same four tests and points to the same Person. The gift never outgrows its job description. It speaks for Jesus, about Jesus, toward Jesus. Anything else is just noise wearing a robe. Street Level The Question Only the Real One Can Answer The phone rings at two in the morning and it is your son's voice. Not a voice like his. His. The crack in it, the way he says Mom, the panic. There has been an accident, he needs money wired now, please do not tell Dad. Except it is not him. With a few seconds of audio lifted from a video online, cheap software can now wear a loved one's voice like a mask, convincingly enough to fool the people who raised that voice from a whisper. So families have started doing something almost old-fashioned. They agree on a code word at the kitchen table, ahead of time, a question no stranger could ever mine from the internet. When the desperate call comes, you ask it. Panic can be faked. Tears can be faked. The voice itself can be faked. The answer agreed on in advance cannot. Voices claiming to come from God still arrive all the time, from pulpits, podcasts, and confident friends, and Scripture treats them the way those families treat the phone. You do not swallow every voice, because fakes exist and they are skilled. You do not stop answering either, because some calls really are from home, and God still speaks to strengthen, encourage, and console His people. You test, against the standard written down long before the phone rang. The words come true. The message agrees with what He already said. The life behind the voice confesses Christ. The fruit feeds somebody. And there is one tell that settles most calls on the spot. A voice that really comes from your Father's house is never offended that you checked. Today’s World The Year the Fakes Got Pulled In 2023 the scientific world set a grim record. More than 10,000 published research papers were retracted in a single year, the most ever counted. More than 8,000 of them came from the journals of a single publisher, Hindawi. Behind the number sat an industry of counterfeit knowledge, paper mills that sell bogus studies and even authorships to order, and peer review that had been compromised or manipulated to wave the fakes through. Many wore the outward costume of real science, the citations, the confident tone, and still slipped past the editors who should have caught them. What gives them away is patient testing against a fixed standard. The counterfeits leave tells, incoherent text, references that have nothing to do with the argument, and tortured phrases twisted just enough to slip past plagiarism software, along with signs that a paper was quietly written by AI. Catch the tells and the costume falls off. That is precisely the posture Scripture asks of the church toward every voice that claims to speak for God. Do not swallow it because it sounds authoritative, and do not dismiss it because fakes exist. Test it, against the words God has already given, against the life behind it, against whether it actually strengthens and feeds anyone. A true word survives the checking. A counterfeit only survives until someone looks closely. Source Nature More than 10,000 research papers were retracted in 2023 — a new record. Nature, 2023. Read the source. Christ at the center The angel's definition settles what prophecy is for. The testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy, which means every true prophetic word ever spoken has been carrying Him. On the road to Emmaus, the risen Christ walked two discouraged disciples through Moses and all the Prophets and interpreted for them the things concerning Himself (Luke 24:27), a Bible study proving the whole prophetic tradition had one subject. He is also prophecy's fulfillment in person, the Prophet like Moses that God promised to raise up (Deuteronomy 18:15), and more than a prophet, the Son in whom God has spoken His final word (Hebrews 1:1-2). That is why the tests all point one direction. Does the voice agree with His word, confess His flesh-and-blood coming, produce His fruit? Prophecy that strengthens, encourages, and consoles is simply Jesus still doing with human mouths what He did on that road, coming alongside the buckling and setting their hearts on fire with Himself. Application Practice the gift's job description today at its street level. Think of one person who is buckling, the friend waiting on test results, the parent running on fumes, the member nobody has seen in a month. Speak to them on God's behalf, one sentence of strengthening, encouragement, or consolation anchored to something God actually said. Not advice. Not a prediction. Something like, God has not forgotten you, and He finishes what He starts. Send it, say it, or write it before the day ends. Discussion Question "When someone claims to speak for God today, what is your honest reflex, swallowing it whole or dismissing it outright (the podcast prophet, the viral prediction, the friend who says God told them something)? And how would applying Scripture's four tests, fulfillment, agreement with the Bible, a Christ-confessing life, and fruit that feeds, change what you do with the next claim that reaches you?" Closing Prayer Father, thank You for being a God who still talks. You revealed Your counsel to Your servants the prophets, You spoke Your final word in Your Son, and You have promised Your church every gift it needs until the building is finished. Forgive us for the two ways we mishandle Your voice. Sometimes we swallow every confident claim because it thrills us, and sometimes we dismiss the whole gift because fakes have burned us. Teach us instead to test, patiently, by Your word, Your Son, and the fruit. Guard Your church from voices that flatter and voices that frighten but never feed. And make us carriers of the real thing this week, mouths You can trust with strengthening, encouragement, and consolation for the people buckling beside us. Let every word we pass along point to Jesus, because that is what Your voice has always done. In Jesus' name, Amen.
docs.2026-08-07.html: Week in Review This week Paul walked into the loudest living room in Corinth and reintroduced the church to itself, one Spirit handing out many gifts, one body wearing many parts, love as the only current strong enough to run any of it, and every word in worship aimed at raising the house. ☩Sabbath: Spiritual Gifts. In a borrowed living room humming with gifts and rivalry, Paul issued the week's command, chase love first, then welcome every gift the Spirit gives. ☩Sunday: Varieties of Gifts. The Spirit's first gift is the nerve to say Jesus is Lord in Caesar's world, and behind that confession comes a catalog of grace gifts handed out exactly as He decides. ☩Monday: Unity Through Diversity. Against a city that filled temple shelves with clay body parts, Paul insisted the church is a living body, every part arranged by God and the weakest ones indispensable. ☩Tuesday: A More Excellent Way. Without love the grandest gifts are Corinthian bronze, expensive noise, so Paul measured love in fifteen verbs and crowned it greater than everything it carries. ☩Wednesday: The Gift of Tongues. Real languages from the Spirit were being fired into the air, so Paul aimed the gift back at meaning, two or three, each in turn, interpreted, everything building up. ☩Thursday: The Gift of Prophecy. The neglected gift speaks for God to strengthen, encourage, and console, it runs until the church is finished, and every claim to it faces Scripture's tests. Historical Context One Room, Every Gift Step back and the whole week happened in one room. Outside its door, an empire ran on the phrase Caesar is lord, and advancement belonged to whoever said it loudest. Up the hill, a healing god's shrine displayed its shelves of clay hands and feet, perfect parts with no body. Down in the foundries, the city poured the most expensive noise in the world, and across the gulf a priestess proved that incomprehensible speech could be a growth industry. Along every road walked somebody claiming to speak for heaven. Corinth was not short on spiritual experiences. It was drowning in them, ranked, priced, and performed. And in the middle of all that, a borrowed living room filled up each week with a dock worker, a patron, a slave, a seamstress, each one carrying something the Spirit had handed them. Every pressure of the city followed them through the door, the ranking, the volume, the hunger to be impressive. Paul's three chapters were written for exactly that room, and his remedy was not a better performance. It was a body, knit by love, speaking to be understood, testing every voice, building one house. The church did not need to out-shout Corinth. It needed to out-love it. That was true of one living room in AD 55. It has stayed true of every room the church has met in since. What This Week Clarifies Set the six studies side by side and three pairs of truths seem to pull against each other. The Spirit alone decides who gets which gift, yet wanting more is commanded. A room humming with gifts gets handed house rules. The God who still speaks tells His church to test every voice that claims Him. None of the three is a contradiction. Each is the week finishing a thought, and each rewards one slow look before Sabbath. The Signed List Still Says Want More Sunday closed every argument about who earned what. The Spirit hands out the gifts exactly as He decides, and complaining about yours criticizes His judgment. Then Monday's chapter ended with a command that sounds like the opposite. Eagerly desire the greater gifts. The week seems to fix the list with one hand and stir up wanting with the other. 1 Corinthians 12:31 Open ↗ But eagerly desire the greater gifts. And now I will show you the most excellent way. Both sentences are Paul, and the week taught the difference between them. What the Spirit settles is who carries which gift. What the command stirs is a different kind of wanting, aimed at the body instead of the mirror. Corinth desired gifts the way it desired bronze, something bright for the shelf, and that wanting really does argue with the Giver. But a church can also want more the way a family wants a longer table, asking boldly for whatever would let it feed more people. That desire trusts the Spirit's judgment instead of second-guessing it. Paul then tips his hand about the word greater. The most excellent way is about to redefine it from the inside, which is why the gift he moves to the front on Thursday is the one that does the most building. The Spirit signs the distribution. Love writes the wish list. Order Is the Sound of a House Going Up The week opened in a living room humming with gifts, everyone arriving with something, a hymn, a teaching, a prayer in another tongue. It closed with what reads like a set of meeting rules. Two or at most three. Each in turn. Someone must interpret. A reader can feel the temperature drop, as if Paul heard the fire and reached for a clipboard. 1 Corinthians 14:26 Open ↗ What then shall we say, brothers? When you come together, everyone has a psalm or a teaching, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation. All of these must be done to build up the church. Hold the two halves of the sentence together and the worry answers itself. The first half keeps every promise the living room made. Everyone still arrives carrying something, a psalm, a teaching, a revelation, and Paul does not shorten the list by a single item. The second half is the test at the door, and it asks nothing about polish or volume. It asks whether the wall is taller when you sit down. Wednesday showed what fails that test, true words filling a room and landing on no one, a visitor backing out the door convinced the church is out of its mind. So the house rules are not Paul cooling the fire. They are the hearth. Flame loose on the floor burns a house down. The same flame, given a hearth, warms every person in the room. Order is where the heat finally reaches somebody. The Test Begins With the Word Beloved Thursday made two claims that sit awkwardly in the same pew. God still speaks, and His gifts stay until the building is finished. And every voice claiming His name must be tested. Most of us quietly pick one, swallowing every confident word because doubting feels like unbelief, or waving the whole gift away because fakes have burned us. 1 John 4:1-3 Open ↗ 1Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God. For many false prophets have gone out into the world. 2By this you will know the Spirit of God: Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, 3and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God. This is the spirit of the antichrist, which you have heard is coming and which is already in the world at this time. John answers with his opening word. Beloved. The command to test the spirits is family language, not a memo from the fraud department. It is the same instinct that gathers a household at the kitchen table to agree on a code word before any desperate call ever comes. Those families are not cynics. They plan the question precisely because the next voice on the line might really be their son, and because counterfeits have learned to wear the voices they love. Testing and treasuring are one motion. That is why Thursday could hand us four tests without once telling us to stop listening. The words come true. The message agrees with what God already said. The life confesses Christ. The fruit feeds somebody. A church that weighs every voice is not doubting that God speaks. It is guarding the line He speaks on. And the weighing carries a tell that settles most calls quickly. A voice truly sent from the Father's house is never offended that you checked. Tomorrow the room fills again, hymns and teachings and gifts arriving in every pair of hands, and the week has already said what to do with all of it. Want what builds. Take your turn. Test whatever claims His name, with love in your posture and the Book open on your lap. The Giver is not nervous about the checking. He wrote the tests, and He signed the list. Still Speaking The Names at the End of the Movie Stay in your seat when the movie ends sometime. The screen fills with names, hundreds of them, scrolling faster than anyone can read. Gaffers. Riggers. Drivers. The person who kept track of the hero's scarf between takes so the story would not fall apart. You were moved twenty minutes ago because every one of those people did their job, and almost none of them will ever be recognized in a grocery store. The faces on the poster did not make the film. The credits did. The church has always run on credits. One member is a ready speaker, another writes, another prays like the room changes when they start, another sings, another can walk a teenager through a hard verse in plain words, another just shows up with a truck on moving day. The same God works all of it in each person (1 Corinthians 12:6), which means nobody gets to despise the supposedly lesser gifts, least of all in the mirror. Folding your hands because you think you can do no mighty work is not modesty. It is a body volunteering to be shorter one limb. The week's cure for both pride and shrinking is the same motion, eyes off yourself, eyes on your Leader, then do what you can, in meekness, sincerity, and love. And do it together, because none of us carries enough alone. God works through other minds than ours on purpose, and the gifts were designed to blend, like voices, like ingredients, like crew departments, for the building up of the body of Christ (Ephesians 4:12). There will be obstacles. There always are, on every set, in every church. We meet them the way a body does, unitedly, hand in hand. The story God is telling will roll credits longer than anyone expects, and no name on that scroll will have been filler. Bring what you carry. The house is still going up. Christ at the Center of the Week Sabbath opened with a Giver, the ascended Christ stocking His church like a builder stocking a job site before the crew arrives. Sunday handed us His name, Jesus is Lord, the confession no one can truly speak without the Spirit and the first gift every believer already holds. Monday He was the Head, so identified with His body that persecuting the church made Him ask, why are you persecuting Me. Tuesday He was the portrait, fifteen verbs of love that read like a biography because they are one, patient with Peter, kind to lepers, keeping no record from the cross. Wednesday He was the Word translating Himself into our language, God refusing to speak over our heads. Thursday He was the subject of every true prophecy, the testimony of Jesus, the voice on the Emmaus road interpreting the things concerning Himself. A week that began with a question about gifts ends holding one Gift that contains the others. He gave gifts to people because He had already given Himself. Weekend Practice Hold a gift audit this Sabbath, out loud, with your household or a friend from church. Three moves. First, name each other's gifts, especially the ones nobody claps for, and be specific about where you have watched them build somebody. Second, each of you pick one place to spend your gift in the coming week, a person, a task, a corner of the congregation, and say it so someone can ask you about it later. Third, thank God by name for one gift He gave somebody else, without a single word of comparison. Bodies grow where gifts get named, aimed, and celebrated. Closing Prayer for the Week Father, we walked into this week asking which gifts matter and we leave it asking a better question, whether love is running the ones You gave us. Thank You for the Spirit who signed our distribution list, for the body that makes our small parts matter, for the fifteen verbs that showed us Jesus, and for a voice that still strengthens, encourages, and consoles. Forgive us for the rankings we kept, the words we aimed at nobody, the gifts we buried because they seemed small, and the voices we swallowed or dismissed without testing. This Sabbath, gather us like a body and not a crowd. Help us name the gifts in each other out loud, spend our own where You point, and keep every voice in our life under Your Book and aimed at Your Son. We bring what we carry. Raise Your house with it. In Jesus' name, Amen.
docs.2026-08-08.html: In brief The most famous chapter Paul ever wrote was mailed into the middle of a church fight. Corinth is still arguing about whose gift ranks highest when thirteen quiet verses arrive and change the subject. Love is patient. Love is kind. Love never ends. This week we slow down and sit inside 1 Corinthians 13, one movement at a time. What love does. What love refuses to do. Whose face appears when the verbs are read slowly. Love is not one more item on the Christian list. It is the portrait of Jesus, painted in verbs, and we are invited to sit for it. Last week Last week ended in a dark theater, watching credits scroll. Hundreds of names, most of them never recognized anywhere, every one of them necessary, and love was the power source that made the whole body of gifts worth anything. But we only drove past love on Tuesday. We saw what happens when it is missing, the expensive bronze noise, the gifts that add up to nothing. Now Paul makes us park the car and go inside. The current that every gift runs on gets its own week, line by line, verb by verb. Historical Context The Word Greeks Almost Never Used A Corinthian had a word for every kind of love. For desire there was erōs, and the city knew that one well, with the goddess of it enthroned on the mountain above the harbor. For friendship there was philia, the warm loyalty between comrades that Greek writers praised as the crown of a good life. For family there was storgē, the bond of a mother and her child. Three famous words, each one busy, each one bent at least partly toward what the lover gets out of it. And then there was a fourth word, agapē, sitting in the back of the vocabulary. Pale. Rare. Almost nobody used it. It had no famous poems, no temple, no story. That blank word is the one the first Christians picked up. The other three were already spoken for, already shaped by appetite and affection and kinship. So when they needed a name for what they had met in Jesus, a love that chooses, gives, and keeps no accounts, they reached past the famous words and filled the empty one. By the time Paul writes to Corinth, the once-forgettable word is becoming the church's signature. This week he sits down and writes its definition, and the definition will turn out to have a face. The city that had a word for every love is about to learn the one it was missing. This Week’s Memory Text 1 Corinthians 13:13 Open ↗ And now these three remain: faith, hope, and love; but the greatest of these is love. Paul ends his greatest chapter by imagining the end of everything else. Prophecies fulfilled. Tongues quiet. Knowledge outgrown. When the dust of history settles, he says, three things are still standing, and then he ranks them. The greatest is love. The word is agapē, Greek for the love that commits itself and gives, whether or not it is ever paid back. Paul's letters use that word family more than 135 times, nearly half of all its appearances in the entire New Testament, and nowhere does he pour more into it than here. Faith and hope are how we hold on to God. Love is what God is. That is why it outranks even its two immortal companions. The verse also hands us this week's map. We will live inside the whole chapter (1 Corinthians 13), and we will need it, because Jesus warned that in the last days the love of many would grow cold (Matthew 24:12). We will watch love lead the Spirit's harvest in a believer's life (Galatians 5:22, 23), overflow with the grace that found Paul (1 Timothy 1:14), and finally trace back to its source, the God who is love (1 John 4:8). Scripture is crowded with great love passages. Nothing separates us from God's love (Romans 8:35-39). Eye has not seen what God has prepared for those who love Him (1 Corinthians 2:9). The one who loves God is known by Him (1 Corinthians 8:3). The Son of God loved me and gave Himself for me (Galatians 2:20). The Father delivered us into the kingdom of the Son He loves (Colossians 1:13). May the Lord cause you to increase and overflow with love (1 Thessalonians 3:12). And still, nothing compares to the thirteen verses ahead of us. This is the summit of it all. This Week’s Road Map ☩Sunday: The Essentialness of Love. Without love, even tongues, prophecy, faith, and sacrifice add up to nothing, and Jesus warns that love can grow cold. ☩Monday: What Love Does. Paul paints love in seven working verbs, patience and kindness and shared joy, love measured in actions rather than feelings. ☩Tuesday: What Love Does Not Do. Eight refusals, from envy to record-keeping, that show love by what it will not allow itself. ☩Wednesday: A Portrait of Jesus. Read the verbs slowly and a face emerges, because only One Person has ever lived every line. ☩Thursday: Faith, Hope, and Love. Gifts expire and knowledge fades, but three things outlast the world, and the greatest is love. ☩Friday: Further Thought & Discussion. The week lands on love as the life of everything, the only cure for a divided church. Christ at the center Here is the seed to plant before Sunday. As you read the famous chapter this week, try reading it as a wanted poster. Somewhere there is a person who is endlessly patient, relentlessly kind, never envious, never rude, keeping no file of wrongs, bearing everything, believing the best, hoping past reason, outlasting every hurt. Hold the description up against everyone you know, including the face in the mirror, and watch every candidate fall short somewhere around the second verse. The chapter is not just poetry. It is a description of Someone, and by midweek Scripture will say His name out loud. Watch for Him early. He is behind the patience on Monday, underneath every refusal on Tuesday, and waiting in full view on Wednesday. The greatest thing ever written about love was always a portrait, and the portrait was always of Him. Application Before Sunday, read 1 Corinthians 13 out loud once, slowly, alone if you can. Thirteen verses takes about ninety seconds. As you read, notice the one phrase that stings a little, the one that sounds least like your last seven days. Write that phrase somewhere you will see it every day this week, the bathroom mirror, a sticky note on the dash, the lock screen on your phone. Do not fix anything yet. Just let the phrase ride along with you. That sting is where this week intends to work. Opening Question for the Week "When you hear the words love is patient, love is kind, which relationship in your life comes to mind first (a spouse, a teenager, a coworker, the person you quietly avoid at church)? And what would change by Friday if that relationship got the first fruits of this chapter instead of the leftovers?" Opening Prayer for the Week Father, we have heard these words at weddings and seen them framed on walls, and we confess that we have admired them more than we have lived them. This week, take the most famous chapter Paul ever wrote and make it unfamiliar again. Slow us down at the verbs. Show us where our patience runs out, where our kindness gets selective, where the record of wrongs is still in the drawer. And as the portrait comes into focus, let us see not a standard that condemns us but a Savior who loves us exactly this way. Give us eyes to recognize His face in every line, and hearts willing to be repainted. We do not want to finish this week having studied love. We want to finish it loving. In Jesus' name, Amen.
docs.2026-08-09.html: In brief Paul stacks up the most impressive spiritual résumé imaginable. The languages of angels. Prophecy that sees everything. Faith that relocates mountains. Every possession given away, his own body handed over. Then he runs the total, and it is zero. Nothing. No gain. One missing ingredient bankrupts the whole portfolio, and Jesus adds the quiet warning that this ingredient does not shatter when it dies. It cools. Love is not the bonus feature of the Christian life. It is the only thing that makes the rest of it count. Yesterday Yesterday you taped a phrase to your mirror, one line from the famous chapter that stung a little on the way past. We met the blank Greek word the first Christians filled with the love of Jesus, and we agreed to sit for the portrait this week. Today Paul does what any good painter does first. He clears the room. Before a single verb of love goes on the canvas, he removes everything we might pose with, the gifts, the knowledge, the sacrifice, the spiritual trophies, and he shows us what they weigh without love. It is a shorter list than we think. Historical Context Generosity Always Sent an Invoice Walk through first-century Corinth and read the walls. Carved into stone after stone are the names of givers. This man paved the plaza at his own expense. That man funded the games, repaired the temple roof, fed the city during the shortage. The inscriptions were the receipts of a system historians call benefaction, and it ran the Roman world. A wealthy person gave lavishly, publicly, and the city paid them back in the only currency that mattered, honor. Front-row seats. Statues. Titles read aloud at festivals. Generosity was real, and it was never free. Every gift sent an invoice for glory. Now listen to Paul's escalation with Corinthian ears. If I give away everything I own, he writes, even if I hand over my body itself, and love is not the engine underneath, I gain nothing. To a culture where giving everything was the ultimate power move, the surest route to a name carved in stone, that sentence lands like a hammer on marble. Paul is naming the loophole the whole system depended on. You can perform every generous act in the catalog for an audience of admirers and never love a single human being in the process. The city knew how to fund a plaza. It did not know how to want nothing back. Into the Word Imagine the church member Corinth would have voted most spiritual. She prays in languages no one has taught her. He explains mysteries that make elders lean forward. Their faith gets results, their giving is legendary, and the whole congregation feels lucky to have them. Paul opens the love chapter (1 Corinthians 13) by building exactly that person, trait by gleaming trait, and then he asks the question nobody in Corinth thought to ask. What is all of it worth if love is not the thing driving it? His arithmetic is about to be brutal. 1 Corinthians 13:3 Open ↗ If I give all I possess to the poor and exult in the surrender of my body, but have not love, I gain nothing. This is the top of a three-rung ladder, and every rung ends in the same place. Tongues of men and of angels without love are noise (1 Corinthians 13:1). Prophecy, all mysteries, all knowledge, mountain-moving faith without love are nothing (1 Corinthians 13:2). Then Paul reaches the summit, total generosity, the body itself given over, and the verdict actually gets worse. I gain nothing. Notice he never calls the gifts useless. Tongues are real, prophecy is real, faith and sacrifice are real, and all of them are good. They are useless only when love is not the engine driving them. The résumé was never the problem. The problem is a résumé with no heart behind it, and God, who reads hearts, refuses to be impressed. So what is this love that carries so much weight? Not the word we spend on strawberries and playlists, and not the chemistry the movies sell. The love of this chapter is a grace the Spirit plants, a settled commitment of our actions, our feelings, and our thoughts toward Christ and toward the people in front of us. Affection, charity, virtue, and kindness are its fingerprints, but none of them is the hand. And because this love is living, Jesus warns that it can also die, not with a bang but by degrees. Matthew 24:12 Open ↗ Because of the multiplication of wickedness, the love of most will grow cold. Jesus is describing the last days, and the danger He names is not persecution or false teaching. It is temperature. The Greek verb here is psychō, to cool, the word for something hot losing its heat one unnoticed degree at a time. Love rarely dies in an explosion. It dies like coffee on a desk, cooling because it sat untouched while we handled more urgent things. Notice the physics of the verse. Lawlessness multiplies in the world outside, and love loses temperature in the people who were supposed to stay warm. The surrounding cold seeps in wherever love is not actively tended. That is why Paul's arithmetic matters so much. A church can keep every program running at full power, cooling the whole time, and never hear an alarm go off. Street Level The Model Home Nobody Ever Lived In In every new subdivision there is one house that exists to be walked through. The model home. The builder furnishes it down to the toothbrush cups. Cookies cool on the counter, the fireplace is on, and a paperback waits on the nightstand with a bookmark a third of the way in. None of it is fake, exactly. The oven really bakes. The granite is real granite. But look at the picture frames. The smiling family in them came with the frames, and it is the same family in the next model, and the next. Nothing in this house has ever actually happened. Nobody has burned a grilled cheese here, or waited up past midnight for a teenager's headlights, or fallen asleep mid-sentence on that couch. It has every feature of a home and has never been one, because the one thing it lacks is not a feature. It is people who love each other inside it. Paul says a spiritual life can be staged the same way. Tongues, prophecy, mountain-moving faith, generosity arranged where visitors will notice it. All of it real, the way the model's oven is real. And his verdict is not that such a life is a smaller home. It is no home at all. I am nothing, he says. Vacant. Love is not the final upgrade on the spiritual feature list. Love is the family moving in, and it is the only thing that has ever turned a house into a home, or a résumé into a life. Today’s World The Age That Measured Its Own Cold In June 2025 the World Health Organization's Commission on Social Connection, co-chaired by former United States Surgeon General Vivek Murthy, published a report with a plain title and a grim ledger. It counted something nobody thought could be counted. Roughly one person in six on this planet is lonely. Loneliness and isolation are linked to about 871,000 deaths a year, around a hundred every hour, by raising the risk of stroke, heart disease, and cognitive decline and by doubling the odds of depression. And the coldest rooms are not the ones we would have guessed. The loneliest people on earth right now are the young, with about one in five teenagers and young adults reporting loneliness, a generation carrying phones that can reach anyone alive in under a second. The commission named the paradox itself. In an age when the ways to connect are endless, more and more people are ending up alone. Jesus made a forecast about temperature. Because lawlessness would multiply, He said, the love of many would grow cold, and twenty centuries later the cooling has epidemiologists. Sit with what their numbers are actually saying. Our generation holds the greatest connective toolkit in human history, tongues of men and of angels at planetary scale, and a hundred people an hour are dying for lack of the one ingredient the toolkit cannot ship. Nobody is lonely for bandwidth. People are lonely for somebody who is glad they exist, and no network can generate that. It has to walk in the door. Which means the oldest assignment in the church is suddenly urgent public health work. Warm somebody. The world has finished proving Paul's arithmetic. Everything minus love still equals nothing. Source World Health Organization, Commission on Social Connection From loneliness to social connection: charting a path to healthier societies. World Health Organization, Commission on Social Connection, 2025. Read the source. Christ at the center There is one place in history where the whole résumé of 1 Corinthians 13 shows up with the engine intact. At the cross, every item on Paul's list converges. Here is a body given over. Here is everything handed away, not a fortune but a life, down to the seamless robe the soldiers gambled for. And this time the sentence ends differently, because love was driving all of it. He was not performing generosity for an audience of admirers. Most of the audience was mocking Him. He was loving specific people on purpose, the thief beside Him, the soldiers under Him, the friends who had scattered, and us, at the greatest possible cost. The benefactors of Corinth gave to be praised. Christ gave to be with us. That is the difference between charity and love, and it is the difference between gaining nothing and gaining everything He came for. Application Think of one person who recently got your competence but not your love. You solved their problem, answered their question, did your job. Today, go back for the part you skipped. Send the follow-up text that has no task in it. Ask how they are actually doing, and stay for the answer. One person, one return trip, today. Discussion Question "Looking back, when did someone need love from you more than anything else and get something less (advice when they needed presence, a fix when they needed a friend, silence when they needed a call)? If a moment like that came back around this week, what would doing it with love actually look like?" Closing Prayer Father, Your math unsettles us, and we need it to. We have counted the wrong things for a long time, the abilities, the accomplishments, the acts of service everyone could see, and today You showed us a total we did not expect. Forgive us for every gift we have run without love in the engine. Forgive us for the times someone needed warmth from us and received efficiency instead. And keep us honest about temperature. We do not plan to grow cold. Nobody does. So tend the fire in us daily, Lord, because the world outside is not getting warmer. Fill us with the love that comes only from Your Spirit, the kind that wants nothing back, and aim it at the people You have put within our reach. We would rather be nothing impressive and full of love than everything impressive and empty. In Jesus' name, Amen.
docs.2026-08-10.html: In brief Ask a hundred people what love is and you will get feelings. Ask Paul and you get footage. Today he hands the Corinthians seven verbs you could catch on camera. Love waits without the sigh. Love does the kind thing first. Love shows up at somebody else's celebration and means it. Love carries, trusts, hopes, and outlasts. There is not a single emotion on the list, because Paul is describing how a person filled with the Spirit behaves, not how they feel. Love is not a feeling we wait for. It is a set of verbs we practice, and the practice becomes a life. Yesterday Yesterday ended with a cup of coffee going cold on a desk, love losing temperature one unnoticed degree at a time, and with Paul's arithmetic still ringing. Everything minus love equals nothing. Which raises the obvious next question. If love is the one ingredient that makes the rest count, what exactly is it? Today Paul answers, and he refuses to hand us a definition we can frame and forget. He hands us a work order. Seven verbs, each one something love does with its hands, each one something you could watch happen across a kitchen table. Historical Context Kindness Already Had a History On Sabbath mornings in Corinth, before there was a church, there was a synagogue, and inside it a reader unrolling a Greek scroll. Most of Corinth's Jews, and the God-fearing Greeks who slipped in beside them, did not read Hebrew. They knew the Scriptures through the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament, and in that translation one family of words kept surfacing whenever the Psalms talked about God. Kindness words. The Lord is good to everyone. His compassion rests on all He has made. Week after week, the congregation heard kindness described not as good manners but as the settled habit of the Almighty. So when Paul's letter reached the church and someone read the words love is kind aloud, the verb did not arrive empty. Paul reached for that same word family, the one the Greek Psalms had spent centuries filling with the character of God. His converts had been singing about a kind God long before they were told to be kind people. That is the quiet force of today's list. Paul is not inventing virtues from scratch. He is taking the family traits of the God of Israel and writing them into the job description of everyone who claims to be His child. Kindness was God's reputation first. Now it is supposed to be ours. Into the Word Somewhere today a person will say I love you and mean I enjoy how you make me feel. Paul writes four verses that make that sentence impossible to leave alone. He takes love out of the heart, where nobody can check on it, and moves it into the daylight of behavior, where everybody can. What follows is the heart of the whole chapter, a portrait of love painted entirely in motion. Read it slowly. Every verb is aimed at somebody. 1 Corinthians 13:4-7 Open ↗ 4Love is patient, love is kind. It does not envy, it does not boast, it is not proud. 5It is not rude, it is not self-seeking, it is not easily angered, it keeps no account of wrongs. 6Love takes no pleasure in evil, but rejoices in the truth. 7It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Paul personifies love, as if it were a person you could follow around for a day, and the first thing you would notice is what it does under pressure. It shows patience, even when circumstances give it every excuse not to, the same long-tempered bearing with one another that Paul begs of every church (Ephesians 4:2). It does the kind thing without being asked. And notice what is missing from the whole passage. Not one feeling. Paul is showing us how a person moved by the Spirit behaves, because for him love is more about actions than emotions. Feelings rise and fall on their own schedule. Verbs are decisions. That means the question this passage asks is never how do you feel about them, but what have you been doing for them lately. Keep walking the list and it gets more surprising. Love rejoices in the truth, and behind that phrase sits a very specific skill, the ability to be glad alongside someone else. It is the joy of the neighbors who celebrated with Elizabeth over her impossible baby (Luke 1:58), the shepherd shouting rejoice with me over one found sheep (Luke 15:6), the woman throwing a party over one found coin (Luke 15:9), the body where one member's honor makes every member glad (1 Corinthians 12:26), and Paul himself, chained and still rejoicing with his friends (Philippians 2:17, 18). Then come the four load-bearing verbs. Love bears, believes, hopes, endures, all things (1 Corinthians 13:7). Bearing and enduring are near twins, the same tough endurance Paul practiced when he chose to put up with anything rather than hinder the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:12). Believing all things means leading with the benefit of the doubt. Hoping all things means expecting good on the far side of hard. Love endures precisely by believing and hoping. It lasts because it refuses to stop expecting. Psalms 145:9 Open ↗ The LORD is good to all; His compassion rests on all He has made. Here is the spring the kindness verb drinks from. When Paul says love shows kindness, he uses chrēsteuomai, a Greek verb that appears only this once in the whole New Testament, but its word family is all over the Greek Old Testament, especially the Psalms, where it describes the Lord's goodness wrapped in mercy. That backstory matters. Kindness in this chapter is not politeness, the smile we give the cashier. It is imitation. The psalm says God is good to everyone, that His compassion covers everything He has made, the deserving and the undeserving alike. So when love shows kindness to someone who has not earned it, it is not being naive. It is copying its Father. Kindness is family resemblance, and the family it resembles is God's. Galatians 5:22-23 Open ↗ 22But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, 23gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law. Set this list beside today's list and watch them overlap. Love leads the fruit. Patience is on both pages. Kindness is on both pages. Joy shows up here, and rejoicing there. That overlap answers the question today's verbs quietly raise, which is where does anyone get the strength to live like this. Paul's answer is in his farming word. Fruit. Nobody bolts fruit onto a tree. It grows from the life inside, and this life is the Spirit's. The verbs of 1 Corinthians 13 are not a self-improvement checklist we grind through. They are what naturally ripens in a person who stays connected to God's Spirit day after day. Our part is real, choosing the verb when the feeling is missing. But the sap is His. We practice what He produces. Street Level The Butterflies Grew Up At every fiftieth anniversary party, somebody finally asks the question. What's the secret? And the husband, who has been dreading the microphone all evening, gives an answer that disappoints the whole room. We just kept showing up, he says. I make her tea. She warms my side of the bed. The crowd wanted butterflies and he handed them chores. But watch that man for a week. He starts her car on cold mornings so the seat is warm before she gets in. He fills the pill organizer every Sunday night, her days and his, whether or not he feels anything in particular while he does it. Ask him which of those mornings he felt in love, and he honestly could not tell you. The feelings came and went a thousand times across fifty years, like weather. The verbs never missed a day. That is what Paul is handing us in today's passage. Not a rush to wait for. Seven verbs to run today, patience and kindness and rejoicing on purpose, practiced on schedule through every kind of feeling-weather. In a love like that, the butterflies do not die. They grow up. They get jobs. And given enough mornings, the practice stops being something a person does and becomes someone the person is, which is exactly what the Spirit grows in anyone who keeps choosing the verb. Fruit does not appear in a day. It ripens on a schedule of small, repeated yeses. Today’s World The Feelings Followed the Verbs In June 2025, researchers at the University of California, San Francisco published the results of a large-scale global well-being study. They called it the Big Joy Project, and the assignment could not have been humbler. For seven days, five to ten minutes a day, each participant performed one small prescribed act, and the daily list reads like Paul's portrait with a login screen. Do a kind thing for someone. Write down what you are grateful for. Celebrate another person's joy on purpose. Nobody was asked to feel anything first. The acts were scheduled, mood or no mood. In all, 48,789 people consented to take part, 17,598 completed the measures before and after the week, and 169 countries were represented. When the team analyzed the results, the week of tiny verbs had measurably raised emotional well-being and positive emotion, lowered stress, and improved self-reported health and sleep quality, with benefits comparable to programs that run ten or twelve weeks. The largest gains landed on the youngest and most disadvantaged participants. Notice the order of operations, because it is the whole finding. The feelings were not the fuel. They were the exhaust. People acted first, on schedule, and the joy showed up behind the acting, which is precisely the architecture Paul built into today's passage. Love is patient. Love is kind. Love rejoices with. Verbs, all of them, available on days when the warm feeling never reports for duty. Scripture assigned these reps two thousand years before anyone measured them, and it also named what the researchers were watching grow. Fruit. A week of deliberate kindness does not make anyone a finished orchard, and no app can pour God's love into a heart. That is the Spirit's work. But the study caught the mechanism in daylight. Choose the verb, and the verb starts changing the person running it. The feelings were never the engine. The verbs were. Source Journal of Medical Internet Research Scaling a Brief Digital Well-Being Intervention (the Big Joy Project) and Sociodemographic Moderators: Single-Group Pre-Post Study. Journal of Medical Internet Research, 2025. Read the source. Christ at the center Every verb on today's list, Jesus performed in sandals, on foot, at street level. Patience looked like three years of explaining the kingdom to twelve men who kept asking about thrones. Kindness looked like a hand laid on a leper who had not been touched in years. Rejoicing with looked like a wedding at Cana, where He kept the celebration alive with the best wine of the day. Bearing all things looked like a Teacher washing the feet of the man about to sell Him. And believing all things looked like breakfast on a beach, where He handed the ministry back to the friend who had denied Him three times, because He saw who Peter would become and not just what Peter had done. We will spend Wednesday gazing at this portrait in full. For now it is enough to notice one thing. Not one verb stayed theoretical. In Jesus, every line of the love chapter got up and walked. Application Pick the verb on Paul's list that comes least naturally to you and run it once today, on purpose. If it is patience, let the slow moment pass without the sigh or the phone. If it is kindness, do the unrequested helpful thing for the person you find hardest. If it is rejoicing with, find somebody's good news today and celebrate it like it happened to you, no comparison allowed. One verb, one deliberate rep, before you sleep tonight. Discussion Question "Which of Paul's seven verbs is hardest for you right now (patience with a slow situation, kindness to a difficult person, honest joy at someone else's success, holding on when trust has been bruised)? And since this love is the Spirit's fruit rather than raw willpower, what would it look like to ask God for that verb this week instead of just trying harder at it?" Closing Prayer Father, thank You for refusing to leave love vague. We have hidden behind the vagueness, calling ourselves loving because we felt warm things while doing nothing. Today You showed us seven verbs, and we felt the list read us back. We confess the sighs that leak out of our patience. We confess the kindness we ration to people who can return it. We confess how much easier it is to weep with those who weep than to honestly rejoice with those who rejoice. Spirit of God, grow Your fruit in us, because we have tried manufacturing it and the plastic version fools no one. Give us one honest rep of the hardest verb today, and the strength to repeat it tomorrow, until Your love stops being something we admire and becomes something our families can feel. In Jesus' name, Amen.
docs.2026-08-11.html: In brief Today Paul paints in negative space. Eight things love refuses to do, and every one of them feels good in the moment. The flash of envy at a friend's news. The subtle brag slipped into conversation. The sharp reply that wins the exchange. The tidy mental ledger where every wrong is filed by date. Paul is not listing random vices. Each refusal matches something his own congregation was busy doing. Love is proven less by the impressive things it does and more by the satisfying things it declines. Yesterday Yesterday you ran one deliberate rep of your hardest verb, patience without the sigh, kindness without the invoice, joy at news that was not yours. Seven verbs showed us what love does with its hands. But Paul knows something about hands. They do damage as naturally as they do good. So today the portrait adds its shadows, eight refusals, the things love will not let itself do no matter how justified they feel. If yesterday was love's job description, today is its code of conduct, and it reads like Paul had been sitting in Corinth's pews taking notes. He had been reading their mail, at least. And ours. Historical Context A Port City Kept Its Books Stand on the Lechaion Road, Corinth's marble spine running up from the harbor, and listen to the sound of business. A stylus pressing figures into a wax tablet. Grain from Sicily, weighed and entered. A loan to a shipwright, terms and date, entered. Corinth sat on the narrow neck between two seas, and cargo from both directions paid its way across, which made the city one enormous counting house. Fortunes lived and died by the ledgers. A merchant who forgot what he was owed did not stay a merchant, so nothing owed was ever forgotten. Everything was written down, and everything written down was collected. Paul reaches straight into that world for one of today's refusals. Love, he writes, does not keep a record of wrongs, and the verb he chooses is a bookkeeping term, the word for entering an item into the account so it can be settled later. Every Corinthian knew that motion of the stylus. Paul's claim is that love refuses to run its relationships like a counting house. It keeps no column of injuries, logs no dates beside offenses, carries no receivables file of things to bring up during the next argument. In the best-audited city in Greece, Paul describes a love that deliberately loses track of what it is owed. That was bad accounting. It still is. It is also the only way any relationship survives. Into the Word Why would Paul spend half his portrait on negatives? Because the Corinthians could have signed the positive list and gone to lunch. It is the refusals that name names. Read the eight again slowly and notice how precisely they trace this church's file, the envy behind the factions, the puffed-up knowledge, the rudeness of the strong toward the weak, the lawsuits chasing personal rights. Paul re-reads his own list back to a congregation that was living its opposite, and somewhere in the reading, the mirror turns toward us. 1 Corinthians 13:4-7 Open ↗ 4Love is patient, love is kind. It does not envy, it does not boast, it is not proud. 5It is not rude, it is not self-seeking, it is not easily angered, it keeps no account of wrongs. 6Love takes no pleasure in evil, but rejoices in the truth. 7It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Count the refusals this time. Love does not envy, does not boast, is not arrogant, is not rude, is not self-seeking, is not irritable, keeps no record of wrongs, and finds no joy when someone else goes wrong. Behind that record-keeping phrase sits the Greek verb logizomai, an accounting word, to enter something into the books. Love refuses the ledger. It also refuses the touchiness that turns every slight into an event, and the smug little lift we feel when a rival stumbles. None of these refusals comes naturally, because each one means giving up something that pays immediately, the win, the credit, the collected debt. That is exactly why they prove love is real. Anyone can perform the positives on a good day. Only love says no to what feels this good. The first refusal deserves a closer look, because Paul has used its verb positively all through this letter. Desire the greater gifts, he says (1 Corinthians 12:31). Desire spiritual gifts (1 Corinthians 14:1). Desire to prophesy (1 Corinthians 14:39). Same Greek verb, turned toward God's gifts, and it is holy hunger. Turned toward a gifted person, it curdles into the thing that made Joseph's brothers sell him south (Acts 7:9) and the thing splitting Corinth into camps, where envy and strife were walking proof of spiritual infancy (1 Corinthians 3:3). Wanting what God gives is worship. Resenting who God gave it to is war. 1 Corinthians 8:1 Open ↗ Now about food sacrificed to idols: We know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up. Here is where boasting and arrogance were actually living in Corinth. The educated members knew an idol was nothing, and their knowledge had inflated them until they could no longer see the brother at the next table whose conscience was still tender from a lifetime in the temples (1 Corinthians 8). Paul does not dispute their facts. He disputes their posture, dripping irony about the wise and strong looking down on the fools for Christ (1 Corinthians 4:10). His two verbs tell the whole story. Puffing up inflates one person, a balloon, all air and skin. Building up raises a house other people can live in. Every congregation is doing one or the other, and rudeness towards the weak is simply arrogance with its elbows out. 1 Corinthians 10:24 Open ↗ No one should seek his own good, but the good of others. Love is not self-seeking, and Paul had already given that refusal a rule of its own. Do not chase your own advantage. Chase the other person's. This is the sentence that sounded most insane in Corinth and sounds most insane now, because both cultures run on securing your own. Notice, though, what Paul is actually proposing. Not a world where nobody's needs matter, but a community where everyone's needs are carried by someone else, each member seeking the good of the other until the circle closes and every person in it is looked after. Rights enforced to the wall leave a room full of winners who cannot stand each other. Rights laid down build the one thing Corinth could not buy, a people who actually belong to one another. Street Level You Were Right and You Said Nothing You told them. Maybe it was the used car with paint too shiny for its mileage, or the plan to fix the roof without calling anyone who fixes roofs, or the guy who was charming the way weather is nice. You said your piece once, gently, and got waved off. Then one Tuesday the phone rings and it has all gone exactly the way you said it would. Here is the moment. The most satisfying sentence in the English language is sitting loaded on your tongue, fully earned, completely true, already assembled. I told you so. You could say it kindly. You could say it with nothing but a look. Every syllable has been paid for. And love picks up that perfect, deserved sentence, and sets it back down. Makes the tea instead. Asks what happens next.
