Helps load the truck. Nobody hands out trophies for that, and the invisibility is the point. Half of Paul's portrait is refusals, and every one of them means walking away from a payoff that was genuinely available. The flash of being envied. The credit. The delicious last word. The little lift of watching your prediction come true. Those wins feel wonderful for about an hour. Love keeps declining them, not because it is weak but because it is busy protecting something better, the person in front of you, who needs a friend right now far more than a verdict. You were right. You said nothing. That silence was love doing its strongest work, in the one place only God could hear it. Today’s World The Ledger Was Costing the Bookkeeper Researchers recently ran the largest forgiveness experiment ever attempted, and they ran it in places with long memories. In a trial published in BMJ Public Health in 2024, a team led by psychologist Man Yee Ho, alongside forgiveness researcher Everett Worthington and Harvard's Tyler VanderWeele, gave 4,598 people at six sites in five countries, Colombia, South Africa, Ukraine, Indonesia, and Hong Kong, a plain do-it-yourself workbook. No therapist, no retreat, about three hours at a kitchen table. The pages walk one real hurt, a specific one with a name and a date, through five steps. Recall it honestly. Work at seeing the offender as human. Remember a time you were the one forgiven. Commit to canceling the debt. Hold on when the books try to reopen. Two weeks later, compared with people still waiting for their copy, the forgivers were measurably better. Less unforgiveness. Less depression. Less anxiety. And greater flourishing, the researchers' word for a life going well as a whole. Notice who the trial was measuring. Not the people who did the wrong. The people holding the record of it. Paul's bookkeeping word pictured a wrong entered in the account so it could be collected later, and the modern data shows what that entry actually collects. It charges the bookkeeper. Every grudge on file was quietly billing its keeper in depression, in anxiety, in the unforgiveness itself, interest accruing for years on debts nobody was ever going to pay. Tearing up the page turned out to be the move that stopped the bleeding, exactly as the chapter said, and exactly as the cross showed. God did not wait to collect what we owed. He canceled the record that stood against us and nailed it to His cross, and He has been inviting His people into that accounting ever since. Love keeps no record of wrongs. That is not naive bookkeeping. It is the only bookkeeping that leaves the bookkeeper alive. Source BMJ Public Health International REACH forgiveness intervention: a multisite randomised controlled trial. BMJ Public Health, 2024. Read the source. Christ at the center Watch the eight refusals hold at the one place they should have shattered. At the cross, Jesus had grounds for every behavior love declines. He could have envied, the Lord of glory watching soldiers gamble for His only robe. He could have boasted, one word summoning legions of angels to end the whole indignity. He was mocked and stayed silent, struck and did not strike back, provoked past any limit a human being has ever faced and never once became what they were. And the ledger. He was accumulating the greatest record of wrongs in history, hour by hour, nail by nail, and He looked at the men writing the entries and said Father, forgive them. The refusals of 1 Corinthians 13 are not weakness dressed up as virtue. They are the strongest will in the universe, declining every exit, staying on the cross out of love for the people who put Him there. Including us. Application You know whose file you keep. The person whose old offenses you can still recite by date. Today, retire one entry. Write the oldest wrong on a slip of paper, pray for that person by name while you hold it, then tear it up and throw it away. You are not saying it never happened. You are saying it will no longer collect interest. One entry, gone for good, today. Discussion Question "Which of the eight refusals is hardest for you to make (dropping the scorecard in your marriage, staying unprovoked with a certain relative, feeling honest gladness when a rival succeeds)? And what do you think would actually change in that relationship if you retired that one behavior for the next seven days?" Closing Prayer Father, today's list found us. We know the taste of every behavior on it, the envy that spikes at someone else's good news, the boast we disguise as an update, the sharp word that felt so right leaving our mouth, and the records. Lord, You know about our records. Some of us have kept certain books for years, accurate to the day. Forgive us for running love like a counting house. Teach us Your accounting instead, the kind that canceled a debt we could never have paid and then burned the ledger at Calvary. Pry the stylus out of our hands. Where we have been touchy, settle us. Where we have been self-seeking, turn our eyes to the person beside us. And when the old files call our name this week, remind us that we tore them up on purpose, in Your presence, because loved people learn to love. In Jesus' name, Amen.
docs.2026-08-12.html: In brief Two days inside the love chapter and most of us are quietly discouraged. Patient, kind, no envy, no ledger. We have failed every line by Tuesday lunch. Here the argument turns and lifts a weight nobody should have been carrying. Paul was not describing us at our theoretical best. He was describing Someone he had met on a road outside Damascus. Every verb in the portrait has already been lived, in sandals, all the way to a cross. The love chapter is not first a mirror of what we must become. It is a portrait of who Jesus already is. Yesterday Yesterday you tore up a ledger entry, one old wrong retired from the books for good. Fifteen verbs are now on the table, seven things love does, eight things it refuses, and an honest reader is left with a problem. Nobody lives this. Measure any of us against the portrait and the frustration is almost instant, which is exactly where the passage meets us. When Paul wrote these lines, he likely had a particular face in mind. The portrait was drawn from a living model, and today we finally get to meet Him in it. Historical Context The Portrait Came Before the Gospels A believer in Corinth in AD 55 had never seen Jesus' face, and neither had anyone she could ask. There was no picture of Him anywhere in the world. Her city was crowded with the faces of its lords, Caesar on every coin in her purse, statues of benefactors along every street, because in the Roman world a ruler made sure you knew exactly what he looked like. The church's Lord had left no statue, no coin, no painted panel. New converts asked the obvious question, what is He like, and the church had no image to hand them. Here is what makes today's passage remarkable. When Paul wrote this letter, not one of the four Gospels was in circulation yet. Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John were still years from being written down. Which means the love chapter is one of the earliest portraits of Jesus ever put on paper, drawn before the Gospel writers picked up their pens, and Paul painted it without a single physical detail. No height, no face, no voice. Just verbs. Patient. Kind. Keeping no record. Bearing all things. The first portrait of Jesus the church ever owned was a portrait of how He loves, and it turned out to be the only likeness that matters. Into the Word Read the fifteen verbs (1 Corinthians 13:4-7) and then open the Gospels, and something uncanny happens. The abstract portrait starts moving. It picks up a towel. It stops for blind men. It sets its face toward Jerusalem. Scripture insists this is no coincidence, because the love Paul described has always had a face, and today's passages trace the resemblance feature by feature until the identification is unmistakable. John 13:1 Open ↗ It was now just before the Passover Feast, and Jesus knew that His hour had come to leave this world and return to the Father. Having loved His own who were in the world, He loved them to the very end. John hangs a single sentence over the entire last night of Jesus' life, and it reads like a caption under a portrait. He loved them to the end. The Greek phrase is eis telos, and telos means the end, the goal, the finish line, so the words carry a double weight. He loved them to the last hour, and He loved them to the uttermost, all the way, nothing held back. Within minutes He is washing feet, and before the next sunset He is on a cross. This is the love He then hands His people as their family rule, love one another as I have loved you, the new command (John 13:34), sourced from the Father Himself, as the Father loved Me, so I have loved you (John 15:9), and repeated so nobody could miss it (John 15:12). The portrait's first feature is its scale. This love does not taper off. It finishes. 1 Timothy 1:16 Open ↗ But for this very reason I was shown mercy, so that in me, the worst of sinners, Christ Jesus might display His perfect patience as an example to those who would believe in Him for eternal life. Love is patient, love is kind (1 Corinthians 13:4), and Paul offers himself as the laboratory proof of both. The man who once hunted Christians calls himself the display case where Christ exhibits extraordinary patience, and he never got over the kindness underneath it, grace overflowing with faith and love (1 Timothy 1:14). Peter says believers have tasted for themselves that the Lord is kind (1 Peter 2:3), and that tasted kindness reshapes people. It gave a timid Timothy a spirit of power, love, and sound judgment (2 Timothy 1:7) and a pattern to hold in faith and love (2 Timothy 1:13). When we wonder whether the portrait's patience is real, Paul points a thumb at his own chest. If it held for me, it holds for you. The resemblance keeps building. Love rejoices in the truth, and Jesus was no stranger to joy. He wanted His own joy planted in His friends, remaining in them, filling them up (John 15:9-11), and He prayed His joy into them on the night of His arrest (John 17:12-14). Love bears and endures all things, and no one has ever endured like Him, the cross itself, the hostility of sinners, for the joy set before Him (Hebrews 12:2, 3), obedient all the way down to death on a cross (Philippians 2:8). Feature by feature, the face is coming into focus. 1 John 3:16 Open ↗ By this we know what love is: Jesus laid down His life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers. John writes the definition the whole week has been circling. We did not learn what love is from philosophy or poetry or even from watching good families. We learned it at the cross, where the Son laid down His life. Behind that moment stands the character of God Himself, because God is love (1 John 4:8), and He loved the world by giving His only Son (John 3:16). Jesus is the exact expression of that nature (Hebrews 1:3), love made visible among us so that we might live through Him (1 John 4:7-12). And the definition comes with a direction. We love because He first loved us, and the proof lands on how we treat the brother in front of us (1 John 4:19-21). Love flows downhill, from the cross into us, through us, outward. Acts 9:15 Open ↗ “Go!” said the Lord. “This man is My chosen instrument to carry My name before the Gentiles and their kings, and before the people of Israel. Love believes all things, and here is what that verb looks like from heaven. Ananias hears the name Saul and recites the file, all the harm he has done, the arrests he is authorized to make (Acts 9:13, 14). Every word of the file is accurate. And Jesus answers with a different tense. Go, for this man is My chosen instrument. Not was a persecutor, though he was. Is My instrument, because Jesus sees people not only as they are but as they will become through His power. The church's worst enemy was three days away from becoming its greatest missionary, and only One Person in the universe believed it. Love reads the record and still bets on the future. It is the most stubborn optimism there is, and it is aimed at you. Street Level Every Uniform Matched and You Still Found Her Every seat in the bleachers is doing the same impossible thing. Twenty-two kids in identical uniforms, same colors, same numbers blurred by distance, too far away for faces, and every parent up there has already found their own. Nobody is squinting at jerseys. You spot the run. The way she checks over her shoulder before the ball comes anywhere near her. The bounce your son has had since he was three. From two hundred feet, faces are useless, and you never needed one. It works everywhere. You would know your mother from behind, in a crowd, by nothing but her walk. You can hear your best friend's laugh through a wall. And long after a grandfather is gone, when the photographs have started to feel flat and strange, what stays vivid is how he folded the newspaper and patted his pockets at the door. We think faces are how we know people. Faces are only how we meet them. We recognize the people we love by how they move. That is why the love chapter can identify Jesus without a single physical detail. Paul gives no height, no face, no sound of His voice, just how Love moves. Patient with the slow. Kind before being asked. Keeping no record. Staying when it costs everything. Read those movements slowly and a specific Person steps out of the sentences, unmistakable, the way your kid comes across a field. A portrait made of behavior turns out to be the most identifying likeness there is. And it means you can still recognize Him now, moving through an ordinary week, patient where no one else would be. You know the walk. Today’s World The Bank That Reads People in the Future Tense Nobody expects stubborn optimism about human beings from a bank. Banks are in the file business, credit histories, risk scores, past behavior read as forecast. Which is what makes the hiring numbers at JPMorganChase so surprising. The company struck the criminal-history checkbox from its job applications, and in 2022 alone it hired more than 4,600 people with records in their past, roughly one in ten of its new hires in the United States in recent years. It helped found the Second Chance Business Coalition, more than 45 major employers making the same bet, and it now runs clinics that help people clear old records entirely. The bet is paying. When old records are expunged, workers' earnings climb about twenty percent within two years. Now set that beside the road to Damascus. Ananias answered the Lord with a file, every entry accurate, the harm, the arrests, the authorizations, and Jesus replied in a different tense. This man is My chosen instrument. Love believes all things, Paul wrote, and here is what that verb looks like wearing a lanyard. Not gullibility. Not pretending the record is blank. It is the wager that a person's worst chapter is not their last one, made by somebody with the power to open a door. A file tells you where a person has been. It carries no data on what grace can still do. Heaven has been hiring on that basis all along, staffing its whole mission with people whose records should have disqualified them, starting with the man who wrote the love chapter. Every believer is a second-chance hire. The least we can do is read each other the way we were read. Source JPMorganChase Second Chance Hiring Strengthens Workforce and Could Add $87 Billion to the Economy. JPMorganChase, 2023. Read the source. Christ at the center Today the whole page has been Christ connection, so let the connection turn personal. The portrait is not hanging in a museum. It is looking at you. The patience Paul exhibited to the world is patience Christ is currently extending to you, on the days you repeat the sin you swore off, in the prayers you keep forgetting to pray. The kindness believers have tasted is kindness He has already shown you, in mercies you have stopped noticing because they arrive so reliably. And the stubborn faith that saw an apostle inside a persecutor is the same faith He has in what His grace can still do with you. We spend so much energy asking whether we love God enough. Today the gaze runs the other way. Before the fifteen verbs are ever our assignment, they are His disposition toward us. Look at the portrait long enough and you will find it is not a standard glaring down at you. It is a Face, turned toward you, to the end. Application Tonight, read the towel scene in John 13:1-17 in one sitting. Watch Jesus the way you would watch someone you were trying to describe to a friend, noting each love-verb as it happens. Pick the single move that strikes you most, the interruption He allows, the feet He does not skip, the betrayer He still serves. Then copy that exact move on someone in your house or circle tomorrow before noon. Discussion Question "Which feature of Jesus' love is hardest for you to believe is aimed at you personally (His patience after your repeated failure, His kindness when you expect disappointment, His confidence in who you could still become)? And who in your life needs you to show them that exact feature this week, maybe because nobody ever has?" Closing Prayer Lord Jesus, we came into this week thinking the love chapter was about us, and today we found You in every line. You are the patience we have been failing at. You are the kindness we ration. You loved Your own to the end, the very ones who would scatter before morning, and You have loved us the same way through every one of our worst days. Thank You for sitting for this portrait in real time, with real nails. Forgive us for reading it as a burden when it was always an introduction. Heal what discouragement these verses have stirred in us, and replace it with wonder. And do in us what only You can do. Believe us into becoming what You already see, the way You believed a persecutor into an apostle. We want to look like this portrait, because we want to look like You. In Jesus' name, Amen.
docs.2026-08-13.html: In brief Paul ends the love chapter at the end of the world. Prophecy has finished its work. Tongues have gone quiet. The partial knowledge we prized has been swallowed up by knowing fully, and the dim bronze mirror has finally turned face to face. Almost everything the Corinthians were fighting over turns out to have an expiration date. Three things walk across that horizon intact, faith, hope, and love, and Paul crowns the third. The gifts are for now. Faith and hope carry us home. Love is the one thing we will still be doing forever. Yesterday Yesterday the portrait turned out to be looking back at us. We watched every verb of the love chapter come alive in Jesus, patient with the worst of sinners, believing an apostle into existence inside a persecutor, loving His own to the end. One question remains, and it is the question we ask about everything precious. How long does it last? Paul answers today by fast-forwarding the film past prophecy, past tongues, past knowledge itself, all the way to the edge of eternity, and then he shows us what is still standing there. The answer is shorter than the Corinthians expected, and better. Historical Context The Finest Mirror Still Showed a Shadow A bride in Corinth tilts a polished disc of bronze toward the window light and studies the warm, wavering shape looking back at her. It is the best reflection money can buy. Corinth's workshops turned out bronze mirrors prized across the empire, ground flat, polished for hours with fine abrasives until they gleamed like honey. And even the finest of them could not do what the cheapest glass mirror does today. The image came back dim, tinted, slightly bent, a shadow of a face rather than a face. Every Corinthian who owned one knew the peculiar frustration of almost seeing yourself. So when Paul writes that for now we see only a reflection as in a mirror, but then face to face, he is not reaching for an exotic image. He is picking up the pride of local industry and telling the truth about it. Your best look at ultimate things, he says, your sharpest prophecy, your deepest study, is a Corinthian mirror, real but dim, true but partial. The gap between the bronze blur and a face across the table is the gap between what we know of God now and what is coming. The mirror was never the destination. It existed to keep you looking until the door opened and the Face walked in. Into the Word Everything the Corinthians ranked each other by came stamped with a date they could not read. That is the quiet bombshell at the end of the love chapter. The gifts they treated as permanent trophies were temporary tools, issued for the church's construction season and scheduled for retirement the moment the work is done. Paul is not diminishing the gifts. He spent two chapters honoring them. He is measuring them against eternity, and against the one thing in the room that eternity will not touch. 1 Corinthians 13:8 Open ↗ Love never fails. But where there are prophecies, they will cease; where there are tongues, they will be restrained; where there is knowledge, it will be dismissed. The Greek behind never ends is the verb piptō, to fall, and Paul puts it in the strongest form he has. Love never falls. Buildings fall, empires fall, and every gift on Corinth's trophy shelf will one day stand down, not because the gifts fail but because they finish. Prophecy is a flashlight for a dark road, unnecessary at sunrise. Tongues are for a church still gathering the nations. Knowledge, the partial kind we piece together now, retires the moment the full picture arrives, when the perfect comes and the partial goes (1 Corinthians 13:10). The gifts cease only when the purpose they exist for is fulfilled. Love has no such clause in its contract, because love is not a tool for reaching the goal. Love is the goal. Scaffolding comes down. The building stays. 1 Corinthians 13:12 Open ↗ Now we see but a dim reflection as in a mirror; then we shall see face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I am fully known. Here is the timeline behind the whole day. Now, and then. Now is the bronze mirror, the dim tinted almost-image, and Paul includes himself in it. I know in part, says the man who wrote a third of the New Testament. Then is face to face, a phrase Scripture saves for its most staggering promises, and very soon it will be literal. We will see our Lord, not a reflection of Him, not a doctrine about Him, Him. And catch the last clause, because it is the best one. I will know fully, as I am fully known. We are not walking toward a stranger. We are walking toward Someone who has known us completely the whole time, through every day we understood so little, and loved us anyway. The mirror ends. The knowing does not. It finally runs both directions. So what happens to faith and hope when sight arrives? In one sense they graduate. Faith, the walking-without-seeing kind (2 Corinthians 5:7), gives way to sight, and hope, which by definition waits for what it cannot yet see (Romans 8:24), finally holds what it waited for. Yet neither one simply vanishes. Faith as trust, the believing that God credited to Abraham as righteousness (Romans 4:3), and hope as the appetite for new delights in a new earth will mark the redeemed forever. Trusting and anticipating are what living creatures do with an infinite God. Still, Paul ranks them, and the reason is worth the whole chapter. Faith and hope are how creatures hold on to God. Love is what God is. Romans 5:1-5 Open ↗ 1Therefore, since we have been justified through faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, 2through whom we have gained access by faith into this grace in which we stand. And we rejoice in the hope of the glory of God. 3Not only that, but we also rejoice in our sufferings, because we know that suffering produces perseverance; 4perseverance, character; and character, hope. 5And hope does not disappoint us, because God has poured out His love into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, whom He has given us. The triad was never Paul's private signature for one letter. It is how the early church talked about the whole Christian life, faith and love in Ephesus (Ephesians 1:15) with eyes opened to hope (Ephesians 1:18), one body walking in one hope, one faith, one love (Ephesians 4:1-5), faith working through love while hope waits eagerly (Galatians 5:5, 6). And here in Romans the three are shown growing in real soil. Faith brings peace with God. Affliction, of all things, gets worked into endurance, character, and hope. Then the chain ends at its power source, God's love poured out in our hearts by the Spirit. The triad is not three separate achievements. It is one life, and love is the part of it that is most like God Himself (1 John 4:8). Street Level Built to Fall Away Watch a rocket launch with a six-year-old and you get to relive the best plot twist in engineering. About two minutes up, the biggest, loudest part of the whole machine, the part doing almost all the work, shuts down, lets go, and falls away toward the ocean. On purpose. The first stage drinks most of the fuel and does the brutal lifting through the thickest air, and when it drops, nobody in mission control gasps. They cheer. Stage separation is not a breakdown. It is a milestone, planned before the rocket was ever built, because the booster was never going where the mission is going. It exists to lift something else, and the surest proof that it worked is the moment it is no longer needed. Paul says the gifts Corinth kept ranking work exactly like that. Prophecy, tongues, knowledge, all of them real thrust, all of them lifting the church through the thick air of a broken world, and every one of them is scheduled to shut down, not because it failed but because it finished. When we finally stand face to face with Him, the last stage falls away with its work complete. Faith and hope make the whole flight with us, and love turns out to be the cargo they were guarding all along, the one thing the entire stack existed to carry home. So spend your strength accordingly. The loudest parts of a life all drop away on schedule. Pack the payload. Today’s World Eighty-Seven Years of Data Landed on Love In 1938, Harvard researchers began following 724 men, hoping to learn what makes a life turn out well. Then the study refused to end. It has now run for 87 years, widening over time to roughly 2,500 people as wives and descendants joined, and its evidence fills every form a lifetime can leave behind, medical records, brain scans, interviews, questionnaires answered decade after decade. A study that long gets to check the answers everybody assumes. Wealth did not turn out to hold the central answer. Neither did fame. What kept surfacing instead, as the files thickened, was plainer and harder to buy. Strong relationships. Again and again, the people with warm, strong bonds were the ones the records found happy and healthy, and that emerged as the study's central finding. Paul stood at the end of the world and said the impressive things all stand down, prophecy finished, tongues quiet, knowledge outgrown, while love never falls. Set the Harvard files beside that claim and the resonance is hard to miss. The prizes our age bets on hardest, wealth and fame, did not hold the central answer to a life turning out well. Strong relationships held it, in the study's own central finding. And what is a strong relationship, at street level, but love given and received across ordinary decades? To be fair to the researchers, their data can trace the tie between good relationships and happier, healthier people. It cannot see past the horizon, and it does not claim to. Paul does. What an eighty-seven-year window glimpses in miniature, eternity will show in full. Faith and hope will walk us all the way to His face. Love is what we will still be doing when we arrive. The study is long. Scripture got there first. Source Harvard Gazette Things money can’t buy — like happiness and better health. Harvard Gazette, 2025. Read the source. Christ at the center Face to face is not an abstraction. It is a particular Face, and we already know something about it. It is the face that was set like flint toward Jerusalem, the face they spat on and struck, the face that looked at Peter across the courtyard after the third denial and did not look away. When faith finally becomes sight, this is the sight it becomes. And notice what survives the crossing with us. Not our gift inventories. Not our theology grades. The love poured into us, practiced by us, spent on unimpressive people in unrecorded moments, walks straight through the door into eternity like it built the place. Of course it does. It did. Faith will retire into seeing Him. Hope will retire into being home. Love will not retire at all, because love is not our ticket to God. It is the family resemblance, and the resemblance is to a Son with scars. Application Spend today's effort on eternity's currency. Before you sleep tonight, tell one person, specifically and out loud, what you have watched God's love do through them. Name the moment. The meal they brought, the call they made, the patience they showed your family. It will take ninety seconds and feel slightly awkward, and it will outlast every deadline you hit this week. You will be practicing the one skill you will still be using a million years from now. Discussion Question "If you audited last month by eternity's ledger, how much of your best energy went to things that expire (the inbox, the scoreboard, the renovation) versus the one thing that never falls? And what is one standing commitment you could trade this month for a direct investment in loving someone, so the exchange actually happens instead of staying a nice idea?" Closing Prayer Father, we spend most of our strength on things with expiration dates, and today You showed us the three that remain. Thank You that our dim view of You is not Your view of us, that we are fully known even now, on the days our knowing feels like a bronze blur. Grow real faith in us, the kind that trusts You in the dark. Grow real hope in us, the kind that leans toward Your return like a child watching the driveway. And above them both, pour out Your love in our hearts by Your Spirit, because we cannot manufacture what only comes from You. When we are tempted to measure our lives by gifts and accomplishments that will one day stand down, remind us what walks into eternity. We want to meet You face to face having practiced Your favorite thing. In Jesus' name, Amen.
docs.2026-08-14.html: Week in Review This week Paul interrupted the gift wars with thirteen verses that turned out to be a portrait, love audited down to a zero without it, painted in verbs and refusals, revealed as the character of Jesus, and crowned as the only thing that never falls. ☩Sabbath: A Portrait of Love. The faint Greek word the first Christians filled with the love of Jesus opened a week spent inside the most famous chapter Paul ever wrote. ☩Sunday: The Essentialness of Love. The most impressive spiritual résumé in the world totals zero without love, and Jesus warned that love's quiet danger is not shattering but cooling. ☩Monday: What Love Does. Seven verbs you could film showed love as practiced action rather than felt emotion, with God's own kindness as the family trait it copies. ☩Tuesday: What Love Does Not Do. Eight refusals traced Corinth's actual habits line by line, and love tore up the ledger of wrongs in a city that kept books on everybody. ☩Wednesday: A Portrait of Jesus. The portrait resolved into a Person who loved His own to the end and still believes people into futures nobody else can see. ☩Thursday: Faith, Hope, and Love. The gifts retire when their purpose is fulfilled, but three things cross into eternity, and the greatest is the one that is God's own nature. Historical Context The City That Had a Word for Everything Look back across the week and one city comes into focus. Corinth had a rich word for every kind of love except the kind that mattered, and it had a system for everything else. Generosity ran on invoices, every public gift repaid in carved honor. Commerce ran on ledgers, every debt entered by date and collected in full. Its lords made sure you knew their faces, stamped on coins and raised on pedestals, while the finest mirrors in the empire handed back only a warm bronze blur. It was a city fluent in desire, friendship, obligation, and rank, a place where everything had a price and everyone knew the exchange rate. Into that fluency came one letter carrying the vocabulary's forgotten word, and thirteen verses that filled it forever. The church in Corinth was not asked to out-argue its city. It was handed a love with no invoice attached, no ledger behind it, no expiration stamped on it, and told to live that love in full view of the marketplace. Corinth taught the world to price everything. The church was learning to give the one thing that has no price, because it had met the One who gave it first. What This Week Clarifies Six days inside one chapter leave a reader holding live wires, tensions that deserve one more look before Sabbath arrives. Here are the three that most need resolving. The Audit and the Countdown Were the Same Lesson Sunday zeroed out the most impressive spiritual résumé imaginable. Thursday stamped an expiration date on every trophy in Corinth's case. Two demolitions in one week, and together they raise an uncomfortable question. If the gifts can be worthless now and are temporary anyway, what are they even for? 1 Corinthians 13:8 Open ↗ Love never fails. But where there are prophecies, they will cease; where there are tongues, they will be restrained; where there is knowledge, it will be dismissed. The week ran the same audit from two directions. Sunday counted the gifts without love and got zero, the model home furnished to the toothbrush cups with no family inside it (1 Corinthians 13:1-3). Thursday counted the gifts against eternity and watched every one of them stand down on schedule, the booster stage falling away with its work complete. Neither pass was an attack on the gifts. Paul spent two chapters honoring them, and both demolitions leave them standing as exactly what they are, real tools with real thrust. What the double audit exposes is location. The value never lived in the inventory. It lives in what the inventory is carrying. That settles how to measure, and not just for Corinth. The questions we reach for first, how gifted is this person, how impressive is this church, how full is this résumé, are inventory questions, and the week retired them. The chapter's question is a cargo question. What is all this lifting? A congregation's programs, a believer's abilities, a family's accomplishments are boosters and scaffolding, honorable and scheduled to fall away, and the test of every one of them is whether love is the thing riding inside. The Portrait Is an Introduction Before It Is an Assignment Be honest about how the middle of the week felt. Fifteen verbs went up on the wall (1 Corinthians 13:4-7), and most of us had failed the list by Tuesday lunch. Read as a report card, the love chapter grades everyone into discouragement. So is that what it is? Galatians 5:22-23 Open ↗ 22But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, 23gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law. Wednesday answered the discouragement by turning the frame around. The verbs were a biography before they were ever a syllabus. Paul was describing Someone he had met, patient with the worst of sinners, kind before being asked, believing a persecutor into an apostle (Acts 9:15), and the portrait's first message to any reader is not measure up. It is this is how you are currently being loved. Monday had already planted the other half of the answer in a farming word. Fruit. Nobody bolts fruit onto a tree, and nobody grinds out this love by willpower. It ripens from a life the Spirit is living inside. Put the two halves together and the chapter's order of operations comes clear. First be loved, because the portrait is aimed at you before it is assigned to you. Then practice the verb on schedule, the way the anniversary couple ran their small faithful chores through fifty years of feeling-weather, because the feelings were never the engine. And ask for the fruit while you practice, since the sap is His and the reps are yours. The week did not lower the standard. It relocated the strength. It Does Not Shatter. It Cools Notice what the week's warnings had in common. None of them was dramatic. No betrayal, no blowup, no villain. A cup cooling on a desk. A stylus entering a wrong in the books. A congregation running every program at full power and losing a degree a day. The threats were all quiet ones. Matthew 24:12 Open ↗ Because of the multiplication of wickedness, the love of most will grow cold. Jesus' forecast for the last days was a temperature warning, and the week kept finding the cold in unexpected rooms. The loneliest people on earth right now are the young, the very generation holding the greatest connective toolkit ever built. The best-audited city in Greece was billing itself to death one filed grievance at a time, because a record of wrongs turns out to be cold storage, and the interest lands on the bookkeeper. Love almost never dies in an explosion. It dies untended, by degrees, while more urgent things get handled. Which is why the cure the week prescribed is so unglamorous. Maintenance. Not a hotter feeling but a tended fire, small verbs run on schedule, one entry torn out of the ledger on purpose, warmth delivered in person to somebody going cold within arm's reach. And underneath the maintenance, a supply line, because this warmth is received before it is produced. God canceled our record first, and loved people learn to love. Tomorrow is Sabbath, the weekly maintenance window, and the practice below is one deliberate hour of it. Still Speaking You Are an Artery, Not a Reservoir Right now, without asking your opinion, your heart is doing the least glamorous work in the world. One thump per second, give or take, pushing about five quarts of blood down hallways you have never seen, some of them thinner than a hair. Blood is not much to look at. But everything your body lives on travels in it. Oxygen rides in it. Fuel rides in it. And when you cut your finger, everything that arrives to close the wound comes by the same road. A hand is only warm because blood keeps visiting it. Pinch off the flow to any part, however strong that part looks, and it begins to die while still attached, still in place, still resembling itself. The body does not run on the excellence of its organs. It runs on what reaches them. That is the anatomy underneath everything this week taught. A church can have organs that would impress any surgeon, prophecy, knowledge, faith, heroic giving, and Paul's audit still comes back zero if nothing is circulating, because no part lives on its own impressiveness. Love is the blood of the Christian body. And here is where the picture turns kind, because blood has a source. You were never asked to manufacture this love out of willpower, five quarts from nowhere. It is pumped. It flows from a heart that is not yours, the heart of Christ, who loved you to the end before you had done one lovable thing, who keeps no record of yours, who looks at your file and still speaks about your future. All week the portrait has been looking at you. Now you know what it was doing. Transfusing. So the week ends with one question. Not whether you admire the chapter. Whether the current gets past you. Loved people are meant to be arteries, not reservoirs. A reservoir stores what it receives and slowly goes stale. An artery is a humble stretch of pipe that simply stays open, and life passes through it to everything downstream. Somewhere within arm's reach of you is a person going cold for lack of what is already flowing into you, patience they have never been shown, kindness with no invoice attached, a friend willing to tear up the file. You do not have to feel mighty to carry that. The heart does one small verb, over and over, a hundred thousand times a day, and nobody in the body goes without. Stay connected to the Heart. Keep the small verbs moving. And let the love that found you keep traveling, through your hands, all the way to the end of the line. Christ at the Center of the Week Trace Him back through the week. On Sabbath He was the reason an almost-empty Greek word needed filling, because nothing in Corinth's vocabulary could hold what He is. On Sunday He was the difference between charity and love, the Giver who gave everything and actually meant us. On Monday the seven verbs turned out to be His daily schedule, patience for slow disciples, kindness for untouchable skin, joy at a wedding, breakfast for a denier. On Tuesday the eight refusals held at the one place they should have broken, a cross where the ledger of our wrongs was being written and He answered it with forgiveness. On Wednesday the portrait said His name out loud, the One who loved His own to the end and believed a persecutor into an apostle. On Thursday His was the Face waiting on the far side of the bronze mirror. A week that began by asking what love is ends where Scripture always ends. Love is not first a definition. It is a Person, and He is ours. Weekend Practice This Sabbath, give one person the full current instead of a spark. Choose whoever the week kept surfacing, the name behind your mirror phrase, the person whose ledger entry you tore up, the one who got your competence but not your love. Set aside a real block of time for them, a shared meal, a long walk, an unhurried visit, phone face-down, and practice the verbs in person. Listen without planning your reply. Serve without being asked. Leave the score unkept. One person, hours not minutes, before the weekend ends. Closing Prayer for the Week Father, we came to this week knowing the love chapter by heart and left it knowing we had barely met it. Thank You for the audit that zeroed out our impressive things, for the verbs that gave love hands, for the refusals that named what we must lay down, and for the moment the portrait looked back at us with the face of Jesus. We confess that our love runs cooler than we admit and keeps more records than we destroy. So do in us what this chapter cannot do on paper. Pour Your love through the whole of us, mind and heart and hands and feet, until it reaches the people You have placed within our arm's length. Guard our congregations from being impressive and cold. Make us patient this Sabbath, kind on Monday, and free of the ledger all week long, until the day faith becomes sight and we find ourselves face to face with Love Himself. In Jesus' name, Amen.
docs.2026-08-15.html: In brief The road into Corinth ran between tombstones, and a common Roman epitaph was a shrug. I was not. I was. I am not. I do not care. Into that city Paul mails a paragraph that puts the whole faith on the line and dares anyone to check his facts. If Christ is still dead, he says, then the preaching is hollow, the faith is hollow, and the grave wins everything. This week walks his argument all the way to its verdict. Christ has been raised, and every promise you are living on stands up with Him. Last week Last week ended in front of a polished bronze mirror, squinting at a dim almost-image and waiting for the day the seeing goes both ways, face to face. That hope has a hidden load-bearing wall. A portrait of Jesus painted in verbs is only good news if the Man in the portrait is alive to keep loving that way. A dead man's love, however perfect, is a museum piece. So Paul spends the longest chapter of this letter on the question every other promise leans on. Did Jesus actually walk out of His grave? This week we stand where Corinth stood and hear his answer. Historical Context The Graves Outside the City Gate You learned a city's beliefs about death before you ever reached its gate. Roman law kept the dead outside the walls, so the tombs crowded both shoulders of the highway, and the last mile of any journey was a corridor of stone monuments where the dead introduced themselves as you passed. Some epitaphs begged the traveler to stop and read, so the name would live a moment longer in a stranger's mouth. And one line was common enough that stonecutters shortened it to seven letters, the way we reduce our commonest phrases to initials. Written out, it said this. I was not. I was. I am not. I do not care. That shrug was the empire's best answer to the grave. The philosophers offered a loftier one, a soul slipping free of the body at last, but out on the road where ordinary people buried their children, hope mostly read like the stones. Gone is gone. Into one of those cities came a letter insisting that a man executed by Rome had been seen alive, eating breakfast, holding out scarred hands, and that His rising was not a ghost story but a first installment. Paul knew exactly which world he was writing into. That is why he does not whisper the claim. He builds the entire Christian faith on top of it, in public, and invites the reader to test the foundation. This Week’s Memory Text 1 Corinthians 15:14-17 Open ↗ 14And if Christ has not been raised, our preaching is worthless, and so is your faith. 15In that case, we are also exposed as false witnesses about God. For we have testified about God that He raised Christ from the dead, but He did not raise Him if in fact the dead are not raised. 16For if the dead are not raised, then not even Christ has been raised. 17And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile; you are still in your sins. Read those verses again and feel how much Paul just put on the table. He hands his opponents the demolition plan for his own faith. If Christ has not been raised, the preaching is hollow, the believing is hollow, the preachers are liars, and every sin ever confessed is still sitting right where it was. Paul refuses to shield the movement from a testable claim or to move Christianity into the safe territory of ideas, where nothing can be checked and nothing can be lost. The Greek word running underneath his argument is anastasis, and it means a standing up again. Dead bodies back on their feet. Paul stakes everything on one dead man having stood up, because on an open road in broad daylight, that Man had stood in front of him. The memory text also hands us this week's route. We will live inside the whole argument (1 Corinthians 15), and watch the risen Jesus prove from Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms that this was always the plan (Luke 24:44-47). We will stand at the resurrection John saw, where those with a part in it are called blessed and holy (Revelation 20:5-6). We will remember that baptism has already buried us and raised us with Him (Colossians 2:12), borrow the settled confidence of an old apostle who knew whom he had believed (2 Timothy 1:12), and end the week beside the graves of people we love, grieving with hope because the dead in Christ will rise (1 Thessalonians 4:13-17). Every road this week leads to the same empty tomb. This Week’s Road Map ☩Sunday: Proclaiming the Resurrection of Christ. The gospel Paul preached stands on a resurrection promised in Scripture and confirmed by eyewitnesses you could still go ask. ☩Monday: The Risen Christ, Our Only Hope! Paul runs the honest math of a dead Christ and counts everything that collapses if the tomb stayed sealed. ☩Tuesday: Christ, the Firstfruits. The resurrection is a harvest, and Jesus is its first armful, the guarantee that everyone belonging to Him follows. ☩Wednesday: The Resurrected Body. How are the dead raised, and with what body? A seed, a night sky, and a promise about these very bones. ☩Thursday: Final Victory Over Death. The trumpet sounds, the sleepers wake in a blink, and death is swallowed by the victory it thought it had won. ☩Friday: Further Thought & Discussion. The week lands on witnesses, on hope with evidence underneath it, and on the reunion no grave can cancel. Christ at the center Here is the seed to carry into Sunday. Last week you learned to recognize Jesus by how He moves, patient, kind, keeping no record of wrongs. This week's question is blunter. Is He moving now? Everything the portrait promised depends on tense. A dead teacher leaves behind a philosophy, and you can admire a philosophy your whole life without ever being surprised by it. A living Lord makes appointments. He forgives in the present tense, intercedes in the present tense, and intends to raise you in the future tense. Watch how this chapter keeps refusing to let Jesus become a beautiful memory. By Wednesday you will see why your own body is written into His victory, and by Friday the question will have turned personal. If He stood up, then nothing about your life, your grief, or your grave is stuck where it is. Application Before Sunday, take a small piece of paper and write one name on it. The name of someone death has taken from you, the one you still catch yourself missing at odd hours. Put the paper in your Bible at 1 Corinthians 15 and leave it there all week. Every day of this study will be read over that name. Do not rush past the ache, and do not explain it away. Just let the week's argument stand next to your loss, and watch what a risen Christ has to say to it. Opening Question for the Week "If you learned beyond all doubt that Christ never rose, what in your ordinary week would actually have to change (the prayer before meals, the money you give, the hope you spoke at a graveside, the way you face your own aging)? And if He truly did rise, what should change by this time next week?" Opening Prayer for the Week Father, we have recited the resurrection in creeds and sung it at Easter, and still we live many of our days as if the tomb were only a metaphor. This week, plant our feet at the actual grave in the actual garden. Where our faith has gone soft with familiarity, make it load-bearing again. Bring our honest questions out of hiding, because You are not afraid of them, and walk them patiently through the evidence Paul left us. Sit with us beside the names we have written and the griefs we still carry. Teach us the difference between wishing and hoping, and anchor our hope to something that happened. And when the week is over, let us say with whole hearts that Christ has been raised, and let that truth change how we face Monday, and the doctor's office, and the cemetery. In Jesus' name, Amen.
docs.2026-08-16.html: In brief A letter is being read aloud in a crowded Corinthian living room, and Paul has just reached the words everyone learned first. Christ died for our sins. He was buried. He was raised on the third day. Then comes the astonishing move. Paul calls the witnesses, Peter, the Twelve, five hundred at once, and adds that most of them are still living. In plain terms, go ask them. The gospel is not good advice to live by. It is good news that happened, and it still saves everyone who holds on to it. Yesterday Yesterday you slipped a piece of paper into your Bible, a name now resting in the middle of the resurrection chapter, and we walked into Corinth past tombstones that shrugged. I was not. I was. I am not. I do not care. Today Paul begins answering the stones, but notice where he starts. Not with comfort, and not yet with your name. With facts. Before this chapter can hold your grief, it has to hold weight, so Paul lays the foundation first. The gospel he preached. The Scriptures behind it. The living eyewitnesses who saw the risen Lord with their own eyes. Historical Context The Words Paul Learned by Heart In a world where most people would never own a book, memory did the work paper does for us. A student sat at his teacher's feet and learned the master's words by exact repetition, until he could recite them without a slip and hand them to students of his own. That hand-off had formal vocabulary. A teacher passed on the tradition. A student received it. When Paul writes that he passed on what he also received, Corinth heard the language of a chain of custody. He is not composing fresh sentences here. He is reciting a fixed formula that was placed in his hands, word for word, by the people who had it before him. Now do the math that historians love about this passage. Paul is writing around twenty-five years after the crucifixion, but he received this creed at the beginning of his Christian life, within just a few years of the events themselves, from the very men named inside it. That timing changes everything. The resurrection was not a legend that crept in generations later, after the eyewitnesses were safely dead. It was the church's founding recitation, already fixed and memorized while the tomb was fresh news. The claim was not born in the dark. It was proclaimed in public while many named and unnamed witnesses were still living and could be questioned. Into the Word When the courier finally reaches this part of the letter, Paul does something disarming. He argues nothing. He rewinds. Let me remind you, he says, of the gospel I preached to you, the one you received, the one you are standing on right now. Some in Corinth had begun treating resurrection as negotiable, a topic for the seminar room. So Paul takes them back to the words that saved them, recites the message in its oldest form, and then calls a witness list long enough to fill a courtroom. Underneath it all sits one quiet, enormous question. Do you remember what you believed? 1 Corinthians 15:1-4 Open ↗ 1Now, brothers, I want to remind you of the gospel I preached to you, which you received, and in which you stand firm. 2By this gospel you are saved, if you hold firmly to the word I preached to you. Otherwise, you have believed in vain. 3For what I received I passed on to you as of first importance: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, 4that He was buried, that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, Four quick verbs carry the opening. Paul preached, they received, they stand firm, and by this gospel they are saved, if they hold firmly to the word (1 Corinthians 15:1-2). Then comes the message itself, recited in the cadence of a memorized formula. Christ died for our sins. He was buried. He was raised on the third day. And twice Paul adds according to the Scriptures, because none of this was an accident God scrambled to redeem. The gospel was promised through the prophets long before Bethlehem (Romans 1:1-4), and believing that God raised Jesus from the dead is the very heartbeat of saving faith (Romans 10:9-10). Notice what sits at the center of the good news. Not advice. Events. Things that happened to a real body in real time, woven so tightly into the gospel that pulling the resurrection out unravels the whole garment. Before calling his witnesses, Paul pauses over a pairing he refuses to separate. What is preached and what is believed are the same thing, or they are nothing. By this gospel you are saved, if you hold firmly to the word that was preached (1 Corinthians 15:2), and whether the voice belonged to Paul or to anyone else, so we proclaim and so you believed (1 Corinthians 15:11). Preaching hands over a fact. Faith closes its hand around it. Neither works alone. Luke 24:44-47 Open ↗ 44Jesus said to them, “These are the words I spoke to you while I was still with you: Everything must be fulfilled that is written about Me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms.” 45Then He opened their minds to understand the Scriptures. 46And He told them, “This is what is written: The Christ will suffer and rise from the dead on the third day, 47and in His name repentance and forgiveness of sins will be proclaimed to all nations, beginning in Jerusalem. The scene is Easter evening, and the risen Jesus is leading a Bible study about Himself. Before He tells the church what to preach, He shows them where it was always written, in Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms, the whole sweep of the Hebrew Scriptures. A Messiah who suffers, rises on the third day, and sends forgiveness out to every nation was never Plan B. It was the plot. So when Paul writes according to the Scriptures, he is echoing his risen Lord's own teaching method. And do not miss the closing line of the scene, you are witnesses of these things (Luke 24:48). Jesus did not leave behind a theory to be defended. He left people who had seen, and He sent them out talking. 1 Corinthians 15:5-8 Open ↗ 5and that He appeared to Cephas and then to the Twelve. 6After that, He appeared to more than five hundred brothers at once, most of whom are still living, though some have fallen asleep. 7Then He appeared to James, then to all the apostles. 8And last of all He appeared to me also, as to one of untimely birth. Here is the courtroom. Cephas, meaning Peter. The Twelve. More than five hundred believers at once, and Paul notes that most are still living (1 Corinthians 15:6), which in plain terms means go ask them for yourselves. Then James, the skeptical brother turned believer. Then all the apostles. Then, last and least in his own eyes, Paul himself. The Greek verb tolling through this list is ōphthē, he was seen, the word for eyes landing on something actually there. Not dreamed. Not wished into being. Seen, by named people in known places, many of whom went on testifying to it in public despite opposition, pressure, and real personal cost. Paul was that confident in the reality of Christ's resurrection. He did not ask Corinth to close its eyes and believe. He asked them to open their eyes and look. Street Level You Know Your Birthday by Faith Nobody remembers being born. Think about how strange that is. Your birthday is the most settled fact you own. You type the date into every form without a flicker of doubt, and yet you were in no condition to witness it. Everything you know about the day you arrived came to you secondhand. Your mother tells the story with details no form ever asks for, the storm that night, the nurse with the cold hands, the exact wrong thing your father said in the waiting room. The relatives retell it at every gathering, and the versions hold together. For most of your life you could test the story any afternoon you wanted, because the witnesses were sitting in the kitchen. You never doubted it. You could always ask. That is the kind of knowing Paul offers Corinth, and notice what he never asks for. He does not ask anyone to believe into the dark. He recites testimony from people who were in the room, fixed early and told the same way from the beginning, and then adds the astonishing detail that most of the five hundred are still living. That is a man handing out addresses. Go ask them. Faith in the resurrection has never meant believing without evidence. It means trusting witnesses who have held up under a lifetime of asking, the same way you trust the people who were present at the one event your whole life stands on. You have run on tested testimony since you learned your own birthday. The gospel simply asks you to do it about a better morning. Today’s World The First Test Is the One That Counts For decades the standard line, in courtrooms and psychology departments alike, was that eyewitness testimony is the weakest evidence there is. In August 2025, two leading memory researchers published a paper that complicates that story. Writing in the journal Memory, Laura Mickes of the University of Bristol and John Wixted of UC San Diego argued that many of the famous wrongful convictions were not so much failures of memory as failures to heed a witness's first answer. A memory, Wixted explains, works like the other trace evidence at a crime scene. DNA can be contaminated. Fingerprints can be contaminated. So can a remembered face, every time it is retested, rehearsed, and coached toward trial. On the first properly run test, before the contamination starts, the evidence suggests a confident identification is far more dependable than its courtroom reputation. In many of the DNA exoneration cases, the witness's earliest response actually pointed away from the man who ended up in prison. The first answer was often sound. The system stopped listening after it. Set that beside what Paul does in today's passage. He does not hand Corinth a story that had simmered privately for decades. He recites the church's first answer, a formula fixed within a few years of the events and received from the named men inside it, then lists the witnesses and adds that most are still living and easy to ask. Scripture preserved the very thing the memory researchers now prize, the earliest record of what the witnesses said, set down before time or pressure could bend it. The parallel deserves honest limits. A study of police lineups cannot test a first-century identification, and no journal article can prove the resurrection. What the research does offer is a reason to take early, well-preserved testimony seriously instead of dismissing witnesses on principle. That is precisely the kind of testimony the church has been carrying for two thousand years, cross-examined by people certain the witnesses had to be wrong, and never revised. Christ died, was buried, was raised, was seen. The first answer is still on the record, and it still deserves a hearing. Source Memory (Taylor and Francis) When eyewitness memory reliably exonerates the wrongfully convicted. Memory (Taylor and Francis), 2025. Read the source. Christ at the center Every thread of today ties back to a Person who insists on being alive. The gospel Paul recites is not the portrait of a martyr we are asked to admire. It is the announcement that the Man who carried our sins into a grave carried them out again, emptied of their power. He was seen. That changes what kind of faith Christianity is allowed to be. We are not curators of a beautiful memory. We are witnesses of a living Lord who still forgives, still calls, and still walks into locked rooms. Look at the witness list itself. Peter, who denied Him, restored by Him. James, who doubted Him, convinced. Paul, who hunted His church, arrested by grace on an open road. The risen Christ has a habit of turning His witnesses into His heralds, and He has not lost it. Application Someone once handed you the message Paul hands Corinth. A parent, a friend, a stranger with more courage than you knew. Today, be one link in that same chain. Tell one person one specific thing you have seen God do, an answered prayer, a change in you, a rescue you cannot otherwise explain. Say it plainly, no sermon attached. If speaking feels too big, write it instead, one text message, sent today. Witnesses report what they saw. Start there. Discussion Question "What actually holds up your confidence that Christ is risen (the eyewitness record, answered prayer, a change you have watched God work in someone, your own walk with Him)? And what else do you treat as completely true even though you never saw it yourself, and what does that tell you about how faith and evidence work together?" Closing Prayer Father, thank You that the gospel is news before it is anything else, news of something You did in the daylight of history. Thank You for the chain of faithful hands that carried it from an empty garden tomb across twenty centuries to us. Forgive us for treating the resurrection like a decoration on our faith instead of the ground underneath it. Steady those of us who believe and still carry questions, and let the witnesses' testimony give our confidence something solid to stand on. Then make us witnesses too. Put one name on our hearts today, and give us plain courage to say what we have seen You do. We do not want to guard this news. We want to hand it on. In Jesus' name, Amen.
docs.2026-08-17.html: In brief A few Corinthian believers had found a slogan they thought sounded wise. There is no resurrection of the dead. Paul does not shout at them. He borrows the idea and walks it to the end of its road, past an unraised Christ, empty preaching, faith holding air, lying apostles, unforgiven sin, until it stops at the graves of everyone they had ever loved. Gone, on their own theory. Then he turns around and points back at the open tomb. If Christ is not risen, we have nothing. Because He is risen, we have everything that matters. Yesterday Yesterday ended in a courtroom, five hundred living witnesses deep, with Paul all but daring Corinth to go knock on doors and ask. Maybe you even sent your own small testimony out into the world, one text message about what you have seen God do. Today the tone changes. Paul stops presenting evidence and turns to face the people shrugging at it, the ones repeating that there is no resurrection of the dead. He will not mock them. He will do something far more unsettling. He will take their idea seriously, all the way down. Historical Context The Soul Was Supposed to Escape Many educated Greeks inherited philosophical traditions that treated the soul as the truest self and the body as a temporary confinement. Death could then look like release. Influential schools in the empire taught people to hope for escape from the body, not its return. So when Paul preached bodily resurrection to the intellectuals of Athens, they did not get angry. They laughed at him (Acts 17:32). Who wants the corpse back? To many Greek hearers, resurrection was not too good to be true. It was too crude to be desirable, salvation running in reverse. Now put that schooling inside the Corinthian church. These believers loved Jesus, but they had been raised on soul-escape, and old maps die hard. Resurrection of the dead sounded embarrassing at dinner parties, so some quietly reclassified it. A metaphor, perhaps. A spiritual truth about the inner life. Nothing so vulgar as graves opening. Paul refuses the trade, because Christianity's hope was never a soul slipping out of creation. It is God raising His creation, body included, because He made it, He called it good, and He does not surrender it. That collision, Greek escape versus biblical rescue, is the fight underneath every verse today. Into the Word Somewhere in the room when this letter was first read aloud sat the people who had actually said it. There is no resurrection of the dead. They were not trying to attack Jesus. They thought they were being sophisticated. Paul hears it as a crack running through a load-bearing wall, and rather than raise his voice, he does something colder and braver. He accepts their premise for the length of eight verses and walks it to the end of its road (1 Corinthians 15:9-19). Come along, he says, into the world you are proposing. It is a shorter, darker walk than they think. 1 Corinthians 15:12 Open ↗ But if it is preached that Christ has been raised from the dead, how can some of you say that there is no resurrection of the dead? You can hear Paul's bewilderment coming through the ink. He has just finished the witness list, Peter and the Twelve and the five hundred (1 Corinthians 15:5-8), and now he asks how a church built on that testimony can shrug at resurrection itself. Notice the trap they had wandered into. They wanted to keep Christ's rising as the one glorious exception while denying that resurrection ever happens. Paul closes that door with two quiet hinges. If there is no resurrection of the dead, then Christ has not been raised (1 Corinthians 15:13), and if the dead are not raised, not even Christ (1 Corinthians 15:16). His rising was not a special effect. It was the first case of the very thing they were denying. There is no keeping Jesus alive inside a worldview where the dead stay dead. So Paul itemizes the cost of their idea, seven consequences in seven relentless lines (1 Corinthians 15:12-19). No risen Christ. Empty preaching. Empty faith. Apostles unmasked as men who testified falsely about God Himself (1 Corinthians 15:15). Futile faith. Unforgiven sin. The believing dead, gone. Then he slows down on the two lines that cut deepest. 1 Corinthians 15:14 Open ↗ And if Christ has not been raised, our preaching is worthless, and so is your faith. The word Paul reaches for paints a container with nothing inside. Take away the resurrection and the sermon becomes a speech about nothing, and faith becomes a hand closed around air. Notice that he does not soften this for the sake of morale, and he includes himself in the wreckage. Our proclamation, he writes, my life's work along with your believing. Readers have long debated the exact shade of that emptiness, whether it means untrue, or without effect, or without purpose, and the honest answer is that a dead Christ delivers all three at once. A message can be sincere, ancient, beautiful, and comforting, and still be an elegantly wrapped empty box. Only one thing rescues preaching and believing from that verdict. The thing preached has to have happened. 1 Corinthians 15:17 Open ↗ And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile; you are still in your sins. Here Paul sharpens the point with the Greek word mataios, which means fruitless, the label for effort that comes home empty-handed. Without the resurrection, faith is a field that never yields a harvest, because the one thing it was planted for, forgiveness, never actually arrived. Feel the weight of still in your sins. It would mean the cross was love poured out with nothing to show for it, and every confession you ever prayed changed nothing. Then comes the line that would have stopped every reader with a grave to visit. Those who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished (1 Corinthians 15:18). The grandmother who prayed for you. The friend who fell asleep trusting Jesus. Gone, on the no-resurrection theory, and our hope would deserve pity, not respect. Paul shows Corinth the whole bill on purpose. Without Easter morning, Good Friday is just a Friday. Street Level The Person Behind the Profile By now everyone knows a version of the story, from a documentary or from someone they love. A person meets someone online, and for a year the relationship is the best thing in their life. Good-morning texts. Long calls after midnight. Inside jokes, plans, a future taking shape. Then a detail snags, a friend starts digging, and the floor gives way. There is no such person. The photos belonged to a stranger. And here is the cruelest part. Nothing they felt was fake. The love was real, the hope was real, the hours were real, and every bit of it lands on nothing, because the one fact underneath it all, that somebody was actually there, was false. Real devotion multiplied by a missing person equals zero. Paul makes Corinth run that same arithmetic on the faith itself. If Christ has not been raised, sincerity rescues nothing. The sermons were really preached, the tears really fell, the believing was honest, and none of it lands anywhere, because there is no one on the other end. He would rather the church feel that cold once than build on it forever. But the reason he can be this ruthless is that he checked. This is the one story where the Person stepped out from behind the profile, in daylight, and was seen. Peter saw Him. James saw Him. Five hundred people at once saw Him, and Paul met Him on an open road with witnesses standing by. So the dark math runs in reverse, and everything built on Him holds. Sincerity was never the foundation. He is. Today’s World The Truck Was Only Rolling Downhill A few years ago an electric-truck startup named Nikola released a promotional video of its gleaming hydrogen semi cruising down a desert highway. Investors saw the future and bought in. By the summer of 2020 the market valued the company around thirty billion dollars, briefly more than Ford, before it had delivered a single production truck. Then a short-selling research firm, Hindenburg Research, published what insiders already knew. The truck in the video had no working powertrain. A crew had towed it to the top of a long grade and let it roll, with the camera angled so the road looked level. Founder Trevor Milton was convicted of securities fraud in 2022 and sentenced to four years. The company limped on, but on February 19, 2025, Nikola filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy with about 47 million dollars left, a fraction of a fraction of what the market once believed. The motion in the video was real footage of a real truck. It was just never driving. Paul runs the same inspection on his own enterprise, centuries ahead of schedule. If Christ has not been raised, the whole faith is a rolling truck. The preaching was real preaching, the believing was real believing, the sacrifices were real sacrifices, and all of it would be coasting on a slope, impressive at a distance, powerless at the core, stopping wherever gravity decides. That is what his word for futile means, effort that comes home empty-handed, and Paul itemizes the cruelest line himself, still in your sins, your dead simply gone. Notice that he publishes the damaging report on his own gospel before any skeptic could, then stakes the verdict on evidence. The engine has been inspected. Witnesses saw the risen Christ, touched Him, ate with Him, and kept on testifying in public through opposition and at great personal cost. And the gospel has climbed hills for two thousand years, against the grade, through persecution, past every confident prediction of its end. Rolling things eventually stop. This has not. Source CNBC Embattled EV maker Nikola files for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection. CNBC, 2025. Read the source. Christ at the center There is a hidden autobiography inside today's argument. Paul opened this passage calling himself the least of the apostles, a former persecutor remade only by grace (1 Corinthians 15:10). Now watch what his own logic does to his own story. If Christ is still dead, then no one met Paul on the Damascus road. No light, no voice, no commission, no grace. Just a brilliant man who wrecked his life for a hallucination. The apostle writing this chapter is himself walking evidence that Jesus is alive, a persecutor turned proclaimer by a Person he insists he saw. And that is why the resurrection is not one hopeful doctrine among several. A living Christ guarantees forgiveness now, resurrection later, and reunion after that, because the One making the promises has already walked out of His own grave. He is not our best option among many. He is the only door that was ever open, and it is open. Application Take a notebook or your phone and finish this sentence honestly. If Christ were still in His grave, the first thing I would lose is ______. Sit with what you wrote for one full minute. Then turn it into a spoken prayer of thanks for that exact thing, because He is not in His grave, and it is not lost. Carry that one sentence of thanks with you through the rest of today. Discussion Question "When you imagine the moment a believer dies, what picture do you actually carry (an immediate arrival in heaven, a dreamless sleep until the trumpet, something fuzzier you have never examined)? And if the dead in Christ are truly resting until resurrection morning, what does that change about how you grieve, and what would you say differently at the next graveside you stand beside?" Closing Prayer Father, today we walked to the edge Paul showed us and looked over it, into a world with a sealed tomb, empty sermons, unforgiven sin, and graves that keep everything they take. Thank You that we do not live in that world. Thank You that the long walk ends at a doorway with the stone rolled aside. Forgive us for the days we live like citizens of the hopeless world anyway, anxious and grasping, as if everything depended on what our hands can hold. Teach us the difference between a wish and a hope with a foundation under it. Comfort those of us missing someone who fell asleep trusting You, and keep their names safe until the morning You wake them. We hand You our doubts, our grief, and our small flickering courage. Be our only hope, and be enough. In Jesus' name, Amen.
docs.2026-08-18.html: In brief Yesterday's walk ended at a cliff, a world where the dead stay dead and hope deserves pity. Today Paul spins around with the sentence that carries all the weight. But Christ has indeed been raised from the dead. Then he reaches for a farmer's word to say what that means. Firstfruits. The first armful cut from the field, lifted up as proof and promise that the whole harvest follows. Jesus did not rise away from us. He rose ahead of us, and everyone who belongs to Him is standing in a field He has already claimed. Yesterday Yesterday Paul walked us to the edge of the world his opponents were proposing and made us look over. Seven consequences, one darker than the next, down to the unbearable last line about believers who have perished, their graves keeping them forever (1 Corinthians 15:12-19). He left us standing at that edge on purpose, long enough to feel the cold coming up from below. Today he takes us by the shoulder and turns us around, and what he shows us is not a philosophy. It is a field at harvest time, and the first armful is already cut. Historical Context The First Armful of the Harvest Early on a spring morning in Israel, a farmer stood at the edge of his barley field with a sickle and cut exactly one armful. Not the whole crop. One sheaf, the first to ripen, carried to the priest and lifted up before the Lord on the day after the Sabbath of Passover week (Leviticus 23:10-11). Until that sheaf went up, nobody in the land ate a bite of the new grain. The first armful stood in for every field in Israel, consecrating a harvest that was still rooted in the ground. The sheaf did two jobs at once. It declared the harvest holy, and it guaranteed the harvest was coming, because what had happened to the first armful would happen to the rest. Same crop. Same soil. Same life. Now count the calendar. Jesus of Nazareth walked out of His tomb on the morning after the Sabbath of Passover week, the exact slot where the wave sheaf was lifted. When Paul calls the risen Christ the firstfruits, he is not decorating his sentence with farm imagery. He is reading the festival calendar out loud. God had been rehearsing Easter every spring for fifteen hundred years. Into the Word After eight verses inside the world where the dead stay dead, Paul has earned the right to his turn, and he takes it in a single ringing sentence. But Christ has indeed been raised from the dead (1 Corinthians 15:20). Every expectation about the future darkens or brightens on that hinge. The delusion Paul dangled in front of Corinth evaporates, and in its place he sets a picture borrowed from the nearest farm. Firstfruits. One harvest word, and suddenly the resurrection is not only something to believe about Jesus. It is something to expect for everyone who belongs to Him. 1 Corinthians 15:20-23 Open ↗ 20But Christ has indeed been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. 21For since death came through a man, the resurrection of the dead comes also through a man. 22For as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive. 23But each in his own turn: Christ the firstfruits; then at His coming, those who belong to Him. Paul answers despair with agriculture. His word is aparchē, Greek for firstfruits, the first armful cut and lifted before God while the rest of the crop still stands in the field.
