Aimed across every line the world draws, until strangers are eating at one table and calling each other family. Giving was never the bill for any of this. It is the family dish, made again. So notice what happened to the collection plate somewhere between Sabbath and tonight. It stopped being an invoice and became an heirloom. When you give, decided and glad and aimed at real need, you are not paying God back. You cannot, and He never asked. You are making the family dish with your own hands, and the resemblance shows while you make it. Maybe the slip of paper from Sabbath, the one with last month's number on it, reads differently now too. Less like a bill you underpaid. More like handwriting practice, a child copying out a word the Father has been writing since before the world existed. And the Giver at the center of it all is not a memory the family honors. He is alive, still the richest Giver at the table, still teaching the recipe to any hands that will take it. So keep the card where you can see it. Make the dish again this week, in your own kitchen, for somebody who cannot pay for it. It only stays alive if you give it away. Christ at the Center of the Week Trace Him back through the days. Sabbath handed us one sentence, you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the whole week has been that sentence unfolding. Sunday read it like a receipt, the glory He had before the world existed traded for a borrowed pillow and a cross, His poverty the only reason for our wealth. Monday listed every clean motive for giving and found His face behind each one, then ran out of words where Paul did, at the indescribable Gift. Tuesday found the date stamp, the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world, a Gift decided before Eden and kept like an appointment through Gethsemane. Wednesday found the attitude, for the joy set before Him He endured the cross, the original cheerful Giver whose gladness no extraction ever produced. Thursday found the destination, a prayer that they may all be one, answered in coins crossing the world's oldest wall because His body had already torn it down. The week never really taught stewardship. It introduced the Steward's older Brother, the One who gave everything, gladly, on schedule, for family. Everything He asks of our hands, He did first with His. Weekend Practice Close the loop you opened on Sabbath. Take out the slip of paper with last month's number and set it next to this week's memory text, though He was rich, yet for your sake He became poor. Let the two talk to each other for a few honest minutes, without guilt, and then decide next month on purpose, a proportion chosen against what you actually have, a date that will keep itself, and one gift aimed across a line at believers you will never meet. Before Sabbath ends, add the gift no account can hold. Give someone your unhurried presence for a whole hour, phone down, the way God gave you His. Closing Prayer for the Week Father, we began this week braced for a lecture about money, and You gave us Your Son instead. We watched Him trade the wealth of heaven for a manger and a cross so that beggars like us could inherit everything, and somewhere between Macedonia's overflowing joy and the convoy walking into Jerusalem, our grip started to loosen. Thank You for a Gift no words can get to the bottom of. Thank You for churches too poor to be asked who begged to give anyway, and for the proof that Your grace can do that in ordinary people like us. Now send us into Sabbath as different givers. Settle our plans in the quiet. Grow Your own gladness in our faces. Aim our surplus at real need, and knit us to family we have never met. We hand You ourselves first, and everything else after, cheerfully, because now we know the grace. In Jesus' name, Amen.
docs.2026-09-12.html: In brief A rock fortress towers over Corinth, and a small tentmaker with a reputation for weak speech writes that his weapons can bring down strongholds. The people mocking him have moved into his church, polished and confident, preaching a Jesus who fits Corinth better than the crucified One. Paul does not out-shout them. He opens four chapters that are gentle and fierce at the same time, and this week we walk through them to learn the difference between what looks strong and what is. A counterfeit falls to God's power, never to our volume. Last week Last week ended at a kitchen table, with the collection plate turned from an invoice into an heirloom and giving revealed as the family resemblance of a God who gives. Now the tone of Paul's letter changes. Someone has arrived in Corinth to challenge the man who planted the church, and the family recipe is about to be tampered with. Historical Context The Fortress Above the City Fell Before Dawn Every morning in Corinth began under a rock. Acrocorinth rose nearly 1,900 feet above the gulf directly behind the city, a limestone mass with walls along its summit and a spring inside that never ran dry. Whoever held that height controlled the land bridge between northern and southern Greece, which is why one Macedonian king called it one of the "fetters of Greece." Armies looked up at it and made other plans. In 243 BC a general named Aratus took it anyway, not by assault but with a small party climbing a hidden path in the dark. When Rome flattened Corinth a century later, the rock lost its city. By Paul's day the summit still crowned the rebuilt colony, and a person walking to the market could see it from almost any street. So when Paul told this church that God's weapons "demolish strongholds," nobody had to imagine one. They lived under one. He meant exactly that kind of walled height, a place built so that whatever hid inside it could not be reached. His strongholds were not stone, though. They were arguments, reputations, and a way of measuring leaders that some newcomers had carried into the church. Those visitors looked strong the way the rock looked strong. This week watches Paul walk toward that fortress with no siege engines at all, only the truth about Jesus and a willingness to look weak, and it watches what happens to the walls. This Week’s Memory Text One sentence from the middle of Paul's argument becomes the week's banner. He is answering people who say his letters roar and his presence squeaks, and instead of defending his personality he tells them what kind of war he is actually fighting, and with what. 2 Corinthians 10:4 Open ↗ The weapons of our warfare are not the weapons of the flesh. Instead, they have divine power to demolish strongholds. Paul does not deny that he is at war. He denies that he fights the way everyone expects. The Greek word for stronghold here is ochyrōma, a fortified place, the walled height you retreat to when the open field is lost. Paul says the real fortresses are built out of reasoning, the confident positions people take up against the knowledge of God, and that flesh cannot bring them down. Charm cannot. Volume cannot. Credentials cannot. Only weapons with God's own power in them do that work, and the rest of this letter shows what they look like. Plain truth about Jesus. Gentleness that refuses to flinch. A willingness to be laughed at. The walls that come down this week come down from the inside. The week walks straight through Paul's last four chapters to Corinth. Sunday and Monday read his opening defense in 2 Corinthians 10:1-17, where a borrowed line from Jeremiah 9:24 settles what a servant of God is allowed to brag about. Tuesday pulls the mask off the newcomers in 2 Corinthians 11:1-15. Wednesday reads the strangest résumé in the Bible, 2 Corinthians 11:22-28. Thursday hears a father's fear for his children in 2 Corinthians 12:20-21 and the exam he hands them in 2 Corinthians 13:5. Under all of it sits the sentence Paul never stopped believing, that he was an apostle by the will of God (1 Corinthians 1:1), which is why the fight was never really about him. This Week’s Road Map ☩Sunday: Spiritual War. Paul answers the charge that he is all bark by naming the war he is actually in and the weapons God issued. ☩Monday: Boasting in the Lord. Comparison only measures you against you, so Paul boasts inside the field God assigned and lets God do the commending. ☩Tuesday: False Teachers Identified. The best counterfeit looks real, so Paul teaches the church to check the Jesus being preached, not the polish. ☩Wednesday: Sufferings for the Sake of the Gospel. Paul plays the boasting game for one paragraph, wins it with a list of scars, then hands the trophy to grace. ☩Thursday: Appeal to the Unrepentant. A third visit is coming with real authority, and the man bringing it prays he will never have to use it. ☩Friday: Further Thought. The week's threads gather around one question, what strength looks like when it belongs to the crucified Jesus. Christ at the center Watch for a pattern this week. Every time Paul is pushed to prove himself, he points somewhere else. Pushed to boast, he boasts in the Lord. Pushed to show strength, he lists the times he was beaten. Pushed to prove that Christ speaks through him, he answers that Christ was crucified in weakness and lives by the power of God, and that he is glad to be weak the same way. The question the week keeps asking is not whether Paul was impressive. It is what Jesus is like, because the whole fight was over which Jesus Corinth would follow, the polished one the newcomers preached or the crucified One Paul had planted there. That is why counterfeits matter so much. A different Jesus is not a minor adjustment. It is a different God. By Friday we should be able to say what the real One looks like when He fights for His people, and it will not look like a fortress. It will look like a cross. Application Before Sunday, write down the name of one voice you have let shape what you believe about God this year, whether a preacher, a podcast, an author, or a friend. Do not judge it yet. Just name it, and beside the name write one sentence describing the Jesus that voice presents. Keep the paper somewhere you will see it. The week is going to hand you tests, and a test is only useful if you already know what you are testing. Opening Question for the Week When has something that looked strong in your spiritual life (a confident teacher, a big claim, a leader who never seemed to lose) turned out to be hollow, and what did it cost you to find out? If God's power really works through what looks weak, where might you be dismissing the very thing He is using right now? Opening Prayer for the Week Father, we are walking into four chapters where Your servant is under attack, and we admit we do not always know a counterfeit when we see one. We like what sounds confident. We trust what looks strong. Give us eyes this week to see the difference between polish and power, and give us the courage to want the real thing even when it comes wrapped in weakness. Guard the churches we love from teachers who preach a different Jesus, and guard our own hearts, because we are capable of building strongholds too. Where we have measured ourselves against other people, measure us against Christ. Where we have been harsh, teach us His gentleness, and where we have been cowardly, teach us His boldness. Open these letters to us the way You opened them to Corinth, so that when the week ends we are not more impressed with Paul but more devoted to the One he served. In Jesus' name, Amen.
docs.2026-09-13.html: In brief Paul leans in and writes "I, Paul," answering the whisper going around Corinth that his letters roar and the man himself is a coward. His first word back is meekness. Then he describes a war, with weapons that carry God's power, arguments demolished like city walls, and thoughts marched away as prisoners to obey Christ. Jesus shows what that looks like, gentle enough to invite the weary and fierce enough to clear the temple. Meekness is not the opposite of strength. It is strength that belongs to love. Yesterday Yesterday we stood under Acrocorinth, the rock fortress every Corinthian could see from the street, and heard Paul claim that his weapons could bring strongholds down. The people laughing at that claim were sitting inside his church. Today he turns to face them, and the first thing he reaches for is gentleness. Historical Context The Philosophers Called the Mind a Citadel Long before Paul, Greek teachers liked to talk about the mind as a fortress. Plato pictured a young man's soul as an acropolis, a high walled place that could be taken over once its guardians were gone. Later teachers went further and said the truly wise man lived inside an inner citadel no grief or tyrant could breach. The traveling lecturers who came through Corinth traded on that image. Their arguments were siege works, their conclusions were walls, and a man who could not be out-argued was a man who could not be taken. Corinth admired that kind of strength, and the newcomers in the church clearly had it. They spoke well. Paul, by his own admission, did not. That is the world 2 Corinthians 10:1-11 walks into, and it explains why Paul picks the vocabulary he does. He borrows the philosophers' own siege language, the words used for tearing down city walls and for leading prisoners away after a battle, and points it at the philosophers' pride. The fortress of clever reasoning is not admired in his letter. It is the target. And the prisoners of war are thoughts, marched off to obey Christ. The gentleness he leads with is not a softer alternative to that campaign. It is how the campaign is fought, and to a city that measured teachers by how impressive they looked in the open square, that was the strangest battle plan anyone had ever heard. Into the Word Somewhere in 2 Corinthians 10:1-11 Paul stops writing "we" and writes "I, Paul." For nine chapters he has spoken for a team. Now the charges are personal, that his letters are all thunder and his presence is a whisper, and he answers them in his own voice. But the first words out of that voice are not a threat. They are an appeal by the meekness and gentleness of Christ. That is the puzzle we carry today. How does a man open a war by being gentle, and how does gentleness end up being the weapon? 2 Corinthians 10:1 Open ↗ Now by the mildness and gentleness of Christ, I appeal to you—I, Paul, who am humble when face to face with you, but bold when away. Paul's first word back is prautēs, Greek for meekness, and it never meant weakness. It meant power under control, a war horse answering a light rein. He appeals by that quality because it belongs to Christ before it belongs to him. He does not deny the charge hiding inside the verse. Humble when face to face, bold when away. He owns both and treats them as one man, not two. Meekness like that can walk into a battle, and the One holding the rein is the same Christ who was mild with sinners and fierce with lies. 2 Corinthians 10:10-11 Open ↗ 10For some say, “His letters are weighty and forceful, but his physical presence is unimpressive, and his speaking is of no account.” 11Such people should consider that what we are in our letters when absent, we will be in our actions when present. Here is the accusation in the Corinthians' own words. Weighty letters, weak man. Paul does not dispute the facts. His answer is not a promise to be scarier next time (2 Corinthians 10:2). It is a promise of consistency. What the letters are, the man will be. That only works if the letters were never bluster, and it means the gentleness they read as cowardice was a choice he would make again in the room. He also refuses their way of measuring. They were looking at outward appearances (2 Corinthians 10:7). He was looking at what was true. 2 Corinthians 10:3-6 Open ↗ 3For though we live in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh. 4The weapons of our warfare are not the weapons of the flesh. Instead, they have divine power to demolish strongholds. 5We demolish arguments and every presumption set up against the knowledge of God; and we take captive every thought to make it obedient to Christ. 6And we will be ready to punish every act of disobedience, as soon as your obedience is complete. Now Paul redefines the fight. His weapons are not the flesh's weapons of charm, volume, and clever argument. They carry divine power, and their targets are strongholds, arguments, and every proud presumption set up against knowing God. That target list is made of ideas, not people. The prisoners of war are thoughts, marched off to obey Christ. That is why he can be gentle and frightening at once. The demolition is aimed at lies, and the people are the ones being rescued. Then the line that governs everything, 2 Corinthians 10:8. His authority exists to build up, never to tear down. The Corinthians assumed gentle and fierce were opposites, and a lot of us still do. So watch the gentlest man who ever lived on the one afternoon He turned the furniture over. Matthew 21:12-13 Open ↗ 12Then Jesus entered the temple courts and drove out all who were buying and selling there. He overturned the tables of the money changers and the seats of those selling doves. 13And He declared to them, “It is written: ‘My house will be called a house of prayer.’ But you are making it ‘a den of robbers.’” This is the same Jesus who said He was gentle and humble in heart (Matthew 11:29), and here He is flipping tables. The money changers had set up shop in the one courtyard where outsiders were allowed to pray, and they were charging admission to God. Gentleness does not shrug at that. Meekness is not the absence of force. It is force that belongs to love and answers to it. He did the same thing with words when He called the Pharisees whitewashed tombs to their faces (Matthew 23:23-27). Jesus did not lose His temper in either scene. He aimed it. If the war is real, what do you fight it with? Paul answers in another letter with a Roman soldier standing in front of him, and not one item on the list is a personality trait. Ephesians 6:12-17 Open ↗ 12For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the powers of this world’s darkness, and against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly realms. 13Therefore take up the full armor of God, so that when the day of evil comes, you will be able to stand your ground, and having done everything, to stand. 14Stand firm then, with the belt of truth buckled around your waist, with the breastplate of righteousness arrayed, 15and with your feet fitted with the readiness of the gospel of peace. 16In addition to all this, take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming arrows of the evil one. 17And take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. Read the list slowly and notice what is missing. There is no charisma on it, no debating trophy, no commanding presence. Every piece of the armor is either something God has done or something God has said, and the word of God is the only weapon on the list that swings. That is how a thought gets taken captive in 2 Corinthians 10:5. You do not shout a lie out of a person. You answer it with what is true and keep answering until the wall gives. The enemy behind false teaching is not the teacher, and the weapon against it was never going to be a bigger voice. Street Level The Most Dangerous Man in the Room Is the Safest One Walk into a martial arts gym for the first time and you can pick out the instructor without being told. He is not the loudest person on the mat. He is the calmest. The beginners are the ones swinging wild, all shoulders and noise, and they are the ones who leave bruises, because they cannot control what they throw. Then it is your turn to spar with him. He could put you on the floor in about a second, and everyone in the building knows it. What happens instead is strange. Every time your hands drop, his glove taps the exact spot you left open. Not hard. Just enough that you feel it and fix it. Twenty of those in three minutes, and you walk off the mat having been hit more times than you have ever been hit, and somehow built up. Nothing he did was pointed at you. All of it was pointed at your mistakes. That is the thing beginners get backward. They assume gentleness means the power was missing. It was there, fully controlled. He was choosing both the force and the target. The power never left the room. It answered to something better than his temper, and the same hands that could have hurt you were teaching you how not to get hurt. His calm was not the absence of danger. It was danger that had decided what it loved. That is what Paul means by the meekness of Christ. His weapons carried real power, enough to bring down walls of argument, and he never pretended otherwise. But the power answered to love, so every blow landed on a lie and none on the people he was writing to. Gentle and fierce were never two settings. They were one strength, aimed at what needed to fall so that the church could stand. Today’s World The Rabbit Hole Gave Way to Patient Evidence Researchers long assumed that people who believe conspiracy theories cannot be reasoned out of them. Push back and they dig in. Then three researchers tried something quieter. They asked 2,190 believers to describe a conspiracy they held and why it convinced them. Each then had a calm written chat with an AI chatbot that answered those exact reasons with evidence, three exchanges over about eight minutes. Belief in the chosen conspiracy dropped by about 20 percent and held there two months later, even among the deeply entrenched. A professional fact-checker rated more than 99 percent of the chatbot's claims true. A follow-up study in October 2025 asked whether the messenger mattered. Some participants were told they were talking to AI. Others were told only that it was an expert, a label that never said human, though many took it that way. The chatbot's tone was plain or warm and human-sounding. None of it changed the result. Beliefs fell about the same in every version. The authors concluded that the power was in the evidence, not in how trustworthy or friendly the messenger seemed. In June 2026 the journal Science posted a formal warning notice, an Expression of Concern, on the original paper. The authors had found errors in how participants were screened and stray data rows from a code-merging mistake. They report that a corrected analysis gives the same result in direction, significance, and size, and the journal is still reviewing it. The study measured belief in conspiracies, not faith, and a chatbot is not the gospel. Still, it documents what Paul told Corinth. Walls built out of arguments do not fall when someone yells at them. They come down when a patient, accurate answer is set against each stone until nothing is left holding the wall up. Sources Science, PNAS Nexus Durably reducing conspiracy beliefs through dialogues with AI. Science, 2024. Read the source. Dialogues with large language models reduce conspiracy beliefs even when the AI is perceived as human. PNAS Nexus, 2025. Read the source. Editorial Expression of Concern. Science, 2026. Read the source. Christ at the center Paul appeals by the meekness and gentleness of Christ because Christ is where both of those words got their meaning. Jesus stood silent in front of Pilate and He cleared the temple with a whip of cords, and it was the same love doing both. Then He fought the biggest battle in history with the weakest-looking weapon anyone had ever seen. A cross. No army, no argument, no impressive presence, just a man dying outside the city while the crowd measured Him by appearances and found Him lacking. That was the demolition. Sin, death, and every proud reasoning that ever stood between a person and the knowledge of God lost their walls that afternoon, and the captives He led away were us. The authority that could have torn us down was used to build us up, because He let Himself be torn down instead. That is what a stronghold looks like when it falls. Application The next time today you disagree with someone (a group text, a coworker, a family member across the table), do two things at once. Keep your conviction exactly where it is, and drop your volume and your sarcasm to zero. Say the true thing plainly, once, and then stop talking. Tonight, write one line about which of the two was harder. That line will tell you whether your weapon has been truth or force. Discussion Question When you are in a disagreement about faith, or about anything that matters, which comes more naturally to you, going quiet to keep the peace or getting louder to win (think about your last real argument)? What would it look like this week to hold the truth just as firmly while handling the person with the meekness of Christ? Closing Prayer Lord Jesus, You are gentle and humble in heart, and You are the One who turned the tables over, and we confess that we usually manage only one of those at a time. Some of us go quiet when we should speak. Some of us get loud when we should listen. Teach us the strength that answers to Your rein. Where there are fortresses in our own minds, arguments we have built to keep from knowing You fully, bring them down, and take every stubborn thought captive to You. Give the people who teach us the humility to build rather than tear down, and give us the discernment to know the difference. Arm us with what is true instead of what is loud, and when the day of evil comes, let us be found standing, not because we were impressive, but because You were. In Jesus' name, Amen.
docs.2026-09-14.html: In brief The newcomers in Corinth wrote their own reviews. They rated each other, compared each other, and the church was impressed, until Paul pointed out that a ruler which only measures you against you cannot measure anything. He pulls out a surveyor's word instead, the measuring rod God used to mark out his field, and shrinks his bragging rights to a single line from Jeremiah. Boast in the Lord. An old man's finish line proves the point. The only approval worth having comes from the One holding the tape. Yesterday Yesterday Paul leaned into the letter with "I, Paul" and answered the charge of cowardice with meekness, a war horse's strength under a light rein. His weapons were truth rather than volume, and his authority existed to build up. Today the newcomers' favorite weapon comes out. It is a tape measure, and they are always the ones holding it. Historical Context Rome Measured the Colony Before Anyone Moved In When Rome refounded Corinth in 44 BC, the first men on the site were not builders. They were surveyors. Working with a sighting instrument called a groma, they laid a grid of straight lines across the land and carved it into square plots, then handed the plots to the freed slaves and veterans Caesar had sent to fill the empty city. Each boundary was marked with a stone, and the stones were treated as sacred. Rome had a god for boundaries, Terminus, and moving a neighbor's marker in the night was a crime people believed carried a curse. Every settler's family knew exactly which field was theirs, who had assigned it, and where their ground stopped and someone else's began. That is the picture under Paul's odd language in 2 Corinthians 10:12-18 about limits, fields, and areas of influence. He talks like a man holding a survey map. God, not Paul, drew the lines, and God assigned him a plot that reached all the way to Corinth. The newcomers were working a field they had not been given and bragging about a crop they had not planted. Corinth had rules about bragging, too. Self-praise was expected in public life so long as you followed the conventions and did not bore or insult your audience, and a generation after Paul the writer Plutarch even published advice on praising yourself without offending anyone. Paul knew the rules. Today he breaks the game itself by asking who owns the measuring stick. Into the Word Picture the newcomers reading their own reviews. They arrived in Corinth with letters praising them, they rated one another highly, and when they wanted to prove they were the real apostles they pointed at each other. The church was impressed. Paul answers them in 2 Corinthians 10:12-18, and his opening line is almost funny. When people measure themselves by themselves, they show their ignorance, because a ruler that only measures you against you cannot tell you anything. So today's question is a simple one. What are you actually allowed to brag about, and who is holding the tape? 2 Corinthians 10:12 Open ↗ We do not dare to classify or compare ourselves with some who commend themselves. When they measure themselves by themselves and compare themselves with themselves, they show their ignorance. This is the hinge of the whole passage, and it is a diagnosis before it is a rebuke. Paul will not even enter the contest, because the contest cannot produce a result. The newcomers graded themselves on a curve made of each other. Every point of comparison was another man doing the same thing, so the whole group could rise together and learn nothing. That is what Paul calls ignorance. Not stupidity. A missing reference point. Comparison feels like measurement, and it never is. Before he says a word about the right ruler, he takes the wrong one away. 2 Corinthians 10:13-17 Open ↗ 13We, however, will not boast beyond our limits, but only within the field of influence that God has assigned to us—a field that reaches even to you. 14We are not overstepping our bounds, as if we had not come to you. Indeed, we were the first to reach you with the gospel of Christ. 15Neither do we boast beyond our limits in the labors of others. But we hope that as your faith increases, our area of influence among you will greatly increase as well, 16so that we can preach the gospel in the regions beyond you. Then we will not be boasting in the work already done in another man’s territory. 17Rather, “Let him who boasts boast in the Lord.” Now Paul reaches for a surveyor's word, kanōn, Greek for a measuring rod, the straight reed used to mark a field, the root of our word canon. God measured out a field for him, and Corinth was inside it. He got there first, he wants to press on beyond it, and he will not brag about work done in another man's plot. His boast stays inside lines Someone else drew. Then even that boast shrinks to one borrowed sentence. Let him who boasts boast in the Lord. Nothing else qualifies. The moment your brag is about the field instead of the One who assigned it, you have picked up the newcomers' ruler again. Jeremiah 9:24 Open ↗ But let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows Me, that I am the LORD, who exercises loving devotion, justice and righteousness on the earth—for I delight in these things,” declares the LORD. Paul borrowed that one permitted boast from a prophet who watched Jerusalem trust its clever, strong, and rich people right up to the day the Babylonians arrived. The verse just before this one rules out all three. What is left is not a fourth achievement. It is a relationship. Boast that you understand and know Me, God says, and then He describes Himself, the One who practices loving devotion, justice, and righteousness on the earth. A person who boasts in knowing the Lord ends up talking about the Lord's character instead of his own. Paul quotes this line in both of his Corinthian letters (2 Corinthians 10:17). It was the only boast he trusted himself with. 2 Corinthians 10:18 Open ↗ For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends. Here is the grade that counts, and it comes from outside the room. The newcomers commended themselves and each other. Paul had already told Corinth that he reached them first and would not claim another man's work (2 Corinthians 10:14-16), but he does not offer even that as proof of approval. Approval is not something a man can issue to himself. It is the Lord's commendation or it is nothing, and the Lord is not reading the reviews. The ruler belongs to God. So does the report card. So what does a life look like when God's rod measures it from start to finish? The start was a calling, an apostle by the will of God (1 Corinthians 1:1). Here is the finish, written from a Roman prison near the end. 2 Timothy 4:7 Open ↗ I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. Read this as an old man's boast and notice what is missing. He does not say he won. He says he fought the fight, finished the race, and kept the faith, three verbs about staying inside the assignment until it was over. The course was marked out by Someone else, the lane was assigned, the finish line was placed, and all Paul could claim was that he stayed in it. Comparison never came up, because that was never how he was graded. The people who commended themselves in Corinth are nameless today. The man who let God hold the ruler has a finish line the whole church still reads. Street Level Every Clock in the House Agreed The kitchen clock was set from the microwave. The microwave was set from the clock on the stove, and the stove got its time years ago from the alarm clock in the bedroom, which somebody once set by the kitchen clock. Nobody remembers doing any of this. What everybody remembers is that the clocks always matched. You could walk from room to room and check, and the house agreed with itself to the minute, and that agreement felt like information. It felt like knowing what time it was. Then one morning you walk into the interview, or the dentist's office, or your kid's recital, and the room is already ten minutes into something. The confusing part is that you did not feel late. You checked. Every clock you own said you were fine, and every clock you own was wrong by the same eleven minutes, and had been for years. That is the trouble with a standard that only refers to itself. Three clocks agreeing tell you nothing about the time. They only tell you about each other. The fix is not a better argument among the clocks. It is the one signal that comes from outside the house, the time your phone pulls off a tower, traced back to a clock nobody in the family gets a vote on. Set to that, and you stop checking the other rooms. You do not need to. Paul's newcomers were a house full of clocks set to each other, and the church mistook their agreement for accuracy. The standard he reached for came from outside the room. God marked out the field, and God does the commending, and that verdict does not answer to any comparison. A person set to it can walk past every other clock in the house without a glance. Comparison ends the moment the real time arrives. Today’s World Everyone Got an A and Nobody Knew Where They Stood In October 2025 Harvard's dean of undergraduate education delivered a report on the college's own grading, and the numbers were blunt. More than 60 percent of the grades it handed out were A's. Two decades earlier the figure was about 25 percent. The median grade had been an A since 2016. The report concluded that grading at the college "no longer performs its primary functions." A grade that says excellent about nearly everyone says nothing about anyone. A student could compare herself with her classmates all day and still not learn how good her work was. The whole grading scale had drifted upward together until it stopped telling strong work from ordinary work. Most of the faculty accepted the diagnosis. That fall the share of A's fell from 60.2 percent to 53.4 percent. Results announced May 20, 2026, showed that the faculty had voted 458 to 201 to limit A's in each course to 20 percent of the students plus four more, starting in fall 2027. The point of the cap was to make the grade carry information again. Amanda Claybaugh, the dean who wrote the report, gave the reason in one sentence. Students are owed grades "that send clear signals, that give them a good sense of their strengths and weaknesses." The report is about transcripts, not souls, and a faculty vote is not the judgment seat of God. What it shows is the pattern Paul named in Corinth. When a group sets its standard by looking at itself, the standard quietly stops telling the truth, and the people inside it are the last to find out. A measurement carries real information only when it comes from outside the room, and Paul says the one that counts comes from the Lord. Sources The Harvard Crimson, Harvard FAS Harvard College's Grading System Is 'Failing,' Report on Grade Inflation Says. The Harvard Crimson, 2025. Read the source. Harvard Faculty Cut A Grades by Nearly 7 Percentage Points in Fall. The Harvard Crimson, 2026. Read the source. Faculty decisively approve grading changes. Harvard Faculty of Arts and Sciences, 2026. Read the source. Christ at the center Jesus did not build His identity on commending Himself. Ask Him for His credentials and He points to the Father, who commends Him out loud at His baptism and again on the mountain. He said plainly that if He glorified Himself, His glory would mean nothing (John 8:54). He stayed inside the field the Father assigned, a small country of fishing villages and hill towns, and His last report from inside it was that He had finished the work He was given (John 17:4). That is the pattern Paul is copying, and it is also the gift Paul is living on. At the cross the Son who deserved every boast was measured as a criminal, so that people with nothing to brag about could be commended by God as His own. That is why the only boast left is Him. Our righteousness is His, our approval is His, and the tape God holds over us reads the same for every one of us. Christ. Application Today, catch yourself in one comparison as it happens (a scroll through someone's highlight reel, a coworker's win, another family's kid, another church's numbers). The moment you notice it, stop and say out loud one thing God has actually assigned to you in this season and one thing about Him you know to be true. Then go work your own field for ten minutes, a call, a chore, a page of Scripture, something inside your lines. Comparison starves when you stop feeding it your attention. Discussion Question Where do you most often catch yourself measuring your walk with God against someone else's (their Bible knowledge, their ministry, their family, how they pray), and what does that comparison do to you when you win it? If the only approval that counts is the Lord's commendation, what would you stop doing this week, and what would you start? Closing Prayer Father, we confess that we know exactly where we rank. We know who prays better than we do, who serves more, who seems closer to You, and we know who we quietly outscore, and we have felt better about ourselves because of it. Forgive us for grading on a curve You never drew. Take the ruler out of our hands. Show us the field You have measured out for us, the people and the work that are actually ours, and make us content to labor there without looking over the fence. Teach us to boast in one thing only, that we know You, and let every boast turn into talk about Your loving devotion, Your justice, and Your righteousness. When we finish, let it be said of us that we kept the faith in the lane You assigned, and let the commendation we wanted most be Yours. In Jesus' name, Amen.
docs.2026-09-15.html: In brief A father has promised his daughter to one husband, and now smooth strangers are in the house talking her out of him. That is how Paul describes Corinth. The newcomers preach a different Jesus, take a fee for it, and wear the costume of apostles so well that the church cannot see the difference. Jesus had already given the test on a hillside. Wolves dress as sheep, so stop grading the wool and watch the fruit. A costume can change in a minute. Fruit takes a season, and the season always comes. Yesterday Yesterday the newcomers held up their tape measure and Paul took it away. A ruler that only measures you against you cannot measure anything, and the only report card that counts is the Lord's commendation inside the field He assigned. Today Paul stops talking about their measuring habits and says plainly who they are. Historical Context The Serpent Had Worn a Costume Before When Paul writes that Satan disguises himself as an angel of light, he says it as if everyone already knows. Many of his readers did. A Jewish retelling of the Eden story that circulated in Paul's day describes the devil coming back for Eve a second time, this time dressed in the shining appearance of an angel, so that she would trust him before he opened his mouth. Whether or not the Corinthians had heard that exact tale, the point behind it was common knowledge in the synagogue. The serpent's power was never his fangs. It was his wardrobe. He got into the garden by looking like he belonged there, and he got Eve talking by sounding reasonable. Corinth understood costumes from the other direction, too. The city's theater held thousands, and the crowd knew that the same actor could play a king in one scene and a slave in the next by changing his mask and robe between entrances. Nobody in the seats mistook the mask for the man. That is what makes Paul's charge in chapter 11 so sharp. The newcomers had changed into apostles' clothing, and the church, which could spot a costume change from the back row of the theater, could not spot this one from the front pew. Today's passages hand over the only test that works when the wardrobe is perfect. Into the Word Long before Corinth, Jesus sat on a hillside and warned a crowd about wolves that would come dressed as sheep. Paul repeated it to a young pastor (1 Timothy 6:3-5), and Peter promised that false teachers would slip in quietly, with greed underneath (2 Peter 2:1-3). So the problem Paul faces in 2 Corinthians 11:1-15 was not new, and neither is ours. If the costume is convincing and the voice sounds right, how does an ordinary believer tell? Matthew 7:15-20 Open ↗ 15Beware of false prophets. They come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves. 16By their fruit you will recognize them. Are grapes gathered from thornbushes, or figs from thistles? 17Likewise, every good tree bears good fruit, but a bad tree bears bad fruit. 18A good tree cannot bear bad fruit, and a bad tree cannot bear good fruit. 19Every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. 20So then, by their fruit you will recognize them. Jesus does not say you will recognize them by their clothing, because the clothing is the whole trick. Vocabulary is no test either. A few verses later He warns that people will call Him "Lord, Lord" and still be strangers to Him (Matthew 7:21). The test is fruit, what a teaching produces in the people who swallow it, and fruit takes time. A grapevine and a thornbush can look alike in March. By September nobody is confused. Jesus asks His people to be patient and trust what grows over what is worn. Paul takes that test into Corinth, but he does not sound like an inspector. He sounds like a father who has just found strangers in the house talking his daughter out of her engagement. 2 Corinthians 11:2 Open ↗ I am jealous for you with a godly jealousy. For I promised you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ. The jealousy here is a father's, not a rival's. Paul had brought Corinth to Christ the way a father in that world promised a daughter to one husband. His job between the promise and the wedding was to keep her faithful. That is why the false teachers made him fierce. They were not competing with him for a following. They were courting the bride. Every warning that follows comes out of that jealousy, and it is godly because the husband is Christ. 2 Corinthians 11:3-4 Open ↗ 3I am afraid, however, that just as Eve was deceived by the serpent’s cunning, your minds may be led astray from your simple and pure devotion to Christ. 4For if someone comes and proclaims a Jesus other than the One we proclaimed, or if you receive a different spirit than the One you received, or a different gospel than the one you accepted, you put up with it very easily. This is the verse the whole day turns on. Paul's fear is Eve's fear, a mind talked out of simple devotion by someone cunning, and verse 4 gives the danger its shape. A different Jesus. A different spirit. A different gospel. All three still carry the right names. Nobody in Corinth was being asked to abandon Jesus. They were being handed a substitute with the same label, and the last clause is the real indictment. You put up with it very easily. The church's problem was not that it could not detect the switch. It was that it never felt the need to check. 2 Corinthians 11:14-15 Open ↗ 14And no wonder, for Satan himself masquerades as an angel of light. 15It is not surprising, then, if his servants masquerade as servants of righteousness. Their end will correspond to their actions. Here is why the costume works. The verb Paul repeats three times across verses 13 to 15 is metaschēmatizō, Greek for changing your outward form, a costume change. Satan does it as an angel of light, and his servants do it as servants of righteousness. The serpent Paul feared for Corinth (2 Corinthians 11:3) has learned to dress well. A convincing false teacher is not a surprise. It is a family trait. The costume is only skin deep, and the ending is not. Their end will match their deeds, which is Jesus' fruit test stated as a verdict. So why did a smart church fall for it? These false apostles (2 Corinthians 11:13) charged for their teaching, and Paul had refused to, which they read as proof he was second rate (2 Corinthians 11:7-12). He calls it proof of love (2 Corinthians 11:11). And the different gospel (2 Corinthians 11:4) still used the name of Jesus. Paul had watched that happen before, in Galatia. Galatians 1:6-9 Open ↗ 6I am amazed how quickly you are deserting the One who called you by the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel— 7which is not even a gospel. Evidently some people are troubling you and trying to distort the gospel of Christ. 8But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be under a curse! 9As we have said before, so now I say again: If anyone is preaching to you a gospel contrary to the one you received, let him be under a curse! The standard Paul measures every messenger against is not the messenger. It is the message they already received. A different gospel is not a gospel at all. His own team does not get a pass, and neither does an angel from heaven, a line aimed at people modeling their act on an angel of light. The received gospel outranks every credential and every glowing reference, because it was never ours to edit. That is why Paul is calm about the newcomers' résumés, fierce about their sermon, and content to leave their ending to God (2 Corinthians 11:15). The wardrobe was never the issue. The Jesus inside it was. Street Level The Shelf Was a Photograph of a Tree The bookshelf in your first apartment looked like oak. It said oak on the box. It had grain, knots, the warm color, the whole wardrobe of a real tree, and it took an hour and a lost screw to put together. Here is what it actually was. Pressed sawdust wrapped in a thin printed sheet, a photograph of wood glued onto something that is not wood. The print is good. That is the point of the print. Nobody manufactures a fake that fails on sight. The whole craft goes into the surface, because the surface is the only part that has to convince you, and it only has to convince you on the day you carry it home. Two things give it away, and neither one is the look. The first is comparison. Set it beside a real oak board and start hunting for the knot. On the fake you will find the same knot again a shelf or two down, because a print has a repeat and a tree never does. The second is time. Load the shelves with real books and wait two winters. The middle bows. Spill one glass of water and the corner swells and never goes back down. What it was made of was there from the first day. It just took weight and a couple of years to show. The tree was never in it. That is why Paul refused to grade the newcomers on their finish. A counterfeit apostle is built to pass the eye. So he handed the church the only two tests a good surface cannot beat. Hold the teaching against the gospel you first received and look for the repeat. Then watch what it does to people under weight and over time. The Jesus inside either matches the original or He does not, and the fruit will say so. Today’s World The Lot Number Was Real and the Pen Was Not Three times in two years, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has warned patients about counterfeit Ozempic pens found in the American drug supply. The latest alert came on December 5, 2025, after Novo Nordisk, the drug's maker, reported that dozens of fake units had been distributed outside the company's authorized channels and had entered the legitimate U.S. drug supply. The pens were built to pass as the real thing. The only visible tell the FDA could describe was two small words, EXP/LOT, printed beside the date instead of above it. Testing of what was inside the pens was still underway when the warning went out. The April 2025 batch is the one worth remembering. Several hundred counterfeit pens carried lot number PAR0362, and that number was genuine. It belonged to a real production run. What gave the fakes away was the serial number printed with it, a string beginning 51746517 that the company identified as illegitimate. The packaging could not settle the question. The pairing had to be checked against the manufacturer, which is why both the company and the FDA told anyone unsure to call Novo Nordisk before using the pen. Novo Nordisk said plainly that it could not confirm the contents or quality of the counterfeit product, and the FDA seized the units. These alerts are about medicine, not doctrine, and the FDA does not grade sermons. But the pattern is the one Paul warned Corinth about. A counterfeit that borrows a genuine name is the hardest kind to catch, and it is caught the way the pens were, by checking it against the record of what was truly issued and refusing to trust what cannot be verified. Paul handed the church its record. It was the gospel that had reached them first. Sources U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Novo Nordisk FDA warns consumers not to use counterfeit Ozempic (semaglutide) found in U.S. drug supply chain. U.S. Food and Drug Administration, 2025. Read the source. Novo Nordisk warns consumers about counterfeit Ozempic® (semaglutide) injection 1 mg in the US. Novo Nordisk via PR Newswire, 2025. Read the source. Christ at the center Set the two of them side by side. Satan changes his outward form into light so that he can lead people away from God. Jesus, who is the Light, took on real flesh so that He could lead people home, and it was no costume. He was born, He got tired, He bled, and He died, and none of it came off between scenes. That is the difference between a masquerade and an incarnation. One puts on glory to hide what it is. The other laid glory down to show what God is. So when Paul begs Corinth to stay devoted to the Jesus he preached, he is not defending a brand. He is defending the only Bridegroom who ever paid for His bride with His own life, who loved the church and gave Himself up for her to present her to Himself without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:25-27). Check His fruit. It is a cross and an empty tomb. No counterfeit has ever produced either. Application Take out the paper from Sabbath, the sentence you wrote about the Jesus your favorite voice presents. Hold it up to three questions today and write your answers underneath. Does this Jesus need a cross, or does He just need my improvement? Does He ever ask something of me that costs me? After a year of listening, am I more devoted to Christ or more devoted to the teacher? If any answer makes you wince, do not throw the voice out yet. Just start watching the fruit on purpose. Discussion Question Think of the teacher, book, or channel you would hand to a new believer. What fruit has it produced in your life this past year (more patience, more honesty, more Scripture, or mostly more opinions)? If its Jesus began to drift into a slightly different Jesus, would you notice, and what one habit could you build so that you would? Closing Prayer Lord Jesus, You promised us to Yourself, and we confess that we have been an easy bride to talk to. We have listened to voices because they were confident, followed them because they were popular, and never asked what they were doing to our devotion to You. Keep us simple. Keep us pure. Give us the patience of the fruit test, the willingness to watch what a teaching grows in a life before we swallow it, and give us the courage to walk away from a different Jesus no matter how bright the costume. Protect the people in our churches who are young in the faith and cannot yet tell wool from a wolf, and make us the kind of believers who help them see. Above all, keep our eyes on the real You, the One who bled for us and rose for us, until no imitation can hold our attention. In Jesus' name, Amen.
docs.2026-09-16.html: In brief Paul finally agrees to play the newcomers' game. Receive me as a fool, he says, and then he boasts, except the boast is a police record. Five floggings, three beatings with rods, a stoning, three shipwrecks, a night treading water, hunger, cold, and the daily weight of every church he loves. He wins the contest and immediately throws the trophy away, because a thorn taught him where his real strength was. Power lands in weakness, so the scars were never the boast. The grace that carried him through them was. Yesterday Yesterday Paul pulled the mask off the newcomers. They had changed into apostles' clothing, and the church that could spot a costume change in the theater could not spot this one in the pew, so Jesus' fruit test became the only test that worked. Today Paul does something stranger. He puts on their costume himself, for one paragraph, to show how ridiculous it looks. Historical Context Thirty-Nine Lashes Meant He Kept Coming Back Every synagogue kept a strap, and every Jewish man knew what thirty-nine meant. The law in Deuteronomy allowed a judge to have a guilty man beaten, but it capped the blows at forty so that a brother would not be degraded in front of his own people. To stay safely under the limit, the practice was to stop at thirty-nine. The blows were counted, the man was bound, and the community that had raised him watched. It was a punishment for insiders. A Gentile would never receive it, and neither would a Jew who had walked away from the synagogue, because the synagogue had no claim on him anymore. That is what makes Paul's number so striking. Five times. He could have avoided every one of them by doing what the newcomers would have called sensible, staying out of synagogues and preaching only where he was welcome. Instead he kept walking back into the one room where he knew the strap was waiting, because his own people were in it. The Roman rods were a different matter, a magistrate's punishment for troublemakers who could not claim citizen protection, the kind Paul took in Philippi. Between the two, his back carried the marks of both worlds he was trying to reach. When he lists them for Corinth, he is not asking for pity. He is showing them what it looks like when a servant refuses to stop coming back. Into the Word Imagine a man who hates bragging being forced into a bragging contest to save his children. That is Paul in 2 Corinthians 11:16-28. He has just exposed the newcomers as counterfeits (2 Corinthians 11:1-15), and now he does the thing he has refused to do for ten chapters. He boasts. But he announces first that it is foolishness, he keeps apologizing while he does it, and the résumé he produces would get anyone else laughed out of Corinth. Today's question is what a boast looks like in the hands of a man who has decided the boast is not the point. 2 Corinthians 11:16-21 Open ↗ 16I repeat: Let no one take me for a fool. But if you do, then receive me as a fool, so that I too may boast a little. 17In this confident boasting of mine, I am not speaking as the Lord would, but as a fool. 18Since many are boasting according to the flesh, I too will boast. 19For you gladly put up with fools, since you are so wise. 20In fact, you even put up with anyone who enslaves you or exploits you or takes advantage of you or exalts himself or strikes you in the face. 21To my shame I concede that we were too weak for that! Speaking as a fool, however, I can match what anyone else dares to boast about. Paul sets the terms before he plays. This is foolishness, he says, not the Lord's way of talking, and he only does it because the church listens to fools. Then comes the line that should have made Corinth wince. They had put up with teachers who enslaved them, took their money, looked down on them, and even struck them in the face, and they had read all of that as authority. Paul's sarcasm is a scalpel. We were too weak to treat you like that, he says, and everyone knew what he meant. The newcomers had mistaken abuse for strength, and the church had mistaken being bullied for being led. So Paul agrees to boast, but he has already told you how to read it. Anything that follows is a fool's speech, and the fool knows it. Then he plays. He matches the newcomers' pedigree point for point (2 Corinthians 11:22-23), the same heritage they were so proud of (2 Corinthians 11:22), and on the one line that matters, servants of Christ, he claims more (2 Corinthians 11:23). Here is his proof of more. 2 Corinthians 11:22-28 Open ↗ 22Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they descendants of Abraham? So am I. 23Are they servants of Christ? (I am speaking as if I were out of my mind.) I am so much more: in harder labor, in more imprisonments, in worse beatings, in frequent danger of death. 24Five times I received from the Jews the forty lashes minus one. 25Three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, three times I was shipwrecked. I spent a night and a day in the open sea. 26In my frequent journeys, I have been in danger from rivers and from bandits, in danger from my countrymen and from the Gentiles, in danger in the city and in the country, in danger on the sea and among false brothers, 27in labor and toil and often without sleep, in hunger and thirst and often without food, in cold and exposure. 28Apart from these external trials, I face daily the pressure of my concern for all the churches. In a city that boasted about victories, Paul boasts about damage. Every line is a loss. Five times the synagogue strap (2 Corinthians 11:24). Rods, a stoning, three shipwrecks, and a day and a night treading water (2 Corinthians 11:25). Danger from every direction, including from people who called themselves brothers (2 Corinthians 11:26). Sleepless, hungry, cold (2 Corinthians 11:27). Read as a résumé, it is a disaster. Read as evidence, it is unanswerable, because every wound came from walking toward people with the gospel when walking away would have been easier. Then the climax, and it is not a wound. It is worry, the daily weight of every church he loves (2 Corinthians 11:28). The newcomers had letters. Paul had scars, and the scars were the letters. If Paul stopped there, he would have won the contest on the newcomers' own terms, the toughest man in the room. He does not stop. He tells them about a thorn he begged God three times to remove (2 Corinthians 12:7), and about the answer he got instead. 2 Corinthians 12:9-10 Open ↗ 9But He said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness.” Therefore I will boast all the more gladly in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest on me. 10That is why, for the sake of Christ, I delight in weaknesses, in insults, in hardships, in persecutions, in difficulties. For when I am weak, then I am strong. This is where the boast moves house. The word Paul uses is astheneia, Greek for weakness, the ordinary word for sickness and frailty, the condition of a person who cannot do it himself. Jesus does not remove it. He answers it. My grace is enough, and My power is finished, brought to its full strength, in exactly that condition. So Paul does something no Corinthian would have predicted after that list. He stops boasting about what he survived and starts boasting about what he cannot do, because that is where the power of Christ settles on him. The insults and hardships stay on the list, but their meaning flips. They are no longer proof that Paul is tough. They are the places where Christ has room to be strong. The list was never the boast. The grace was. Street Level You Woke Up in Your Own Bed Almost everybody has one of these memories. You fell asleep in the back seat on the way home from somewhere, a long drive, a late night, your head against the window. The next thing you knew, it was morning and you were in your own bed with your shoes off. No memory of the driveway. No memory of the stairs. Somewhere in there a parent unbuckled you, got you up onto a shoulder, opened the front door with a hip, and climbed the stairs in the dark carrying dead weight that kept sliding, then went back down for the bags. You never saw any of it. You just woke up home. Ask the parent about it years later and they remember the cost. The arm that went numb halfway up. The back that complained the next morning. The night they nearly dropped you on the landing. None of it got mentioned at breakfast, and none of it was the point. The point is who got carried. The kid who insisted he was awake and could walk stumbled in on his own and remembers every step. The kid who was out cold, who could not have taken one step, arrived in bed without lifting a finger. The parent's strength did all of it, and it only did all of it for the one who could not. Paul's scars are the parent's numb arm, the price of getting people home, and love does not mention them until it is made to. But the boast lands somewhere else. Grace covers what is missing, and Christ's power rests on the person who has stopped pretending to walk. "When I am weak, then I am strong" is a sleeping child's sentence. He did not get himself to bed. He was carried. Today’s World The Scientist Who Admitted Limits Was Trusted More A team of psychologists asked what happens to a scientist's credibility when she admits the limits of what she knows. Across five preregistered studies with 2,034 participants, published in Nature Human Behaviour in late 2024, readers met a scientist named Dr. Moore in an article. In one version a colleague says she "is not afraid to assert what she knows." In the other, she "is not afraid to admit when she doesn't yet know something." Readers trusted the second Dr. Moore more, believed her research more, and in a later study were more willing to follow a scientist's advice. The effect held whether the scientist was a man or a woman and across racial backgrounds. Certainty did not buy credibility. Admitted limits did. One more finding keeps this honest. In the final study the researchers had the scientist signal humility in different ways. When she spoke about herself, admitting she does not yet know everything, readers saw her as humble and still believed her research. When she instead listed the weaknesses of her own results, readers rated her as humble too, but belief in the research fell below that of a scientist who said nothing at all. Humility landed when it belonged to the person. Attached to the work as a disclaimer, it cost her. The study measured trust in research, not faith, and says nothing about grace. What it shows is the instinct Paul was counting on in Corinth. A voice that admits what it cannot do is more believable than a voice that never loses, and the admission has to be real. Paul's weakness was never a speaking tactic. It was the plain report of a man who knew where his own strength ran out and had met the One whose power begins there. Source Nature Human Behaviour The effect of seeing scientists as intellectually humble on trust in scientists and their research. Nature Human Behaviour, 2024. Read the source. Christ at the center The voice that told Paul "My power is perfected in weakness" was not speaking in theory. It belonged to a man who had been flogged, mocked, and nailed up outside a city while people measured Him by appearances and walked away. By every standard Corinth used, the cross was the weakest moment in history, and it was where God did His mightiest work. That is why Jesus can answer a thorn with grace instead of removal. He knows weakness from the inside, and He knows what His Father accomplished through it. So when Paul boasts in his weaknesses, he is not being brave. He is standing where his Lord stood and expecting the same thing to happen, resurrection power showing up in a body that cannot save itself. That is the gospel in one sentence. We are not saved by getting strong. We are saved by a crucified Savior whose grace is enough, and the places we cannot fix are the places He most likes to work. Application Write your own list today, but not of things you have survived. Write the three places you feel weakest right now (a marriage that is strained, a body that keeps failing you, a job that is not working, a temptation you keep losing to). Beside each one, copy out the sentence Paul heard, "My grace is sufficient for you," and pray that line over that place before you go to bed. Do not ask for the weakness to be explained. Ask for Christ's power to rest on it, and leave the list where you will see it tomorrow. Discussion Question When you have to prove yourself (a job interview, your spouse's family, a new church), what do you put forward first and what stays hidden? Paul led with his scars and then with his weakness, so what would change in one relationship this week if the weak place became the first thing you were willing to show? Closing Prayer Lord Jesus, we have spent a lot of energy looking strong. We have hidden the thorns, dressed up the failures, and hoped nobody would notice the places where we cannot do it ourselves, and we confess that we have sometimes trusted teachers for the same reason, because they looked like they never lost. Teach us to read the list of scars the way You read it, as the marks of love that kept walking toward people. Then teach us the harder thing, to stop boasting about what we survived and start bringing You what we cannot fix. Rest Your power on our weak places today, on the marriage, the body, the job, the habit, and let people see a strength in us that is plainly not ours. Make us servants who keep coming back to the people who need You, whatever it costs. In Jesus' name, Amen.
docs.2026-09-17.html: In brief A father is packing for a third trip home, and he is afraid of what he will find. Not the strangers this time. His own children, still quarreling, still gossiping, still refusing to turn from sexual sin, two letters after he begged them to stop. Paul gives notice that this visit comes with authority, and then he prays he will never have to use it. Then he hands them one exam question. Is Christ in you? The test was never meant to condemn them. It was meant to prove them real, and a real coin rings true. Yesterday Yesterday Paul played the boasting game for one paragraph and won it with a list of scars, five floggings, three shipwrecks, a night in the sea. Then he threw the trophy away, because a thorn had taught him that Christ's power lands in weakness. Today the same weak man announces that he is coming back, and this time he will not spare anyone. Historical Context Athens Paid a Man to Test Every Coin in the Market Four centuries before Paul, the city of Athens passed a law that tells you how seriously the Greek world took counterfeits. It hired a public coin tester and sat him in the marketplace with a set of scales and a cutting tool. Anyone could bring him a silver coin. If it rang true, he handed it back approved, and by law the seller had to accept it. If it was a plated fake, he cut a gash across its face on the spot and confiscated it. The tester's whole job was to make honest trade possible, because a market where nobody trusted the money was a market where nothing moved. Corinth, a trading city with its own mint, lived by the same rule. Every coin was a question until somebody tested it. Paul reaches for that world when he tells the church to examine themselves. The verb he chooses is the coin tester's verb, the word for testing something in order to approve it, and it changes the mood of the whole chapter. He is not setting a trap. He expects the coin to ring true. He also brings a second piece of ancient procedure with him, the rule from the law of Moses that no charge stands without two or three witnesses. His two earlier visits have already testified. The third one will settle the matter. A city that cut fakes in half in the marketplace understood exactly what Paul meant, and it understood the mercy in it too. The tester wanted to hand the coin back. Into the Word Read the whole stretch from 2 Corinthians 12:14-13:10 and you can hear a suitcase being packed. Paul is coming a third time, and he says the thing every parent says, I am not after your money, I am after you (2 Corinthians 12:14). Everything he has written, all the defending and boasting, has been for one purpose, to build them up (2 Corinthians 12:19). But building sometimes requires demolition, and today's question is what love does when it comes home and finds the same sins still living in the house. 2 Corinthians 12:20-21 Open ↗ 20For I am afraid that when I come, I may not find you as I wish, and you may not find me as you wish. I fear that there may be quarreling, jealousy, rage, rivalry, slander, gossip, arrogance, and disorder. 21I am afraid that when I come again, my God will humble me before you, and I will be grieved over many who have sinned earlier and have not repented of their acts of impurity, sexual immorality, and debauchery. Two lists, and the order matters. The first one is the church's everyday weather (2 Corinthians 12:20), quarreling, jealousy, rage, rivalry, slander, gossip, arrogance, disorder. Paul catalogs the same rot elsewhere (Romans 1:29-31 and Galatians 5:19-21), and the first two items were already Corinth's problem in his first letter (1 Corinthians 3:3). Two letters later, still there. The second list is the sexual sin some had never turned from (2 Corinthians 12:21). Notice that the respectable sins and the scandalous ones share one paragraph. Gossip sits next to immorality with no line between them. And notice what Paul dreads. Not confronting them. Being humbled and grieved by them. He is not afraid of them. He is afraid for them. So he gives notice, the way a parent does before the car pulls in. The man who opened this section with the meekness of Christ (2 Corinthians 10:1) said then that he would be ready to deal with every disobedience once the church's own obedience was complete (2 Corinthians 10:6). The time has come. 2 Corinthians 13:1-4 Open ↗ 1This is the third time I am coming to you. “Every matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses.” 2I already warned you the second time I was with you. So now in my absence I warn those who sinned earlier and everyone else: If I return, I will not spare anyone, 3since you are demanding proof that Christ is speaking through me. He is not weak in dealing with you but is powerful among you. 4For He was indeed crucified in weakness, yet He lives by God’s power. For we are also weak in Him, yet by God’s power we will live with Him concerning you. The third visit is the third witness (2 Corinthians 13:1), and Paul says plainly that this time he will not spare. They wanted proof that Christ speaks through him, and the proof is going to look like the cross. Jesus was crucified in weakness and lives by the power of God, and Paul says his own ministry runs on the same two rails, weak in Him, alive by God's power toward them (2 Corinthians 13:4). That settles what kind of discipline is coming, and it is not Paul losing his patience. It is resurrection power arriving in a room that has been treating the crucified Lord as if He were weak. The weakness they mocked in their apostle was never the absence of power. It was the shape power takes on its way in. You would expect a man with that kind of authority to pray for a clean win. Paul prays the opposite. He asks God that they will do what is right even if it makes him look like he failed, because their restoration is the whole point (2 Corinthians 13:7-9). Then he hands them the exam. 2 Corinthians 13:5 Open ↗ Examine yourselves to see whether you are in the faith; test yourselves. Do you not realize that Jesus Christ is in you—unless you fail the test? They had been testing Paul for months. He turns the test around and gives them the coin tester's word, dokimazō, Greek for examining something to approve it, the way silver is proved and handed back as genuine. That is the mood of the exam. Paul expects them to pass, and he tells them the answer. Jesus Christ is in you. Being in the faith is not a feeling or a membership card. It is Christ living in a person, and a person He lives in cannot stay comfortable with the lists in chapter 12. The power that raised Him leads to turning, and the turning is how the coin rings true. Failing means nothing is under the plating. So the week's question lands where Paul always aimed it. Not whether Paul is real. Whether Christ is in them. Street Level The Inspector Came Back to Hang an A Anyone who has worked in a kitchen knows the feeling when the health inspector walks in with the clipboard. She has real authority. If she finds the wrong thing, she can close the doors that afternoon, and she would rather do almost anything else. Closing restaurants is not why she took the job. So the first visit ends with a list, not a padlock. The thermometer nobody uses. The towel draped over the sink. The raw chicken stored on the shelf above the lettuce. Small things, the kind a busy crew stops noticing, and every one of them on the same sheet as the big ones. Then she gives you a date. "I will be back in thirty days." The thirty days are the whole point. The return visit is not a trap. It is a test built to be passed, and everybody knows what it is checking, because she wrote it down. She is not coming back to admire the new sign or the fresh paint. She is coming to see what the kitchen has stopped doing. The towel gone. The thermometer in use. The chicken on the bottom shelf. If the changes are real, she signs the form and hangs the letter in the window, and the whole neighborhood can read that this place was examined and approved. The closure order stayed in her folder the entire time. It never had to come out. Paul is packing for the return visit. He has the authority, he has given the date, and his prayer is that he never has to use it. The exam he hands Corinth is built the same way. It is meant to approve, it comes with the answer already on it, Christ in you, and it is graded by what has stopped. The gossip, the rivalry, the sin nobody flagged. When those go, the grade goes in the window. Today’s World The Rudeness Nobody Wrote Up Still Ran the Bill The Society for Human Resource Management is a professional association for people who run hiring and workplace policy. It tracks rudeness in everyday life and on the job with a quarterly survey called the Civility Index. Its Q3 2025 report, drawn from 1,478 U.S. workers surveyed in July 2025, found that 74 percent had experienced or witnessed uncivil behavior in everyday life during the month before. Of those, 51 percent said at least one incident they saw happened at work. The count includes acts a worker witnessed, not only ones aimed at them. By the association's own estimate, workplace incivility costs American organizations about 2.1 billion dollars every day in lower productivity and missed work. Workers who ran into it said they deliberately stayed home an average of 1.7 days that month. The report's most telling numbers are about tolerance. Thirty-five percent of workers said their manager ignored acts of incivility, and 44 percent said their manager could have done more to prevent it. The association concludes that the scores show a continued need "to curb incivility before it escalates to more harmful levels." Small rudeness that no one corrects does not stay small. It escalates, it costs, and it keeps people home. A workplace survey is not a verdict on a church, and its authors were not reading 2 Corinthians. But the pattern they measure is the one Paul feared. His first list was not the scandalous sins. It was gossip, rivalry, and quarreling, the respectable rudeness a community learns to live with. He treated those as seriously as the sins nobody excuses, because he knew what small disorder grows into when a church looks away. The exam he handed Corinth was built to catch it early, while turning was still the easy part. Source SHRM SHRM Civility Index Q3 2025 Results. SHRM (Society for Human Resource Management), 2025. Read the source. Christ at the center The unrepentant in Corinth did not get an execution notice. They got an appeal, and the appeal came from a man copying his Lord. Jesus is the One who was crucified in weakness and lives by the power of God, and He is also the One who is coming back, with authority. Yet the Judge who is coming is the same Jesus who took the verdict first. He was cut like a counterfeit so that counterfeits could be made genuine. That is why Paul can hand the church an exam with the answer already written on it. Christ is in you. Not because they had been good, but because He had been given. The power that leads to turning from sin is not willpower. It is the risen life of Jesus inside a person, the same power that walked out of the tomb. So the test is not a threat hanging over believers. It is a promise being checked. If He is in you, it will show. Application Take the eight words from 2 Corinthians 12:20 (quarreling, jealousy, rage, rivalry, slander, gossip, arrogance, disorder) and read them as a checklist of your own last week, not somebody else's. Circle one. Before the day ends, do what repentance does with it. Apologize to the person, delete the thread, give back the credit you took, or simply confess it to God by name. Then say out loud the answer Paul already gave you, "Christ is in me," and go act as if it is true, because it is. Discussion Question Which sins on Paul's first list would people in your church treat as respectable (gossip, rivalry, quarreling), and which would get someone disciplined? If Paul puts them all in one paragraph and expects Christ's power to turn us from every item, what would an honest self-examination look like for you, and who could you trust to help you do it? Closing Prayer Lord Jesus, You are coming back, and we want to be found as You wish to find us. We confess that some of the sins on Paul's list have become so ordinary in us that we stopped calling them sin, the quarreling we call conviction, the gossip we call concern, the rivalry we call ambition. Examine us. Test us, and let the test prove You are in us, because we have no other hope of passing it. Where we have not turned from what we know is wrong, turn us today by Your power, the same power that raised You from the dead.
