Give our churches the courage to correct one another the way Paul did, with authority held in reserve and restoration as the whole aim, and make us people who pray for each other's wholeness more than for our own vindication. Ring true in us, Lord. In Jesus' name, Amen.
docs.2026-09-18.html: Week in Review A rock fortress, a tape measure, a costume, a synagogue strap, and a coin tester. That was Corinth's week, and underneath every scene sat one question, what strength looks like when it belongs to the crucified Jesus. ☩Sabbath: Dealing With False Teachers. Under Acrocorinth, Paul claimed weapons that demolish strongholds, and the memory text set the week's rule that a counterfeit falls to God's power, never to our volume. ☩Sunday: Spiritual War. "I, Paul" answered the charge of cowardice with meekness, strength under a light rein, aimed by an authority that exists to build up rather than tear down. ☩Monday: Boasting in the Lord. The newcomers' ruler only measured them against themselves, so Paul boasted inside the field God assigned and left the commending to God. ☩Tuesday: False Teachers Identified. Wolves wear wool and Satan wears light, so the test is the fruit and the Jesus being preached, never the costume. ☩Wednesday: Sufferings for the Sake of the Gospel. Paul won the boasting game with a list of scars and then moved the boast to weakness, where Christ's power rests. ☩Thursday: Appeal to the Unrepentant. The third visit comes with authority and a prayer never to use it, and the exam has the answer written on it. Christ in you. Historical Context A City That Trusted Whatever Looked Strong Put the week's scenes side by side and a portrait of Corinth emerges. A fortress on the rock above town that everyone assumed could not be taken. Lecturers who bragged that their minds were citadels. Survey stones that told each family exactly what was theirs. A theater where a costume change fooled nobody, and a pulpit where one fooled everybody. A synagogue strap that only ever landed on men who kept coming back. A coin tester whose whole job was telling silver from plating. Corinth was a city that respected strength, measured it constantly, and had learned the hard way that a great deal of what looked strong was hollow. Into that city came a small man whose speaking was said to be of no account, and everything about him read as weak by local standards. No fee, no polish, no letters of praise, a back full of scars and a thorn he could not pray away. The newcomers who followed him read the room perfectly and gave Corinth what it trusted. Paul gave it the cross instead. He argued like a siege engineer, measured like a surveyor, unmasked like a theater critic, and tested like the man with the scales, and at every turn he pointed the city's own instincts toward a strength it had never considered, a crucified Lord who lives by the power of God. That is the world these four chapters were written for, and it is not far from ours. What This Week Clarifies The Gentle Man Was Never Bluffing The week opened with a puzzle it never quite let go of. Paul appeals by the meekness of Christ on Sunday and promises on Thursday that he will not spare anyone. A reader could be forgiven for wondering which Paul is the real one, the gentle one or the fierce one, and whether the gentleness was a tactic he planned to drop the moment it stopped working. 2 Corinthians 10:8 Open ↗ For even if I boast somewhat excessively about the authority the Lord gave us for building you up rather than tearing you down, I will not be ashamed. This is the sentence that holds both Pauls together. His authority came from the Lord, and it came with a purpose stamped on it, building up rather than tearing down. Gentleness is not the opposite of authority. It is what authority looks like when its job is construction. Force is not the opposite of gentleness either. It is what the same authority does when lies stand where people need to live. Sunday's war horse and Thursday's third visit are one animal answering one rein. Paul could threaten without bluffing and soften without surrendering because the target never moved. Lies come down. People get built. He was not ashamed of that authority because it was never his to be proud of. This settles a question many of us carry into every hard conversation, whether being kind means being soft. It does not. It means knowing what you are building and refusing to tear down the person while you take down the lie. Strength with a purpose can afford to be gentle. Strength without one cannot afford to be anything else. The Trophy Went Back on the Shelf Monday drew a hard line. Boast in the Lord and in nothing else. Then Wednesday read like a chapter of boasting, floggings and shipwrecks and sleepless nights, one after another. It is fair to ask whether Paul broke his own rule two days after making it. And Wednesday raised a second puzzle. Paul boasted in weakness, yet the rest of the week faulted Corinth for being weak. Are those the same weakness? 2 Corinthians 12:9-10 Open ↗ 9But He said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness.” Therefore I will boast all the more gladly in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest on me. 10That is why, for the sake of Christ, I delight in weaknesses, in insults, in hardships, in persecutions, in difficulties. For when I am weak, then I am strong. Paul did not break Monday's rule. A boast about victories can be copied by anyone with a good story. A boast in the Lord has to land somewhere the boaster is not, and Paul found it in his weakness, where the power of Christ came to rest. Every scar was a spot where he could not save himself and grace was enough. But not every condition called weakness is the weakness Paul boasts about. His was brought honestly to Christ and leaned on grace. Corinth's dodged the truth, put up with sin and bullying leaders, and leaned on whoever spoke most impressively. Paul's weakness made room for Christ's power. Corinth's weakness only made room for the wolves. This settles what it means to boast in the Lord, and which weakness counts. It is telling the truth about the places you could not do it, and naming who did. Weakness that leans on Christ becomes the place His power lands. Weakness that refuses His truth is not a virtue, and it still needs repentance. The Exam Had the Answer Printed on It Five days of the week were spent learning to test other people. Check the fruit. Check the Jesus being preached. Check the gospel against the one you received. Then Thursday turned the test around and pointed it at the church itself, and a reader could feel the floor tilt. Was that a trap? After a week of examining false teachers, who exactly ended up on trial? 2 Corinthians 13:5 Open ↗ Examine yourselves to see whether you are in the faith; test yourselves. Do you not realize that Jesus Christ is in you—unless you fail the test? The test Paul hands the church is the same one he applied to the newcomers all week, and that is the point. A fruit test that only points outward becomes a way of feeling superior, which is the newcomers' disease. So Paul turns it around and tells the church how to pass. Jesus Christ is in you. He does not ask them to prove they are impressive. He asks them to notice who lives in them and whether His life is showing in what they turn from. That is why Thursday's coin tester belonged here. The examination was designed to approve, and the standard was never Paul, never a teacher, never a feeling. It was the presence of Christ. This settles the fear that self-examination is a spiritual dead end. It is only a dead end if you are looking for your own goodness. Look for Christ instead, and the exam becomes a promise being checked. If He is in you, the turning will show, and the turning is enough. Still Speaking They Park the Trucks on It First Before some new bridges open, engineers do something that looks reckless. They line up loaded dump trucks, drive them out to the middle of the span, and park. Then they measure how far the deck bends under the weight. Nobody on the crew is hoping it fails. The test exists to sign the certificate, and the numbers they want to see are not zero. Steel is built to give a little under load and come back, and the small sag they measure is the design doing its job. What no engineer will do is certify a bridge by looking at it. Massive stone looks strong. Thin steel looks weak. Neither look holds a truck. Corinth certified by looking, and so do we. We are drawn to the confident voice, the full room, the leader who never seems to lose, and we are quietly ashamed of the places in our own lives and churches that visibly sag. Underneath that is a suspicion that a faith which cannot out-argue or out-shine its rivals must be losing. Paul spent four chapters taking that suspicion apart. His weapons were not the weapons of the flesh (2 Corinthians 10:4), and the Lord he preached was crucified in weakness and lives by God's power (2 Corinthians 13:4). The cross looked like the span giving way. It was the load being carried. Every weight sin and death could bring rolled onto that one place, and it held, and three days later it came back. That changes what your weak places are. The marriage that strains, the habit you keep losing to, the church with more folding chairs than people, none of these is proof that the structure is fake. They are the spans where weight actually lands, and Paul heard the answer for them from Jesus Himself, that grace is enough and power is perfected in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9). A counterfeit never learns this, because a counterfeit is all surface. It photographs beautifully, it has never been asked to hold anything, and it looks like the stronger of the two until the day something heavy has to cross it. Then the fruit shows (Matthew 7:16). So stop measuring your faith by how solid it looks next to someone else's. And stop fearing the test. A load test is not a threat to a real bridge. It is the day the bridge gets to prove what was under it all along. Paul's exam works the same way. Christ in you is the steel, and the examination is designed to certify that He is there. Let the trucks roll on. Feel the give. That is not the sound of something failing. It is the sound of a strength that was never yours, holding. Christ at the Center of the Week Every day this week ended in the same place. Sabbath promised that the real Jesus would not look like a fortress but like a cross. Sunday found His meekness and His overturned tables to be one love. Monday saw Him point to His Father for commendation and finish the work His Father assigned. Tuesday set His incarnation against Satan's costume, real flesh against borrowed light. Wednesday heard His voice tell a suffering apostle that grace was enough, because He had learned weakness from the inside. Thursday saw Him as the Judge who took the verdict first and now lives in the very people He warns. Put those together and you have the answer to the week's question. The strength of Jesus is not a louder or more impressive version of the strength Corinth admired. It is a different kind altogether, power that walks into weakness on purpose and comes out the other side alive. That is why a counterfeit Jesus is so easy to sell and so deadly to buy. The fake always looks stronger, right up to the moment it has to save somebody. The real One was crucified in weakness and lives by the power of God, and He is in you. Weekend Practice Before Sunday, set aside twenty minutes to take the exam on purpose. Read 2 Corinthians 13:5 out loud, then answer three questions in writing. Where did Christ's presence show up this week in something I turned away from? Where did I boast, even silently, in a place I was strong, and how would that story sound with grace in the lead? Which voice in my life, if any, has been passing the costume test but failing the fruit test? Finish by reading the memory text one more time and thanking God that the fight was never yours to win by looking strong. Closing Prayer for the Week Lord Jesus, You were crucified in weakness and You live by the power of God, and this week has shown us how little we understand that. We have admired fortresses. We have measured ourselves by each other. We have trusted costumes and been impressed by volume, and we have hidden our weaknesses as if they disqualified us from Your service. Forgive us, and teach us strength all over again. Give our churches leaders whose authority builds and never tears down, teachers whose Jesus needs a cross, and members patient enough to watch the fruit before they follow the voice. Where a different Jesus has crept into our thinking, demolish that stronghold with truth and take our thoughts captive to You. Then do the hardest thing of all. Move our boast off our victories and onto Your grace, so that the story of our lives tells people about You. Examine us this weekend, and let the examination find You in us, turning us, holding us, ringing true. In Jesus' name, Amen.
docs.2026-09-19.html: In brief Somewhere in Corinth a reader reaches the last lines of a letter that has argued, pleaded, and warned for thirteen chapters, and the room waits to hear how it ends. It ends with a blessing. Grace from Jesus, love from God, fellowship from the Spirit, handed to all of them, the loyal and the stubborn alike. This week walks through that one sentence a name at a time and finds the whole gospel folded inside it. The last word Paul had for a divided church was not a rule. It was a gift with three names on it. Last week Last week ended on a bridge with the trucks parked in the middle of it, the measured give under weight being the sound of a strength that was never ours, holding. Christ in you was the steel. This week Paul writes the closing sentence of his last surviving letter to Corinth, and it is a blessing with three names in it. Historical Context Greek Letters Usually Ended With Be Strong Read through a stack of ordinary Greek letters dug out of the Egyptian sand from Paul's century and many of them end the same way, with a one-word farewell that means be strong. It worked the way our sincerely or take care works, a formula so ordinary that nobody read it twice. It was common enough that the Jerusalem church used it when it wrote to the Gentile believers in Antioch (Acts 15:29). Be strong. Then the letter was rolled up and handed to whoever was sailing that way. None of Paul's surviving letters ends that way. He had been writing to Corinth for several years by this point. The two letters we have mention others that did not survive, and a visit so painful he did not want to repeat it (2 Corinthians 2:1). Thirteen chapters of this letter have just told the church to examine itself. So the reader in the house church reaches the final paragraph (2 Corinthians 13:11) braced for one more warning and hears five quick commands instead. Rejoice. Be put back together, the same word Paul used at the start of his first letter when he begged them to mend their divisions (1 Corinthians 1:10). Encourage one another. Agree. Live in peace. Then, where be strong should go, he writes a sentence with three names in it. Strength was never going to come from the Corinthians. It was going to come to them. This Week’s Memory Text Every one of Paul's surviving letters ends with grace. Only this one ends with all three names at once, and it went to the church that had given him the most grief. 2 Corinthians 13:14 Open ↗ The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with all of you. Notice who is standing where. The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ. The love of God. The fellowship of the Holy Spirit. Paul names Jesus first, and he gives Him the title Kyrios, the Greek word for Lord, a master with the right to command. In the Greek Old Testament Paul grew up reading, that same word stood in for the personal name of God Himself. So a man raised to guard the oneness of God sets the Lord Jesus in one breath with God and the Spirit and asks all three to be with a church. The creeds that later spelled out the Trinity were still centuries away. Paul simply blessed people the way he had met God, as grace, as love, and as company. Then he says be with all of you. Not the loyal ones. All of you. The week takes the blessing apart one name at a time and then puts it back together. Sunday starts with grace, the Lord who was rich becoming poor for you (2 Corinthians 8:9), the word that opens and closes every surviving letter of his (Romans 16:20). Monday sits with the love of God, who is love and proved it by sending (1 John 4:8-11). Tuesday hears a title found nowhere else in Scripture, the God of love and peace. Wednesday asks what fellowship with the Spirit means and whether the Spirit is a someone or a something (Philippians 2:1-2). Thursday watches all three work one rescue in three verses (Galatians 4:4-6). And under all of it runs the comfort Paul opened this letter with (2 Corinthians 1:3-7), received from God so it could be handed on. This Week’s Road Map ☩Sunday: The Grace of Jesus. Grace opens and closes every surviving letter Paul wrote, and Sunday asks what it cost. ☩Monday: The Love of God. God is love, and the proof is a sending, a Son handed over while we were still sinners. ☩Tuesday: The God of Love. Paul gives God a title found nowhere else in Scripture, and its peace is the kind that mends a whole person. ☩Wednesday: The Fellowship of the Holy Spirit. The Spirit is a Person who searches, teaches, and testifies, and fellowship with Him is where fellowship with each other begins. ☩Thursday: Our Triune God. Grace, love, and fellowship come from Father, Son, and Spirit together, in one rescue told in three verses. ☩Friday: Further Thought. The week gathers around one blessing and asks what changes for people sent out under it. Christ at the center Watch where Jesus stands in this blessing. He is named first, ahead of the Father, which is not the order anyone expects, and it is hard to believe it is an accident. The Corinthians did not come to know the love of God by reasoning their way up to it. They met it in a Man who was rich and became poor for them, and only afterward could they say the Father is love and the Spirit is with us. Grace is the door. This week is going to ask what that grace cost, why the Father sent Him, and how the Spirit makes His company real in a room full of ordinary people. Paul had already learned that his own hard days were for their comfort (2 Corinthians 1:6), because that is the shape of the One he served. So keep one question open until Friday. If the blessing begins with Jesus, what does it tell you about God that He introduces Himself through a crucified Son? Application Before Sunday, read 2 Corinthians 13:14 out loud once. Go slowly, and put your own name in place of all of you. Then sit with whichever of the three names you needed most. If you are able, think of one person you expect to see this week who could use some of what you just received. Comfort is given so it can be passed along (2 Corinthians 1:4). Hold that person's name through the week. Opening Question for the Week Of grace, love, and fellowship, which one feels most like something you have already received and which feels most like something you are still waiting on (think of the last time you needed each)? What would it take for the missing one to feel like a gift rather than a requirement? Opening Prayer for the Week Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, You end Paul's hardest letter with a blessing, and we would like to begin our week under it. We come as the people that letter was written to, some of us loyal, some of us stubborn, all of us tired in places we do not talk about. Open these texts to us. Show us what grace cost, what love sent, and what fellowship with the Spirit feels like on an ordinary Tuesday. Where we have turned You into a rule, make Yourself a gift again. And be with all of us, the way Paul asked. In Jesus' name, Amen.
docs.2026-09-20.html: In brief A secretary dips his pen somewhere in Macedonia, and the first real word Paul gives him for Corinth is grace. Thirteen chapters later the last word is grace again. Today follows that word from the top of the letter to the bottom, through a trade that left the rich One poor, into a promise that receivers will reign, and out to the sign-offs where grace is the last thing a church hears. Grace is not Paul's way of being polite. It is the only word big enough to open and close a letter to people like us. Yesterday Yesterday a reader in Corinth reached the last line of Paul's hardest letter and found a blessing with three names in it instead of one more warning. Jesus was named first. Today we start where Paul started, with the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ. Why is it the first word and the last word of everything he wrote? Historical Context The Next Letter Was Written From a Corinthian Guest Room Picture the winter after this letter arrived. Paul made the visit he had promised. Luke records three months in Greece (Acts 20:2-3) without naming the city. Paul's own greetings fill in the gap. During that stay he dictated his longest surviving letter, Romans. He sends greetings from his host, Gaius, and from a city official named Erastus (Romans 16:23). He introduces the woman carrying the letter as Phoebe from Cenchreae (Romans 16:1-2), the harbor town on Corinth's eastern shore. Those clues are why most scholars place the writing of Romans in Corinth. If that is right, look at how Romans begins and ends. It opens with grace and peace to everyone in Rome (Romans 1:7). It closes with grace, right after a promise that Satan will be crushed (Romans 16:20). Both lines were likely written a short walk from the people who had given Paul the most trouble. He used the same greeting for Corinth itself (1 Corinthians 1:3), for the Galatians (Galatians 1:3), and for Philippi (Philippians 1:2). The grace he sent to Rome probably had a Corinthian return address. It was the same grace he had already spent on Corinth. Into the Word Every one of Paul's surviving letters starts the same way, and it is not the way letters started. A Greek letter opened with the writer's name, the reader's name, and a one-word hello. Paul keeps the names and swaps the hello for a blessing, then ends with the blessing he began with. A word a writer cannot get into or out of a letter without is a word he thinks you cannot live without. So what is this grace, and what did it cost to make it the first and last thing Paul had to say? 2 Corinthians 1:2 Open ↗ Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Notice what comes before the argument. Before Paul defends himself, before he names a single sin, before he asks for a single coin, he says grace and peace to a church that has doubted him, sued one another, tolerated a scandal, and been charmed by rival teachers. Grace is not the reward for the letter going well. It is the ground the letter stands on. When the letter is over, he says it again (2 Corinthians 13:14), the way he had ended the first letter too (1 Corinthians 16:23). Whatever else Corinth had earned in those years, it had not earned that word. That was the point of it. Paul had defined the word for Corinth a few chapters earlier, in the middle of asking for money, with a sentence about a trade. 2 Corinthians 8:9 Open ↗ For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though He was rich, yet for your sake He became poor, so that you through His poverty might become rich. Grace is not a mood God is in. It is something that happened, and Paul says the Corinthians already know it. There was a Person who was rich, and He became poor. Not by accident and not by defeat. For your sake. That phrase gives grace a direction. It moves from Him toward you, and it leaves Him with less and you with more. Paul spells out how low the trade went in another letter, obedient to death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:8). That is why grace can be the first word to a church like Corinth. It was never a comment on them. It was a report about Him. Grace given is one thing. What does it do to the people who receive it? Paul answered that in the letter he wrote next, from a Corinthian's guest room. Romans 5:17 Open ↗ For if, by the trespass of the one man, death reigned through that one man, how much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness reign in life through the one man, Jesus Christ! Paul sets two kings side by side. Through one man's trespass, death got a throne and ruled everyone born after him. The gift is not like the trespass (Romans 5:15), and the difference is who ends up on the throne. Those who receive the abundance of grace will reign in life. The Greek verb is basileuō, to rule as a king. The people who did nothing but receive are the ones who end up reigning. Grace does not make beggars with their hands out forever. It makes heirs, and it stands them up. Death reigned by one man's fall. Life reigns through one Man's gift, and He shares the throne with the people He paid for. Then watch how Paul says goodbye. The first of his four closings has a battle in it. Romans 16:20 Open ↗ The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. Two sentences sit side by side. The God of peace will crush Satan, an old promise from the garden coming due (Genesis 3:15), and He will do it under your feet. The crushing is God's. The feet are yours. Then, without a breath in between, grace be with you. God does the winning, the people He loves stand on the result, and grace holds them there in the meantime. Paul signed off the same way to the Galatians (Galatians 6:18), the Philippians (Philippians 4:23), and the Thessalonians (1 Thessalonians 5:28). Each church heard grace as the last thing before the scroll was rolled up. Ephesians 6:24 Open ↗ Grace to all who love our Lord Jesus Christ with an undying love. One more closing. Paul wishes it on everyone who loves the Lord Jesus with a love that does not wear out. Grace is not aimed at making people comfortable. It is aimed at making people love Him, and keep loving Him. That is why Paul could pray for grace to reach more and more people (2 Corinthians 4:15) without worrying it would run thin. He had heard the supply reported by Jesus Himself, over a thorn that never went away, my grace is sufficient for you (2 Corinthians 12:9). Grace was the first word Corinth heard from Paul and the word Paul heard from Jesus about his own pain. It was enough both times. Street Level The Receipt Said One Dollar Imagine a hardware store in a small town, forty years under one man's name. A chain is opening out by the highway, and a developer's offer on the building would fund the rest of his life. Instead he calls the woman who has run his register for six years into the back office and slides a folder across the desk. A bill of sale. Purchase price, one dollar. She laughs. She has done the math on that store the way you do the math on a house you will never afford. Six years at a register do not add up to it. Then she sees his signature already on the line. A dollar sale is not a joke, and it is not a loan. It is a sale, so the whole thing transfers. On Monday she unlocks the front door with the same key she has carried for six years, and the key is not what changed. She sets the hours now. When a customer asks for the owner, she is the owner. The man who signed is living on less than he could have, on purpose. He still reads her the books straight in the months she loses money. He does not come for the store. It was hers the day he signed it. That is the direction Paul built into the word grace. He was rich, and for your sake He became poor, so that you would end up rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). The loss runs toward the One who had everything. The standing runs toward people who put in nothing but their name. Grace does not keep you on at the register, hoping. It puts your name on the deed. Today’s World The Keys Came Before the Test Housing First runs on one reversed rule. The apartment comes first. Getting it does not depend on being sober, finishing treatment, or passing any other readiness test. Urban Institute researchers tested that order in Denver on 724 people. They had spent years cycling between the street, the emergency room, and the jail. Half were offered supportive housing with no readiness requirements. Half got the usual services. Of those who moved in, 86 percent were still stably housed a year later and 77 percent after three years, counting only those still living. The group offered housing also used shelters 40 percent less. The study did not find every life repaired. It found that housing given first held, even for people whose lives were not fixed yet. The keys stayed in their hands. That is the order Paul used with Corinth. Grace was the first word of the letter, before anything had been put right, and the last word too. Help that arrives before you earn it, and stays when you stumble, is not softer help. It is the kind that holds. Source Urban Institute Breaking the Homelessness-Jail Cycle with Housing First: Results from the Denver Supportive Housing Social Impact Bond Initiative. Urban Institute, 2021. Read the source. Christ at the center Be honest about the other half of the ledger for a moment. Take the things you have said and done this year, the ones you would least like read aloud, and ask what they deserve. Scripture's answer is not flattering. Sin earns death (Romans 6:23), and no amount of later kindness pays that bill down. Grace does not argue with the verdict. It moves the sentence onto Someone else. The rich One became poor, the sinless One took the cross, and He did it for your sake, on purpose, before you had done a single thing to make it reasonable. That is why grace is a Person before it is a doctrine. You cannot receive it from a distance any more than you can receive a rescue from a distance. Jesus is the grace of God with a face and hands and scars, and what He offers instead of what you deserve is Himself. Take it, and start living like someone who was paid for. Application Borrow Paul's habit for one day. Write the word grace at the top of the first thing you write this morning and at the bottom of the last thing you write tonight. In between, each time you catch yourself keeping score against someone, including yourself, say one sentence under your breath. He was rich, and for my sake He became poor. Notice by bedtime whether the score still feels worth keeping. Discussion Question What do the things you have said and done this year deserve, and what does it do to you that grace was Paul's first and last word to people exactly like that (think of the one thing you would least want read aloud)? Where this week does grace need to become the first word instead of the last resort? Closing Prayer Lord Jesus, You were rich and You became poor, and You did it for us, on purpose, before we had done anything to deserve it. Thank You. We confess that we still treat Your grace like a last resort, something we reach for after our own efforts run out. Make it our first word instead. Let it be the ground we stand on when we open our mouths, and the sound we leave behind when we close them. Teach us to receive without bargaining, and then stand us up. Where we are tired and the thorn has not gone away, say to us what You said to Paul, and let it be enough. In Jesus' name, Amen.
docs.2026-09-21.html: In brief An old apostle writes three words everyone has seen on a poster, God is love, and then refuses to let them stay a slogan. He tells you what the love did. It sent. Today follows that one verb from the Father's decision, through a night conversation Jesus had with a nervous teacher, to a cross that arrived before anyone had cleaned up, and out to a list of everything that cannot pry that love off you. God's love is not a feeling He has about you. It is a Son He sent for you. Yesterday Yesterday we followed grace from the first line of Paul's letter to the last and found a trade inside it, the rich One made poor for our sake. Grace had a direction, from Him to us. Today asks where that direction came from. Paul's blessing names it next, the love of God (2 Corinthians 13:14). Historical Context The Ancients Had Stories About Dying for a Friend A Corinthian who wanted to feel something about sacrifice went to the theater. Euripides had written a play about a queen named Alcestis who agreed to die in her husband's place when nobody else would, and audiences had been weeping over it for centuries. Romans told their children about the consul Decius Mus, who rode into the enemy line at the battle of Vesuvius and gave his life so that Rome would win. Stories like those were the kind the ancient world admired, and they tended to share a shape. Someone worthy died for someone worth it. A wife for a husband. A general for his city. A friend for a friend. Paul does not deny that such devotion existed. In the letter he wrote from Corinth he grants that someone might dare to die for a good man (Romans 5:7). Then he writes a sentence that runs against the grain of those stories, that Christ died for us while we were still sinners, still enemies (Romans 5:10). The admired sacrifices were aimed at a spouse, a city, a friend, someone judged worth it. Paul aims Christ's death at the people who were against Him. Perhaps the most quoted sentence in the Bible was spoken at night to one nervous religious teacher (John 3:16), and what it describes is a love story with an unexpected cast. The ones who deserved nothing got the Son. Into the Word John writes the three words everyone knows, God is love (1 John 4:8), and then, before anyone can turn them into a mood, he tells you exactly what he means. Love is something God did. The word he leans on, over and over, is sent. So today we follow that verb. Where did the sending start, what did it cost, when did it happen, and what does it mean for people who keep expecting love to be taken back? The question underneath all of it is simple. What changes when you learn that God's love has a verb? 1 John 4:8-11 Open ↗ 8Whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love. 9This is how God’s love was revealed among us: God sent His one and only Son into the world, so that we might live through Him. 10And love consists in this: not that we loved God, but that He loved us and sent His Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins. 11Beloved, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another. John starts with a hard line. Whoever does not love does not know God, because love is not a fact you can learn about God from a distance. You only know it from inside it. Then he tells you how anyone got inside. God's love was revealed among us in a Son sent into the world. Love consists in this, he says, and the direction is the whole point (1 John 4:10). Not that we reached up. He reached down, and the Son He sent dealt with the sins in the way. John had seen it with his own eyes (1 John 4:14). Only then does the ought arrive. We love one another because we were loved first. Love is not the feeling God has about you. It is the Son He sent for you. Where did John learn to talk like that? From a conversation Jesus had at night with a teacher who came with questions he could not ask in daylight. John 3:16-17 Open ↗ 16For God so loved the world that He gave His one and only Son, that everyone who believes in Him shall not perish but have eternal life. 17For God did not send His Son into the world to condemn the world, but to save the world through Him. The size of the love is measured by the size of the gift. So loved that He gave, and what He gave was His monogenēs Son, a Greek word meaning one of a kind, which older Bibles render only begotten. There was no spare. Then Jesus gives the purpose, not to condemn a world that had earned it, but to save it. Sending was how He described His own life. He kept calling the Father the One who sent Me (Matthew 10:40), and He taught that to welcome Him was to welcome the Sender (Mark 9:37). Peter later announced that heaven holds Him until the restoration of all things, and that the Father will send Him again (Acts 3:20-21). The rescue mission is not over. The Father who sent Him the first time has promised to send Him back. When did He send Him? Not after we cleaned up. Paul gives the timing in one sentence, and it is the sentence the old stories could never have told. Romans 5:8 Open ↗ But God proves His love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Proves is present tense. God keeps demonstrating His love, and the exhibit He points to is always the same one. Christ died for us, and the clock reads while we were still sinners. Not after a change of heart. Not once we had shown promise. Still. Yesterday grace had a direction. Today love has a timestamp, and the timestamp is what makes it love rather than reward. A love that waits for you to deserve it is only a fair trade, and Corinth already knew plenty about fair trades. This was something else. The admired stories stopped at friends and family. God's story started with enemies, and it started while they were still enemies. If that is when it started, when does it stop? Paul answers with a list, and the list is one of the most reassuring things he ever wrote. Romans 8:37-39 Open ↗ 37No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through Him who loved us. 38For I am convinced that neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities, neither the present nor the future, nor any powers, 39neither height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord. The list is an inventory of what people fear. Dying. Living, which can be harder. Spiritual powers. The present and the future. Paul is convinced none of it can separate us from the love of God, and the reason is in the last five words. The love is in Christ Jesus, anchored in a Person who has been through death and back, so nothing on the list can get behind it. That is why Paul could tell Corinth that love builds up (1 Corinthians 8:1), that gifts without it add up to nothing (1 Corinthians 13:1-3), and to do everything in love (1 Corinthians 16:14), and why John could say we ought to lay down our lives for each other (1 John 3:16). Fear of losing love keeps score. People who know they cannot be separated from it are free to stop counting. Street Level Every Line Was in Her Handwriting Picture the visitors' entrance of a state prison on a Saturday morning, and a woman in her sixties at the front desk, signing the visitor sheet. Then she sits in a plastic chair until an officer comes out and tells her what he told her last Saturday. He refused. Her son is inside on a sentence he earned, and he will not come out to the glass. Not for her. He has not come out in eleven months. She drives home. Next Saturday she signs the sheet again. Nobody would call it dramatic. Her name is on every sheet in the drawer, week after week, with the column for his answer empty. She is not pretending he did nothing. She knows the charge and the length of the sentence better than he does. She is not waiting for him to change, either. She comes while he is still refusing, and the sheets prove it, one line at a time. John's definition of love is that God loved us first and sent His Son. Paul's proof of it is a date, Christ dying for us while we were still sinners. Every line is in His handwriting. The Son was sent before anyone came out to the glass, and no refusal from inside can erase a Saturday already spent in that chair. The one the love is aimed at can go on saying no. The sheets in the drawer will not change. Or, some Saturday, he can come out and find that she never stopped signing. Today’s World A Recruiter for the Child Still Waiting Wendy's Wonderful Kids assigns an adoption recruiter to children who have waited a long time for a family, often older children. The recruiter takes on each child's search as a particular search, meeting the child and looking for a family among the adults who already know that child. A former teacher. A coach. A relative nobody had called. The child did not have to ask for any of it. A randomized study of 956 children, published in 2015, found that children with a recruiter were 1.7 times as likely to be adopted, with larger gains for older children. A recruiter cannot make a young person say yes, and not every child found a family. But the search began before any child asked. That is the order John gives for God's love. He loved us and sent, before anyone went looking for Him. Source Journal of Public Child Welfare Experimental Evaluation of a Child-Focused Adoption Recruitment Program for Children and Youth in Foster Care. Journal of Public Child Welfare, 2015. Read the source. Christ at the center Everything today hangs on one question. Who exactly did God send? If the Son were anything less than God Himself, then John's sentence falls apart, because the love of God would turn out to be God delegating. He would have loved us by making someone else pay. The Word who was with God in the beginning was God (John 1:1), and that is what makes the sending love rather than management. The Father's gift was not the sacrifice of a lesser being. He gave His one-of-a-kind Son, who is fully God and who gave Himself willingly. The One who came did not come to condemn (John 3:17), and He arrived while we were still against Him, which means the love of God is not an idea you have to climb toward. It walked into Galilee, then up a hill outside Jerusalem, and it has not gone anywhere since. Nothing in all creation can separate you from it, because it has a name, and the name is Jesus. Application Give love a verb today. Think of one person who has done nothing lately to earn your kindness, then choose one small thing you can do for them before the day ends that does not depend on how they respond. Make the meal, send the note, pray for them by name for five whole minutes. Do it first. Do it while they are still whoever they are. That is the order God used with you. Discussion Question When you say God loves you, are you picturing a feeling He has or a thing He did (think of the last time you doubted it, and what would have settled the doubt)? Which item on Paul's list of things that cannot separate you from His love do you secretly believe could? Closing Prayer Father, You did not wait for us. You sent Your Son while we were still turned away, and we thank You for a love that came first and came at Your own cost. Forgive us for treating it like a mood You might be in today and out of tomorrow. Settle it in us the way You settled it in Paul, so that nothing on his list, and nothing on ours, can talk us out of it. Then send us. Give us one person to love before they deserve it, and the nerve to do it without keeping score. In Jesus' name, Amen.
docs.2026-09-22.html: In brief Walk through Corinth and the gods you pass have titles. The god of the sea. The goddess of desire. The emperor's goddess of peace, carved in marble back in Rome. Then a tentmaker ends a hard letter with a title found nowhere else in Scripture, the God of love and peace. Today collects the names Paul gave God and finds one thing under all of them. God's titles are not departments He runs. They are the character He gives away. Yesterday Yesterday the love of God turned out to have a verb. God sent His Son while we were still enemies, and nothing on Paul's list can pry that love loose. Today Paul turns the noun into a name. He calls God the God of love, and it is the only place Scripture uses that exact title. Historical Context The Gods Had Titles for Everything They Ran Every other spring the road east out of Corinth filled with athletes and gamblers. They were headed for Isthmia, where the games were held under the eye of Poseidon, god of the sea and of the earthquake. Up on the rock above town stood the shrine of Aphrodite, goddess of desire. Zeus had a title for one job after another. Protector of guests. Keeper of oaths. Sender of rain. A god's title told you his territory, and his territory told you what he could do for you or to you. Devotion to gods like these was often a matter of keeping them favorable. Rome added one more to the collection. Pax, the goddess of peace, got an altar from Augustus in the capital, built to celebrate the quiet that follows a Roman victory. So when a letter read aloud in a Corinthian house called the Lord the God of love and peace, the phrase would have sounded strange. Love as a god's title pointed to Aphrodite and the desire she governed. Peace as a title pointed to Rome and the calm that follows a conquest. Paul takes both words and hangs them on the one God as a description of who He is rather than what He controls. Then he attaches a promise. This God will be with you. Of everything in that sentence, the promise may have been the strangest part. Into the Word Paul has a habit worth noticing. When he wants to bless people, he names God by what God is about to give them. The God of endurance. The God of hope. The God of all comfort. Today we collect those titles, and the collection starts with the rarest one. The phrase the God of love appears only once in the whole Bible, in the closing lines of this letter, spoken to a church Paul had just spent four chapters warning. Why there? And what does it mean that every one of God's titles turns out to be something He hands over? 2 Corinthians 13:11 Open ↗ Finally, brothers, rejoice! Aim for perfect harmony, encourage one another, be of one mind, live in peace. And the God of love and peace will be with you. Five commands and then a promise, and the promise is where the weight sits. Rejoice, be put back together, encourage one another, agree, live in peace, and the God of love and peace will be with you. Paul is not selling God's presence as a wage for good behavior. He is describing the room God's presence fills. A church at war can be visited by the God of peace and never notice Him, the way a shouting match never notices the quiet man in the doorway. Put the fight down and His company becomes plain. And notice which title Paul reaches for at the end of his hardest letter. Not the God of judgment, though He is that. The God of love. The one place in Scripture that phrase appears is the close of Paul's surviving correspondence with Corinth. That title was not a one-off. Paul had been naming God this way for years, and when you set the names side by side a portrait comes into focus. Romans 15:13 Open ↗ Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace as you believe in Him, so that you may overflow with hope by the power of the Holy Spirit. A few lines earlier Paul had called Him the God who gives endurance and encouragement (Romans 15:5), and here He is the God of hope. Watch the mechanism. God is not hopeful the way a person is hopeful, crossing His fingers about the future. He is hope's source, and the prayer is that He would fill people with joy and peace so that hope overflows out of them by the power of the Holy Spirit. That is how every title on Paul's list works. God gives what God is. Endurance from the God of endurance, comfort from the God of comfort, and at the close of the same chapter, peace from the God of peace (Romans 15:33). None of it is manufactured on our side. It is poured, and it runs over. Of all the titles, the God of peace is the one Paul used most, and the word he chose for peace is bigger than the absence of a fight. 1 Thessalonians 5:23 Open ↗ Now may the God of peace Himself sanctify you completely, and may your entire spirit, soul, and body be kept blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. The Greek word is eirēnē, and for a Jew like Paul it carried the weight of the Hebrew shalom, not just quiet but wholeness, everything in its right place and nothing missing. That is why the God of peace can sanctify you completely, spirit and soul and body, without changing the subject. Peace is what a whole person looks like. It is why He is a God of order and not confusion when His people gather (1 Corinthians 14:33), why He walks beside people who practice what they have learned (Philippians 4:9), and why the same God of peace can crush Satan under your feet (Romans 16:20). Peace that mends a whole person has to deal with what broke him. So His peace is not passive. It puts things back. 2 Corinthians 1:3 Open ↗ Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of compassion and the God of all comfort, Here is the title Paul opened this letter with, and it belongs next to the one he closed it with. Father of compassion, God of all comfort. Compassion in the plural, mercies, one for every kind of trouble. Comfort with the word all in front of it, so no situation lands outside His supply. Between this opening and the closing blessing (2 Corinthians 13:14) sit thirteen chapters of conflict, and the two titles hold them like bookends. That tells you something about the God of love. He is not a nicer god than the God of comfort, or a softer god than the God of peace. He is the same God, seen from inside a hard year. Whatever the year took, the title still held. Street Level The Calm Was Already on the Line Imagine a kitchen at seven in the evening. A man's wife has collapsed between the table and the stove, and he is on the phone with an emergency dispatcher, shouting. He shouts the address, shouts that she is not breathing right, shouts at her to hurry. On the other end is a woman he will never meet. Help is already on its way. The address went out the moment she had it, and the ambulance is rolling while he is still shouting into the phone. So she stays on the line and lowers her voice. She tells him she is right here and she is not going anywhere. She tells him to put the phone on the floor beside his wife and put his hands where she says. Then something happens. He stops shouting. Not because she asked for quiet. Because the calm on the line is the only steady thing in that kitchen and he needs it. He counts with her. He presses when she says press. For four minutes the calm in that woman is the calm in his hands, and he did not earn a second of it. If he writes to thank her later, he will not know her name. He will call her what she gave him. The calm one. Paul names God the same way, by what He is and what He hands over. From the God of hope, hope. From the God of peace, a whole person. So when he writes live in peace, and the God of love and peace will be with you, he is not putting a price on the visit. The help was on the line before the shouting stopped. Stopping is how you hear it. Today’s World The Salmon Were Back in Three Weeks Four dams once blocked salmon from parts of the Klamath River in Oregon and California. Fish coming up from the ocean stopped below the lowest one. The river's tribes led a decades-long campaign to take them out, through hearings, lawsuits, and negotiation. In 2024 the dams came down. It was the largest river restoration project in American history, and it reopened nearly 400 miles of habitat. On September 26, 2024, the last barrier in California came out. On October 15, less than three weeks later, state biologists found fall-run Chinook spawning in Jenny Creek, four miles above the old dam site. The first salmon in those tributaries since 1961. Nobody carried them there. A year on, a conservation group counted more than 10,000 fish over two feet long passing the old dam site, most likely Chinook. The group says it will take years of monitoring to know how the river recovers. Paul's word for peace means more than a truce. It means things put back where they belong. A settlement that only stopped the lawsuits would have left the concrete in the river. The peace that mends takes the barrier out, and what was missing comes home. Sources California Department of Fish and Wildlife, Office of Governor Gavin Newsom, California Trout Klamath River Chinook Salmon Reoccupying Historic Habitat, Spawning Above Former Dam Locations. California Department of Fish and Wildlife, 2024. Read the source. Klamath River dams fully removed ahead of schedule. Office of Governor Gavin Newsom, 2024. Read the source. One Year After Klamath Dam Removal, Salmon Surge into Newly Opened Habitat: CalTrout and Partners Track Recovery Through Comprehensive Monitoring. California Trout, 2025. Read the source. Christ at the center How would anyone know that the God behind the universe is a God of love and peace rather than a god to be managed? Corinth's temples suggested otherwise, and so does plenty of human experience. The title was not announced. It was shown. God made peace through the blood of Jesus' cross (Colossians 1:20), which means the God of peace paid for the peace Himself instead of billing the people who broke it. And the love in the title is the love Monday traced, the Son sent while we were still enemies. Jesus is where the God of love and the God of peace turn out to be the same God with one saving purpose. When He said He was leaving His peace with the disciples, not the way the world gives (John 14:27), He meant the shalom that mends a whole person, and He was hours from paying for it. The God of love and peace will be with you. He already came. Application Pray today using one of Paul's titles for God, and choose the one that matches what you are short on. God of hope, God of all comfort, God of peace, God of love. Say it out loud, then tell Him in one sentence why you picked it. Then take one step toward peace that needs nobody's permission, such as writing the apology you owe or dropping the argument you were rehearsing, whether or not anyone else moves. Discussion Question When something goes wrong, which god sits under your reaction, one who must be appeased or the God of love and peace (think of what you assumed the last time a prayer went unanswered)? Where are you being asked to live in peace right now, and what would change if you believed He is the source and not the referee? Closing Prayer God of love and peace, we have managed You more often than we have loved You, bargaining like people who thought You had to be kept happy. Forgive us, and show us Your face in Jesus until the bargaining stops. Fill us with the peace that mends the whole person, spirit and soul and body, and put back what this year has knocked loose. Where we are at war with someone, give us the first move, and where a church we love is arguing, help it lay the fight down long enough to notice You standing in the doorway. Be with all of us, the way Paul asked. In Jesus' name, Amen.
docs.2026-09-23.html: In brief In a Corinthian lecture hall a philosopher explains that spirit is a fiery breath running through everything. Across town a letter says the Spirit searches the mind of God, teaches, reminds, testifies, decides who gets what, and cries Father from inside a person's chest. One of those is a force. The other is Someone. Today follows the verbs Paul and Jesus give the Holy Spirit and asks what fellowship with Him means. The Spirit is not a power you use. He is a Person you keep company with, and that company is where every other fellowship begins. Yesterday Yesterday Paul gave God a title found nowhere else in Scripture, the God of love and peace, and every title on his list turned out to be something God hands over. The last name in the blessing is still waiting. Today we ask who the Holy Spirit is, and what it means to have fellowship with Him. Historical Context The Philosophers Said Spirit Was a Kind of Fire If you had asked an educated Corinthian what spirit was, he would not have looked puzzled. He would likely have given you the Stoic answer, since Stoicism was one of the most influential philosophies of Paul's day. Spirit was a fine, fiery breath, a blend of air and fire that ran through every stone, tree, and body in the universe. It held things together the way tension holds a bowstring, and it was as physical as the string. The Stoics could call that breath divine, even reason itself, and they urged people to live in step with it. But it was a principle woven into the world, not a Person you could meet. You could reason about it. Nobody expected it to know your name. Paul used that same everyday word, the one that also meant breath and wind, and then gave it verbs no Stoic would have used. This Spirit searches. He teaches. He reminds. He testifies. He decides. He can be grieved (Ephesians 4:30), and He calls God Father from inside a person. It is easy to keep the philosophers' version, a divine energy you tap into, which is why it matters that the letters give the Spirit verbs only a someone can do. Nobody has fellowship with a bowstring. You can only keep company with a Someone, and Paul closes his letter by asking that this Someone be with all of them. Into the Word Paul stacks up four ifs in a letter to the Philippians, and he does not doubt one of them. Any encouragement in Christ, any comfort from His love, any fellowship with the Spirit (Philippians 2:1), any affection and compassion. Look at the company that third item keeps. Every other item in the list is something that happens between persons. So the question today is simple to ask. Is the Holy Spirit a something or a Someone, and what changes if you can keep company with Him? Philippians 2:1-2 Open ↗ 1Therefore if you have any encouragement in Christ, if any comfort from His love, if any fellowship with the Spirit, if any affection and compassion, 2then make my joy complete by being like-minded, having the same love, being united in spirit and purpose. Paul writes about the Father and the Son as two Persons in a relationship all through these letters, the God and Father of our Lord Jesus (2 Corinthians 1:3), the God and Father of the Lord Jesus who knows Paul is not lying (2 Corinthians 11:31). Here he lists the Spirit as the third party in that relationship, which is an odd place to put an impersonal energy. Then comes the result. Fellowship with the Spirit is meant to produce a like-minded church, one love and one purpose. The order matters. We do not build fellowship and then invite God into it. It is what fellowship with Him produces when it spills over. Paul learned to talk about the Spirit this way from Jesus, who described Him to the disciples on the night before He died. John 14:16-17 Open ↗ 16And I will ask the Father, and He will give you another Advocate to be with you forever— 17the Spirit of truth. The world cannot receive Him, because it neither sees Him nor knows Him. But you do know Him, for He abides with you and will be in you. Jesus is about to leave, and He does not promise a feeling or a power. He promises another Advocate, someone called to your side, a helper who shows up in person. Another means Jesus had been the first one. The world cannot receive this Advocate because it neither sees nor knows Him, but the disciples do know Him, the way you know someone rather than something. Jesus adds that this Advocate will teach and remind (John 14:26) and will testify about Jesus Himself (John 15:26). Teachers, reminders, witnesses. Every one of those is a job that requires a mind and a voice. Romans 8:15-16 Open ↗ 15For you did not receive a spirit of slavery that returns you to fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption to sonship, by whom we cry, “Abba! Father!” 16The Spirit Himself testifies with our spirit that we are God’s children. In this passage the Spirit's work shows up in what people call God. They received the Spirit of huiothesia, the Greek word for adoption, a legal act in Roman life that made someone a full son with an heir's standing. It was how Julius Caesar made Augustus his heir. By this Spirit we cry Abba, the family word for Father, and then the Spirit Himself testifies with our spirit that we are God's children. A witness takes the stand and speaks. A force testifies to nothing. This same Spirit lives in the church as God's temple (1 Corinthians 3:16) and in each believer's body (1 Corinthians 6:19), set in our hearts as God's seal and pledge (2 Corinthians 1:22). Fellowship with Him begins with being told who you are. 1 Corinthians 2:10-11 Open ↗ 10But God has revealed it to us by the Spirit. The Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God. 11For who among men knows the thoughts of man except his own spirit within him? So too, no one knows the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God. Company with a Person also means being told things you could not find out alone. The Spirit searches even the deep things of God, and Paul explains why that matters with a comparison. Only your own spirit knows your thoughts, and only the Spirit of God knows His. So the One who lives in you is the One who knows the mind of God from the inside, and He speaks it in words He teaches (1 Corinthians 2:13). That is why Paul refused to build Corinth's faith on clever preaching and rested it on a demonstration of the Spirit's power instead (1 Corinthians 2:4-5). A force does not know anything. The Spirit knows the mind of God, and He tells. 1 Corinthians 12:11 Open ↗ All these are the work of one and the same Spirit, who apportions them to each one as He determines. One more verb, and it may be the most personal of all. He apportions the gifts to each one as He determines. He decides. Across three chapters (1 Corinthians 12-14) Paul describes a church humming with gifts, and behind every one stands a will choosing who gets what, all of it for building up the church (1 Corinthians 14:12). The same Spirit gives life where the written code could only condemn (2 Corinthians 3:6), and where He is present there is freedom (2 Corinthians 3:17). Put the verbs together. Searches, knows, teaches, reminds, testifies, dwells, seals, decides, frees. That is not a list of things a force does. It is a portrait of Someone at work. Street Level The Monitor Never Said Her Name Picture a hospital room in the middle of the night. A woman is hours into labor and losing the thread. A monitor beside the bed records the baby's heartbeat and each contraction and draws them across a screen as two lines. The information is real. The nurses and the doctor read those lines, and what they read shapes what they decide. The screen itself decides nothing and knows nothing. It has never once said her name. There is also a doula in the chair by the bed, hired to stay. When the next contraction comes she does not look at the screen. She looks at the mother's face and says, low, you are doing this, one at a time. She suggests trying a new position and helps her turn. She hands the husband, frozen by the window, a cup and tells him to count out loud, and suddenly the room has one purpose instead of two frightened people and a machine. Nobody hired her for strength. They hired her for company. Paul lists fellowship with the Spirit beside encouragement in Christ and comfort from His love. The Spirit searches, teaches, reminds, and testifies that we are God's children. His power is real. But you were not handed a screen to read. You were given Someone who knows the mind of God and knows your name, and the one purpose Paul wanted for the church is what His company does to a room. Today’s World Fifteen Years With the Same Doctor Norway gives its residents a named family doctor, which let researchers ask whether it matters to keep the same doctor for years. In a 2022 study, Hogne Sandvik and colleagues followed 4.5 million people through 2018, sorted by how long each had kept the same doctor. Compared with people in their first year with a doctor, those past fifteen years with the same one had 28 percent lower odds of an emergency hospital admission and 25 percent lower odds of dying that year. The longer the relationship, the lower the numbers. The same national system served everyone. What differed was how long each person had stayed with the same doctor. The study is observational, so it shows an association, not proof of cause, and it does not show that the doctor's personal knowledge made the difference. Still, the pattern suggests that ongoing care from the same person may matter in ways that access to a system alone does not capture. That is the difference Paul had in view when he set fellowship with the Spirit beside encouragement and comfort. Source British Journal of General Practice Continuity in general practice as predictor of mortality, acute hospitalisation, and use of out-of-hours care: a registry-based observational study in Norway. British Journal of General Practice, 2022. Read the source. Christ at the center Every verb the Spirit has points at one Person. He testifies about Jesus. He reminds the disciples of what Jesus said. He cries Father with the word Jesus taught. So the fellowship of the Spirit is not a separate department from the grace of Jesus. It is Jesus keeping His promise not to leave them as orphans (John 14:18). When Paul reminds Corinth what happened to them, he puts the two names together, washed, sanctified, justified, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God (1 Corinthians 6:11). The church itself is a letter from Christ written with the Spirit of the living God on human hearts (2 Corinthians 3:3). The Author and the ink are not rivals. The One who was rich and became poor for you now lives in you by His Spirit, closer than He was to the disciples who could touch Him. Application Speak to the Holy Spirit today as a Someone, once, on purpose. Not a request for power. A sentence of company, the kind you would say to a friend who walked into the room, then two minutes of quiet with your phone face down. Before the day ends, notice one place where you and another believer are not like-minded, and pray for that person by name instead of rehearsing your side. Discussion Question Have you been treating the Holy Spirit as a Someone or a something (think about the last time you mentioned Him at all, and what you wanted)? If fellowship among believers is what fellowship with Him produces, which strained relationship in your church or family might change if you started with Him instead of with them? Closing Prayer Holy Spirit, we confess we have talked about You more than we have talked to You, and we have reached for You like a power source when You came to us as a Person. Forgive us. Testify to our spirits again today that we are God's children, and teach us the things about Him we could never have found alone. Search us, since You already know us. Then do what Paul prayed for. Let our fellowship with You spill over into one love and one purpose with the people around us, especially the ones we have been avoiding. Stay with us, the way Jesus promised You would. In Jesus' name, Amen.
